title: Five Health Facilities Shut Down in Mwenye After ADF Attacks
excerpt: Lubero, North Kivu – January 26, 2026 — Five health centers and several health posts have closed in the Mwenye area following renewed insecurity marked by the killing of civilians attributed to suspected Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) rebels. Facilities in Mausa, Pombi, Mandelya,
title_en: Five Health Facilities Shut Down in Mwenye After ADF Attacks
excerpt_en: Lubero, North Kivu – January 26, 2026 — Five health centers and several health posts have closed in the Mwenye area following renewed insecurity marked by the killing of civilians attributed to suspected Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) rebels. Facilities in Mausa, Pombi, Mandelya,
body_en:
Lubero, North Kivu – January 26, 2026 — Five health centers and several health posts have closed in the Mwenye area following renewed insecurity marked by the killing of civilians attributed to suspected Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) rebels.
Facilities in Mausa, Pombi, Mandelya, Musenge, and the Masoy referral health center have ceased operations. The Masoy center, located in the main town of Mwenye, has reportedly been closed for about a week.
This development has worsened the humanitarian crisis in an area already heavily affected by persistent violence.
Civil society leaders have condemned the silence of the authorities, saying the insecurity has paralyzed socio-economic activities across the Mwenye group in the Baswagha chiefdom, deepening a sense of abandonment among residents.
“Given the situation we are experiencing, nurses have been a great help to the population. Even members of armed groups and their families were receiving care free of charge. But the pressure on the Biambwe health center forced our nurses to close the facility,” said Kambale Muthano Jérémie Mutumwa, president of the New Congolese Civil Society. “This complicates life for the entire population, because all facilities in Mandelya, Pombi, Mausa, Masoya, and Musenge have now closed. We are not against healthcare workers. We only ask the government to ensure the safety of the population, including health facilities, so that professionals can work in decent conditions.”
Faced with this situation, healthcare workers are urgently calling on military authorities to intervene and fully implement Operation Shujaa, a joint operation between the FARDC (Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo) and the UPDF (Ugandan People’s Defence Force).
Since 2024, the Mwenye area has remained in a state of chronic instability, marked by massacres of civilians, mass displacement, the closure of schools, and now the shutdown of health facilities.
The latest violence occurred on the night of Tuesday, January 21, when suspected ADF fighters killed five civilians and burned about ten houses in the village of Mavwe-Mavwe, in the Mandelya district. Four women were among the victims.

Kinshasa, January 26, 2026 — The government of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has strongly contested a recent report by Human Rights Watch on the security situation in Uvira, South Kivu, following the withdrawal of the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebellion. The government warned that separating current risks from the actions and strategies of the occupying forces is both legally inaccurate and politically dangerous.
In a statement released on Thursday, January 22, the Ministry of Communication emphasized that the Human Rights Watch report, titled “DR Congo: Civilians in South Kivu at Serious Risk”, primarily focuses on post-withdrawal risks without adequately situating them within the broader context of an illegal armed occupation characterized by systematic abuses against civilians and a deliberate strategy to destabilize the city.
“The withdrawal of the AFC/M23 from Uvira, which occurred on January 17, 2026, followed a period marked by looting, large-scale theft, threats, intimidation, and community stigmatization, all of which severely affected civilian security and social cohesion. This withdrawal was accompanied by premeditated disorder, deliberately orchestrated to prolong insecurity and create residual effects after the occupying forces departed,” the statement read.
According to the government, the primary responsibility for endangering civilians lies with the rebels, due to the illegal occupation, the manipulation of fear among residents, forced transfers and displacement of members of the Banyamulenge community, and the deliberate chaos left behind.
The government stressed that downplaying or reversing this responsibility is inconsistent with established facts and warned against any equivalence between the aggressed state and the occupying forces. “It is legally inaccurate and politically dangerous to dissociate the current risks in Uvira from the acts and strategies implemented by the occupying forces before and during their withdrawal. The DRC reaffirms its commitment to international human rights mechanisms, which must respect the full factual truth, the hierarchy of responsibilities, and the principle of non-equivalence,” the statement said.
The government also reiterated its willingness to cooperate with international mechanisms, provided their analyses and recommendations adhere to rigorous interpretations of international law and do not dilute responsibilities or reverse facts.
Since the rebel withdrawal, the redeployment of FARDC troops, the Congolese National Police, and other security services has facilitated the gradual restoration of state authority, the protection of civilians and their property, and the containment of risks, contributing to the preservation of public order.
Uvira, a strategic city in South Kivu, had previously fallen under the control of AFC/M23, strengthening the rebels’ influence in North and South Kivu. The city is seen as a key stronghold, potentially facilitating a rebel advance toward the Greater Katanga region, the economic heartland of the DRC.

title: Vodacom Network Disrupted in Goma Following Technical Center Intrusion
excerpt: Goma, North Kivu – January 26, 2026 — Vodacom Congo (DRC) reported a disruption of its services in Goma after an intrusion at its technical center, resulting in a temporary loss of network monitoring and control. The incident affected voice calls, SMS, internet access, and M-Pesa
title_en: Vodacom Network Disrupted in Goma Following Technical Center Intrusion
excerpt_en: Goma, North Kivu – January 26, 2026 — Vodacom Congo (DRC) reported a disruption of its services in Goma after an intrusion at its technical center, resulting in a temporary loss of network monitoring and control. The incident affected voice calls, SMS, internet access, and M-Pesa
body_en:
Goma, North Kivu – January 26, 2026 — Vodacom Congo (DRC) reported a disruption of its services in Goma after an intrusion at its technical center, resulting in a temporary loss of network monitoring and control.
The incident affected voice calls, SMS, internet access, and M-Pesa mobile money services. The company apologized for the inconvenience, describing the situation as “beyond its control”, and stated that its teams worked to restore service. By the afternoon, connectivity had returned after several hours of outage.
Goma has been under the control of the AFC/M23, a Rwandan-backed rebel group, for the past year. While no direct link has been established between the intrusion and the security situation, telecommunications infrastructure is known to play a significant role in the ongoing conflict in eastern DRC, according to previous UN Group of Experts reports.
Vodacom remains the market leader in mobile telephony in the DRC, with 25.8 million active subscribers as of September 2025, representing a 35.2% market share. Over the same period, the company generated $198.1 million in revenue, or 31.9% of total market revenue, second only to Airtel. Vodacom also leads in mobile internet subscribers (12.78 million) and mobile money accounts (15.3 million active accounts).

title: Looting of Health Facilities Leaves Over 44,600 People Without Access to Care
excerpt: Uvira, South Kivu – January 27, 2026 — The ongoing conflict in Uvira has significantly worsened the humanitarian situation, with the looting of health facilities affecting more than 44,600 people, including 19,287 internally displaced persons and 25,313 returnees, severely limiti
title_en: Looting of Health Facilities Leaves Over 44,600 People Without Access to Care
excerpt_en: Uvira, South Kivu – January 27, 2026 — The ongoing conflict in Uvira has significantly worsened the humanitarian situation, with the looting of health facilities affecting more than 44,600 people, including 19,287 internally displaced persons and 25,313 returnees, severely limiti
body_en:
Uvira, South Kivu – January 27, 2026 — The ongoing conflict in Uvira has significantly worsened the humanitarian situation, with the looting of health facilities affecting more than 44,600 people, including 19,287 internally displaced persons and 25,313 returnees, severely limiting their access to essential healthcare.
A security and humanitarian overview for South Kivu province covering December 2025 reveals that the intensification of armed clashes in Uvira has caused widespread displacement, disrupted livelihoods, and halted critical humanitarian operations. Thousands of people have fled within the city and territory, while others have crossed into Burundi seeking refuge.
Assessments in the Ruzizi Health Zone indicate tens of thousands living in precarious conditions across multiple health areas, including Kiliba, Runigu, Kabunambo, Sange État, Sange CEPAC, Nazareni, Rusabagi, Ndunda, Kigurwe, and Kimuka. Many displaced families are sheltered in collective centers, such as schools and churches, while more than eight health facilities have been looted, drastically reducing or entirely halting operations.
The Kalehe territory also experienced massive displacements and disruption of socio-economic activities. Fighting along the Katasomwa–Ramba and Bushaku–Chambombo axes displaced nearly 2,900 households, now housed in Lemera, Luzira, Kasheke, Kalehe Centre, Bushushu, Nyamukubi, and Tchofi. These populations face severe vulnerabilities, including food insecurity, lack of shelter, limited access to healthcare, clean water, and sanitation.
In the Walungu territory, armed clashes led to population displacements, the suspension of socio-economic activities, and the destruction of numerous schools, churches, and health facilities in health zones such as Kaziba, Nyangezi, and Mubumbano. Assessments in Kamanyola and Kashenyi health zones indicate thousands of returnees and displaced persons facing acute food insecurity, malnutrition, and limited access to safe water and healthcare.
Since early 2025, the escalation of the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebellion in North and South Kivu has displaced hundreds of thousands, resulting in hundreds of deaths, thousands of injuries, and blocked access for humanitarian aid. Despite these challenges, humanitarian actors continue to provide emergency medical care, food aid, and essential services, negotiating access to affected areas wherever possible.
Humanitarian experts emphasize the urgent need for safe and unimpeded access to vulnerable populations. Meanwhile, progress in regional mediation initiatives, including the US-led Washington process and Qatar-facilitated talks, has yet to produce tangible improvements on the ground. Many voices are now calling on all stakeholders to honor commitments, silence the guns, and provide a chance for lasting peace after nearly three decades of conflict.

title: Kinshasa Urges UN to Fully Enforce Resolution 2773 Amid Persistent Rebel Occupations
excerpt: Kinshasa, January 27, 2026 — Nearly a year after the adoption of United Nations Security Council Resolution 2773, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is calling on the UN to fully assume its responsibilities in addressing the deteriorating security situation in the eastern pro
title_en: Kinshasa Urges UN to Fully Enforce Resolution 2773 Amid Persistent Rebel Occupations
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, January 27, 2026 — Nearly a year after the adoption of United Nations Security Council Resolution 2773, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is calling on the UN to fully assume its responsibilities in addressing the deteriorating security situation in the eastern pro
body_en:
Kinshasa, January 27, 2026 — Nearly a year after the adoption of United Nations Security Council Resolution 2773, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is calling on the UN to fully assume its responsibilities in addressing the deteriorating security situation in the eastern provinces of the country.
The resolution, unanimously adopted in February 2025, condemned Rwanda for supporting the AFC/M23 rebellion and demanded the immediate withdrawal of its troops from Congolese territory. It also called on the AFC/M23 to cease hostilities in the DRC. Despite these mandates, the implementation of Resolution 2773 remains largely ineffective, and the eastern DRC continues to face intense insecurity, nearly a year after the occupation of Goma by the rebel movement.
During the 10096th session of the UN Security Council on Monday, January 26, 2026, Ambassador Jocelyne Kabengele Lukundula, Deputy Permanent Representative of the DRC to the UN, urged the Council to rigorously implement all resolutions and prioritize the promotion and strengthening of the rule of law. She stressed that this requires:
Full enforcement of adopted resolutions,
Increased support for fragile states,
Ensuring humanitarian operators have unimpeded access to provide assistance to civilians, and
Better coordination among UN bodies to strengthen collective peace efforts.
“Regional organizations, particularly African ones, play a critical role in peaceful dispute resolution and in reinforcing states’ legal and institutional capacities,” Ambassador Kabengele Lukundula said. “The DRC remains committed to multilateralism, law, and justice as guarantees of lasting and inclusive peace.”
On the ground, the security situation in North and South Kivu has worsened since the resolution’s adoption. The AFC/M23 rebellion, supported by Rwanda, continued its territorial expansion, establishing its own parallel administration beyond Kinshasa’s control. While the movement temporarily withdrew from Uvira under US pressure, it retains control over other eastern areas, maintaining security and public services under its authority.
Diplomatic processes, including the Washington process between Kinshasa and Kigali and the Doha talks with the AFC/M23, have produced limited progress. Parties continue to accuse each other of failing to honor commitments, fueling ongoing tensions.
Despite prior denials, Rwanda has now acknowledged security cooperation with the AFC/M23, further complicating efforts to stabilize the region. Humanitarian and security conditions remain critical, with civilian populations facing displacement, attacks, and limited access to essential services, highlighting the urgent need for UN action and the effective enforcement of Resolution 2773.
The DRC continues to call on the UN Security Council to act decisively, ensuring that the resolution translates into tangible security improvements for populations affected by decades of conflict in the eastern DRC.

title: Great Lakes Crisis Returns to EU Foreign Ministers’ Agenda

title_en: Great Lakes Crisis Returns to EU Foreign Ministers’ Agenda
excerpt_en: Brussels, January 27, 2026 — The ongoing crisis in the Great Lakes region is back at the center of attention for the European Union (EU), as a meeting of EU foreign ministers is scheduled for Thursday, January 29, 2026, in Brussels with the security and humanitarian situation in
body_en:
Brussels, January 27, 2026 — The ongoing crisis in the Great Lakes region is back at the center of attention for the European Union (EU), as a meeting of EU foreign ministers is scheduled for Thursday, January 29, 2026, in Brussels with the security and humanitarian situation in the region as the main agenda item.
The announcement comes amid the first anniversary of Goma’s occupation by the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebellion and follows recent interventions by the United States and Qatar to mediate the crisis between Kinshasa and Kigali and between the Congolese government and the AFC/M23.
The EU Special Representative for the Great Lakes Region, Johan Borgstam, met with Prime Minister Judith Suminwa in Kinshasa on Monday, January 26, 2026, to discuss priorities ahead of the Brussels meeting. Borgstam emphasized the EU’s commitment to the DRC and stressed the importance of understanding the humanitarian and security needs on the ground.
“This visit allows the Prime Minister to convey relevant messages to the European ministers on January 29. It’s about demonstrating the EU as a supportive, reliable, and predictable partner for the DRC,” Borgstam said.
The EU is currently the largest humanitarian partner in the Great Lakes region, financing programs for agencies such as UNHCR and WFP, and supporting refugee camps, including the Busuma camp in Burundi, which hosts 68,000 Congolese refugees. Borgstam highlighted recent deliveries of 73 tons of humanitarian supplies, reflecting the EU’s concrete support for displaced populations.
In addition to humanitarian assistance, the EU has played a significant role in sanctions against individuals linked to the Rwandan Defence Force (RDF) and the M23 rebellion, following the occupation of Goma and Bukavu. Among those sanctioned are:
Ruki Karusisi, commander of the RDF special forces in eastern DRC
Eugène Nkubito, commander of RDF’s 3rd Division deployed in North Kivu
Brigadier General Pascal Muhizi, commander of RDF’s 2nd Division
Bertrand Bisimwa, president of M23
Désiré Rukomera, responsible for recruitment and propaganda
John Imani Nzenze, M23 colonel
Jean-Bosco Nzabonimpa Mupenzi, deputy finance chief of M23
Jean Bahati Musanga, former finance head and current governor of the rebellion’s administration in Goma
Borgstam warned that, despite diplomatic processes such as the US-led Washington process and Qatar’s Doha talks, the situation on the ground remains tense. Violence continues to escalate, and mutual accusations of non-compliance with agreements persist between the DRC, Rwanda, and the AFC/M23.

title: Mobondo Militiamen Surrender Weapons as Government Urges Return of Displaced Persons
excerpt: Kwamouth, January 27, 2026 — In a significant step toward peace in the Kwamouth territory, several Mobondo militiamen have surrendered their weapons in villages such as Etumba na Ngwaka, following a government-led peacekeeping mission. The weapons were handed over to the Armed Fo
title_en: Mobondo Militiamen Surrender Weapons as Government Urges Return of Displaced Persons
excerpt_en: Kwamouth, January 27, 2026 — In a significant step toward peace in the Kwamouth territory, several Mobondo militiamen have surrendered their weapons in villages such as Etumba na Ngwaka, following a government-led peacekeeping mission. The weapons were handed over to the Armed Fo
body_en:
Kwamouth, January 27, 2026 — In a significant step toward peace in the Kwamouth territory, several Mobondo militiamen have surrendered their weapons in villages such as Etumba na Ngwaka, following a government-led peacekeeping mission.
The weapons were handed over to the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) in the presence of Minister Delegate for Defense in charge of Veterans, Eliezer Ntambwe, who has been leading the mission for a week. While local reports suggest about 100 weapons have been surrendered, the minister indicated that the final tally will be submitted to Kinshasa at the conclusion of the mission.
Some leaders of the Mobondo militia, along with their traditional healers, have also joined the peace process, signaling a broader willingness among the movement’s members to reintegrate into civilian life.
Minister Ntambwe highlighted that the Mobondo phenomenon has evolved beyond its original ethnic conflict roots between the Teke and Yaka communities, becoming increasingly associated with livestock raiding and other criminal activities. “Those who started this Mobondo story are already with us, including their traditional healers. This proves there is a will to leave this movement,” Ntambwe stated.
The minister conveyed a message from the President of the Republic, encouraging former combatants to resume normal lives and leave the movement, which had drawn in many participants, including some innocent civilians seeking protection.
Ntambwe also urged displaced populations to return to their villages, assuring them that security measures have been deployed by the 11th and 14th Military Regions and the Republican Guard to protect civilians and their property.
“This peacekeeping mission primarily aims to facilitate the surrender of Mobondo militiamen in this part of the country,” the minister explained. He emphasized that insecurity in the region has hindered the implementation of several government programs, underscoring the broader importance of stabilizing Kwamouth.
The surrender of weapons and the ongoing reintegration efforts mark a critical step toward restoring security and normalcy in the affected communities, while allowing the government to implement development and social programs more effectively.

excerpt: Kalemie/Uvira, January 27, 2026 – 17:38 — After several weeks of suspension due to insecurity in Uvira, traffic on Lake Tanganyika between the cities of Kalemie (Tanganyika Province) and Uvira (South Kivu) officially resumed on Tuesday, January 27, 2026. The decision was announce
title_en: Lake Tanganyika Traffic Resumes Between Kalemie and Uvira After Weeks of Disruption
excerpt_en: Kalemie/Uvira, January 27, 2026 – 17:38 — After several weeks of suspension due to insecurity in Uvira, traffic on Lake Tanganyika between the cities of Kalemie (Tanganyika Province) and Uvira (South Kivu) officially resumed on Tuesday, January 27, 2026. The decision was announce
body_en:
Kalemie/Uvira, January 27, 2026 – 17:38 — After several weeks of suspension due to insecurity in Uvira, traffic on Lake Tanganyika between the cities of Kalemie (Tanganyika Province) and Uvira (South Kivu) officially resumed on Tuesday, January 27, 2026.
The decision was announced by Governor Christian Kitungwa Muteba of Tanganyika Province. The suspension had been implemented in response to the threat posed by the AFC/M23 rebellion, which had temporarily seized control over parts of Uvira, creating risks of infiltration and disruption across the lake.
“With the progressive restoration of state authority, ordered by the Government of the Democratic Republic of Congo, and the resumption of economic and migratory activities previously interrupted for security reasons, lake traffic between Uvira and Kalemie will resume as of January 27, 2026,” the governor’s statement read.
The reopening of this vital transport route is expected to boost trade, migration, and humanitarian activities, providing relief to local populations and economic operators who rely on the lake for daily commerce and travel.
This development comes after the withdrawal of the AFC/M23 rebellion from Uvira and reflects the ongoing efforts of the central government and provincial authorities to restore security and normalcy in eastern DRC.
Residents and businesses have welcomed the resumption, highlighting the lake’s importance as a key commercial and social link connecting the East and Southeast regions of the Democratic Republic of Congo.

excerpt_en: Kalemie/Uvira, January 27, 2026 — After several weeks of suspension, lake traffic on Lake Tanganyika between the cities of Kalemie and Uvira officially resumed on Tuesday, January 27, 2026, authorities announced. The decision was confirmed by Christian Kitungwa Muteba, Governor o
body_en:
Kalemie/Uvira, January 27, 2026 — After several weeks of suspension, lake traffic on Lake Tanganyika between the cities of Kalemie and Uvira officially resumed on Tuesday, January 27, 2026, authorities announced.
The decision was confirmed by Christian Kitungwa Muteba, Governor of Tanganyika Province, in an official statement. The suspension had followed the deterioration of the security situation in Uvira, the second-largest city in South Kivu, which had been under the threat and control of the AFC/M23 rebellion. The instability posed serious risks to neighboring Tanganyika Province, particularly the danger of infiltration by lake.
As a result, all lake movements — including trade, passenger transport, and migration — had been strictly prohibited by provincial authorities. With the withdrawal of the rebellion from Uvira and improvements in security, the government has now lifted these restrictions as part of broader efforts to restore state authority.
“As part of the progressive restoration of state authority, ordered by the Government of the Democratic Republic of Congo, and the resumption of all economic activities and migratory movements previously interrupted for security reasons, lake traffic between the cities of Uvira and Kalemie will resume as of January 27, 2026,” Governor Kitungwa Muteba stated.
The reopening has been welcomed with relief by economic operators, travelers, and lakeside communities, for whom this route represents a vital corridor for commercial, social, and humanitarian exchanges between eastern and southeastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

title: Manguredjipa Paralyzed After Deadly Protest Against Insecurity in Lubero
excerpt: Manguredjipa, January 28, 2026 — Socio-economic activities slowed sharply in Manguredjipa, the main town of the Bapere sector in Lubero territory, on Wednesday, January 28, 2026, marking the second day of unrest triggered by a protest against rising insecurity linked to Allied De
title_en: Manguredjipa Paralyzed After Deadly Protest Against Insecurity in Lubero
excerpt_en: Manguredjipa, January 28, 2026 — Socio-economic activities slowed sharply in Manguredjipa, the main town of the Bapere sector in Lubero territory, on Wednesday, January 28, 2026, marking the second day of unrest triggered by a protest against rising insecurity linked to Allied De
body_en:
Manguredjipa, January 28, 2026 — Socio-economic activities slowed sharply in Manguredjipa, the main town of the Bapere sector in Lubero territory, on Wednesday, January 28, 2026, marking the second day of unrest triggered by a protest against rising insecurity linked to Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) attacks.
Shops remained closed, agricultural work was suspended, and traffic was severely disrupted. On the previous day, local women had erected barricades at the main entry and exit points of the town. Some protesters marched barefoot, while others demonstrated topless, a traditional sign of indignation in the face of persistent violence.
The demonstration, organized on Tuesday, January 27, turned violent, leaving two people dead and three others seriously injured. The victims, all young boys, were reportedly killed by gunfire attributed to security forces during the protest. Among the injured were a woman, a six-month-old infant, and another young boy, all evacuated to medical facilities for urgent treatment.
The unrest also caused significant material damage. The residence of the sector chief was vandalized, a motorcycle was set on fire, and several household appliances were destroyed. These incidents led to the closure of the local market, further paralyzing economic life.
The protest came just 72 hours after an ADF attack in the village of Musenge, in the Baswagha chiefdom, during which several houses, a health center, and a Catholic church were burned down. The attack also caused mass displacement and the deaths of two FARDC soldiers.

title: DRC Humanitarian Response Refocused on 7.3 Million People Amid $1.4 Billion Funding Appeal for 2026
excerpt: Kinshasa, January 28, 2026 — Facing a severe funding shortfall, the humanitarian community in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has announced a major reprioritization of its 2026 response, targeting 7.3 million people—less than half of the nearly 15 million in critical need.
title_en: DRC Humanitarian Response Refocused on 7.3 Million People Amid $1.4 Billion Funding Appeal for 2026
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, January 28, 2026 — Facing a severe funding shortfall, the humanitarian community in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has announced a major reprioritization of its 2026 response, targeting 7.3 million people—less than half of the nearly 15 million in critical need.
body_en:
Kinshasa, January 28, 2026 — Facing a severe funding shortfall, the humanitarian community in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has announced a major reprioritization of its 2026 response, targeting 7.3 million people—less than half of the nearly 15 million in critical need. The government and its humanitarian partners launched an urgent appeal on Wednesday for USD 1.4 billion to address the country’s most pressing humanitarian needs.
The revised plan reflects a sharp reduction from 2025, when 11 million people were targeted. According to humanitarian officials, this shift represents a strict prioritization of populations facing the most immediate threats to survival, as the country grapples with ongoing armed conflict, mass displacement, climate shocks, and recurring epidemics.
The impact of underfunding has already been severe. In 2025, reduced operational capacity led to the closure of more than 1,000 nutrition centers, leaving over 390,000 children suffering from severe acute malnutrition without essential care. An estimated 1.5 million people lost access to primary healthcare due to facility closures, medicine shortages, and weakened epidemic response. Monthly food assistance targets were reduced by up to 73%, exposing vulnerable communities to heightened hunger and deprivation.
“The combination of immense needs and limited resources forces us to make extremely difficult, sometimes impossible, choices,” said Bruno Lemarquis, Humanitarian Coordinator in the DRC. “We call for renewed and strengthened financial commitments to preserve lives, dignity, and prevent millions from being deprived of vital support.”
The 2026 plan comes amid a deeply disrupted humanitarian environment, particularly in North Kivu, South Kivu, and Ituri, where intensified fighting since January 2025 has reshaped needs, disrupted supply chains, and imposed growing administrative and security constraints. Access to affected populations has become increasingly dangerous and complex.
Mr. Lemarquis called for a paradigm shift in the humanitarian approach. “Humanitarian assistance saves lives, but it does not resolve the root causes of crises,” he said. “Peace must be at the center of our efforts. Solutions are primarily political. We must move beyond constant reaction and establish a culture of anticipation and prevention, while strengthening the Humanitarian–Development–Peace Nexus for real, lasting impact.”
He also praised the resilience and solidarity of Congolese communities, particularly host families who share scarce resources with displaced people, describing them as the country’s first line of humanitarian defense. He emphasized the central role of the government in facilitating humanitarian operations on the ground.
Despite its scale and duration, the humanitarian crisis in the DRC remains one of the world’s most protracted and underfunded. The 2025 Humanitarian Response Plan, budgeted at USD 2.54 billion, was funded at only 22%, even as needs continued to rise. International funding shortages—compounded by recent reductions in humanitarian assistance from key donors—have had particularly severe consequences in eastern DRC.
At the global level, the United Nations’ 2026 humanitarian plan targets 87 million people worldwide and requires USD 23 billion. While major pledges have been announced, humanitarian officials warn that without sustained and predictable financing, millions of vulnerable people in the DRC will remain without life-saving assistance.

title: General Strike Paralyzes Shabunda as Residents Demand End to Insecurity and Wazalendo Abuses
excerpt: Shabunda, South Kivu January 29, 2026 — The town of Shabunda has been paralyzed since the beginning of the week by a general strike, as residents protest rising insecurity, alleged abuses by the “wazalendo”, and demand the withdrawal of these armed groups from the town. The strik
title_en: General Strike Paralyzes Shabunda as Residents Demand End to Insecurity and Wazalendo Abuses
excerpt_en: Shabunda, South Kivu January 29, 2026 — The town of Shabunda has been paralyzed since the beginning of the week by a general strike, as residents protest rising insecurity, alleged abuses by the “wazalendo”, and demand the withdrawal of these armed groups from the town. The strik
body_en:
Shabunda, South Kivu January 29, 2026 — The town of Shabunda has been paralyzed since the beginning of the week by a general strike, as residents protest rising insecurity, alleged abuses by the “wazalendo”, and demand the withdrawal of these armed groups from the town.
The strike, launched by civil society on Tuesday, January 27, follows a series of incidents attributed to certain wazalendo elements. Since Monday, schools, markets, and most commercial activities have been shut down, while vehicle traffic has come to a standstill.
“Shops, stores, markets… are not operating. Traffic is suspended,” said a local resident. Another added, “Schools have been closed for four days, which is seriously disrupting classes, especially during first-session exams for secondary students.”
According to Isaac Rashidi, president of Shabunda territory’s civil society, the “ghost town” operation was declared in response to repeated acts of insecurity. He cited the proliferation of illegal roadblocks, extortion of money from civilians, and repeated killings allegedly committed by some wazalendo fighters.
Mr. Rashidi further reported that an altercation last Friday between wazalendo and residents left four people dead, including three civilians, and several others wounded.
“We are asking the security council and the provincial government to order all wazalendo in the central zone to go to the front lines,” he said. “Only the FARDC, the police, and the official security services should remain in Shabunda.”
Civil society has also called on officials of the Armed Reserve for Defense (RAD) to restore order in the management and deployment of wazalendo in this part of South Kivu.

title: AU Facilitators Meet Tshisekedi to Relaunch Regional Mediation Ahead of Visits to Kigali and Bujumbura
excerpt: Kinshasa — January 29, 2026 — President Félix Tshisekedi on Thursday received a delegation from the African Union (AU) Panel of Facilitators at the African Union City complex, as part of renewed diplomatic efforts to promote peace in the Democratic Republic of Congo and the wider
title_en: AU Facilitators Meet Tshisekedi to Relaunch Regional Mediation Ahead of Visits to Kigali and Bujumbura
excerpt_en: Kinshasa — January 29, 2026 — President Félix Tshisekedi on Thursday received a delegation from the African Union (AU) Panel of Facilitators at the African Union City complex, as part of renewed diplomatic efforts to promote peace in the Democratic Republic of Congo and the wider
body_en:
Kinshasa — January 29, 2026 — President Félix Tshisekedi on Thursday received a delegation from the African Union (AU) Panel of Facilitators at the African Union City complex, as part of renewed diplomatic efforts to promote peace in the Democratic Republic of Congo and the wider Great Lakes region.
Discussions focused on mediation initiatives aimed at ending the violence, particularly in the eastern provinces. “We are on a tour. We will listen to everyone and see what can be done for the well-being of this population that has suffered greatly for decades. Behind all this, there is human suffering that must be stopped,” said Sahle-Work Zewde, former President of Ethiopia.
According to the Congolese presidency, President Tshisekedi welcomed the facilitators’ efforts and reaffirmed his commitment to achieving a lasting and verifiable peace in eastern DRC, as well as to strengthening regional stability, in line with commitments made by all parties.
The delegation included Olusegun Obasanjo, former President of Nigeria; Sahle-Work Zewde, former President of Ethiopia; Mokgweetsi Eric Keabetswe Masisi, former President of Botswana; Catherine Samba-Panza, former President of the Central African Republic; Yackoly Kokou Johnson, Togolese Minister Delegate representing mediator Faure Gnassingbé; and Ambassador Akok Manyuat Madut, representing the African Union Commission. The facilitators are also scheduled to visit Kigali, Bujumbura, and Kampala.
The African Union has recently outlined the structure of its mediation for the peace process in eastern DRC following a high-level meeting held in Lomé on January 16 and 17. The mediation is led by Togolese President Faure Gnassingbé, appointed as AU mediator, and supported by a Togolese team drawn from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Presidency.
Five co-facilitators, all former African heads of state, have been assigned specific thematic areas: Olusegun Obasanjo for military and security issues; Sahle-Work Zewde for humanitarian affairs; Uhuru Kenyatta for dialogue with local armed groups; Mokgweetsi Masisi for regional economic cooperation; and Catherine Samba-Panza for civil society, reconciliation, and women’s issues.
The mediation mechanism also includes an independent joint secretariat bringing together Togo, the African Union, the East African Community, the Southern African Development Community, and the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region. The African Union Commission coordinates with international partners, including the United Nations, Qatar, the European Union, and the five permanent members of the UN Security Council.

title: Identification Operation Launched for Military and Police Personnel in Kisenso
excerpt: An operation to identify military and police personnel officially began on Friday, January 30, in the Kisenso district of Kinshasa, aimed at tightening control over law enforcement officers and armed forces members residing in the area. The initiative, launched by Kisenso Mayor G
title_en: Identification Operation Launched for Military and Police Personnel in Kisenso
excerpt_en: An operation to identify military and police personnel officially began on Friday, January 30, in the Kisenso district of Kinshasa, aimed at tightening control over law enforcement officers and armed forces members residing in the area. The initiative, launched by Kisenso Mayor G
body_en:
An operation to identify military and police personnel officially began on Friday, January 30, in the Kisenso district of Kinshasa, aimed at tightening control over law enforcement officers and armed forces members residing in the area.
The initiative, launched by Kisenso Mayor Godé Athswel, follows a surge in insecurity linked to unidentified men in uniform in several neighborhoods of the capital. These individuals are accused of extortion, home invasions, and other acts of violence.
Mayor Athswel said the operation is intended to protect residents and neutralize criminals who have infiltrated the security services.
“We took the precaution of identifying all soldiers in the Kisenso district, whether armed or not, and recording their weapon serial numbers for rigorous verification, in order to guarantee the safety of our population,” he stated.
Objective: Restoring Public Trust
Although the security situation in Kisenso is described as relatively calm, authorities acknowledge that in other parts of Kinshasa, deserters from military training are reportedly involved in looting and violence. The identification campaign is therefore seen as a key step toward restoring trust between the population and the security forces.

title: Belgium Urges European Action and Humanitarian Air Access via Goma
excerpt: Brussels Belgium January 30, 2026 — Belgium has renewed its call for stronger European engagement in response to the worsening security and humanitarian crisis in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), urging the European Union to treat the conflict as a priority rather than
title_en: Belgium Urges European Action and Humanitarian Air Access via Goma
excerpt_en: Brussels Belgium January 30, 2026 — Belgium has renewed its call for stronger European engagement in response to the worsening security and humanitarian crisis in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), urging the European Union to treat the conflict as a priority rather than
body_en:
Brussels Belgium January 30, 2026 — Belgium has renewed its call for stronger European engagement in response to the worsening security and humanitarian crisis in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), urging the European Union to treat the conflict as a priority rather than a forgotten crisis.
Speaking at an EU meeting on Thursday, January 29, Belgian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot emphasized that the situation on the ground continues to deteriorate, despite ongoing diplomatic efforts.
“Belgium is deeply sensitive to the tragedies unfolding in the Democratic Republic of Congo. While we welcome political mediation initiatives undertaken in Washington and Doha, the situation on the ground is worse than ever. This is extremely worrying from a humanitarian perspective,” Prévot said.
According to him, this persistent decline prompted Belgium, alongside other EU member states, to place the eastern DRC crisis on the meeting agenda. He expressed concern over how rarely the issue is discussed at the European level. “I am surprised that this is only the second time in a year that eastern Congo has been addressed. This cannot be a forgotten conflict. The European Union has a role to play,” he insisted.
While reaffirming Belgium’s support for ongoing mediation processes, Prévot called for tangible outcomes, including a ceasefire and a return to lasting peace. He also reiterated his country’s position on respecting Congolese sovereignty and territorial integrity.
“We hope these mediation efforts will lead to genuine ceasefire and peace solutions. We must advocate for the withdrawal of the M23 and Rwandan troops so that the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the DRC are preserved,” he stated.
However, the Belgian minister stressed that the immediate priority remains humanitarian. He painted a stark picture of the suffering endured by civilians, particularly women and children, who are disproportionately affected by sexual violence.
“The urgent need at this moment is for European action to address the humanitarian situation, where a woman is raped every four minutes and a child every thirty minutes,” he said.
In this context, Prévot called for concrete measures to facilitate aid delivery, including the reopening of Goma International Airport for exclusively humanitarian purposes.
“It is urgent to activate Goma airport to deliver massive amounts of humanitarian aid. Let there be no doubt: there is no intention to use this airport for military purposes. Belgium’s objective is a broader European commitment to children who have long suffered the tragic horrors of this conflict,” he clarified.
The reopening of Goma airport remains a sensitive and central issue in political discussions. Kinshasa has announced an initiative to reopen the airport to facilitate humanitarian assistance, while the M23 and Rwanda insist that any decision should be made within the framework of the peace process and in respect of territorial control on the ground.

title_en: Violent Clashes Between AFC/M23 and FARDC in Chanjikiro
excerpt_en: Walikale North Kivu, January 30, 2026 — Violent fighting erupted on Thursday, January 29, 2026, between AFC/M23 rebels and the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), supported by the Wazalendo and the Armed Reserve of the Defense (RAD), in Chanjikiro, within th
body_en:
Walikale North Kivu, January 30, 2026 — Violent fighting erupted on Thursday, January 29, 2026, between AFC/M23 rebels and the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), supported by the Wazalendo and the Armed Reserve of the Defense (RAD), in Chanjikiro, within the Kisimba group of Walikale territory, North Kivu province.
According to local administrative authorities, the attackers advanced from Mpety and launched an offensive against government positions at around 2:00 p.m. local time.
Heavy and light weapon fire was reported, with loud explosions heard across the area, triggering widespread panic among civilians.

body_en:
Walikale North Kivu, January 30, 2026 — The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) have continued their military operations against AFC/M23 rebels in Walikale territory, aiming to dismantle rebel positions and reduce their operational capacity in this part of North Kivu.
Following the repulsion of a rebel attack in Chanjikiro, the Congolese army, through its air force, carried out airstrikes on Thursday, January 29, 2026, targeting AFC/M23 positions in Mindjendje, near Mpety, within the Kisimba group.
Local administrative authorities reported that the strikes occurred in the early evening, around 4:00 p.m. local time, shortly after the clashes in Chanjikiro.
A FARDC drone was deployed during the operation to strike what security sources identified as a key rebel logistics base in the Pinga area. Significant material damage was reported at the targeted site.
These airstrikes follow similar operations in recent days against positions in Mindjendje and Mpety, reflecting an intensification of FARDC military efforts in Walikale territory.

title: Faure Gnassingbé Travels to Kigali to Meet with Paul Kagame
excerpt: Kigali Rwanda, January 30, 2026 — Rwandan President Paul Kagame received Togolese Prime Minister Faure Gnassingbé, the African Union (AU) chief mediator for the peace process in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), in Urugwiro Village, as part of ongoing diplomatic consult
title_en: Faure Gnassingbé Travels to Kigali to Meet with Paul Kagame
excerpt_en: Kigali Rwanda, January 30, 2026 — Rwandan President Paul Kagame received Togolese Prime Minister Faure Gnassingbé, the African Union (AU) chief mediator for the peace process in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), in Urugwiro Village, as part of ongoing diplomatic consult
body_en:
Kigali Rwanda, January 30, 2026 — Rwandan President Paul Kagame received Togolese Prime Minister Faure Gnassingbé, the African Union (AU) chief mediator for the peace process in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), in Urugwiro Village, as part of ongoing diplomatic consultations on the Great Lakes crisis.
The two heads of state held a private meeting before a broader session with the AU Panel of Facilitators, which includes former African heads of state: Olusegun Obasanjo (Nigeria), Sahle-Work Zewde (Ethiopia), Mokgweetsi Masisi (Botswana), and Catherine Samba-Panza (Central African Republic).
The discussions focused on the security situation in eastern DRC, the progress of ongoing diplomatic initiatives, and ways to strengthen coordination between regional and continental mediation efforts to promote peace, security, and stability in the Great Lakes region.
“I thank President Paul Kagame for the quality of the discussions held today in Kigali. Our discussions focused primarily on the challenges of peace and stability in the Great Lakes region, particularly in eastern DRC, as well as on strengthening bilateral cooperation,” said Faure Gnassingbé.
The presidency recalled that this situation was central to the high-level summit held in Lomé on January 16 and 17, 2026, dedicated to the coherence and consolidation of the peace process in the DRC and the region. “The President of the Council is continuing consultations to reach an African solution to this conflict, which is affecting the population,” the source added.
The previous day, Congolese President Félix Tshisekedi received a delegation from the AU Panel of Facilitators in Kinshasa, focusing on mediation efforts to end the violence in the east of the country. “We are on a tour. We will listen to one another and see what can be done for the well-being of the population, which has suffered greatly for decades,” said Sahle-Work Zewde.
Félix Tshisekedi commended the facilitators’ efforts and reaffirmed his commitment to a lasting and verifiable peace in eastern DRC and the strengthening of regional stability, in line with commitments made by the parties.
The delegation also included Yackoly Kokou Johnson, Togolese Minister Delegate, and Ambassador Akok Manyuat Madut, representing the African Union Commission. The facilitators will continue their regional tour in Bujumbura and Kampala.
The African Union outlined the structure of its mediation for the peace process in eastern DRC following the Lomé meeting, placing Faure Gnassingbé in authority and supported by five co-facilitators, each responsible for a specific component, with a joint secretariat involving the AU and several regional organizations.

title: Tshisekedi Highlights Rwanda-AFC/M23 Collaboration, Calls for UN Action
excerpt: Kinshasa, January 31, 2026 — President Félix Tshisekedi addressed ambassadors and diplomats at the New Year's greetings ceremony at the Palais de la Nation, reacting to Rwanda’s official admission of collaboration with the AFC/M23 rebel group in eastern DRC. This acknowledgment w
title_en: Tshisekedi Highlights Rwanda-AFC/M23 Collaboration, Calls for UN Action
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, January 31, 2026 — President Félix Tshisekedi addressed ambassadors and diplomats at the New Year's greetings ceremony at the Palais de la Nation, reacting to Rwanda’s official admission of collaboration with the AFC/M23 rebel group in eastern DRC. This acknowledgment w
body_en:
Kinshasa, January 31, 2026 — President Félix Tshisekedi addressed ambassadors and diplomats at the New Year's greetings ceremony at the Palais de la Nation, reacting to Rwanda’s official admission of collaboration with the AFC/M23 rebel group in eastern DRC. This acknowledgment was made by Mathilde Mukantabana, Rwanda’s Ambassador to the United States, before the US House of Representatives.
According to Tshisekedi, the admission reduces the scope for denial, clarifies responsibilities, and obliges the international community, particularly the United Nations, to implement Security Council resolutions.
“For years, we have denounced, with evidence, the external support fueling armed violence on our soil. Now, a high-ranking Rwandan official has officially confirmed security coordination with the AFC/M23 rebels. This is not a PR exercise or a political strategy. It exposes the decisive support provided to an armed insurgent movement operating on Congolese sovereign territory,” declared Félix Tshisekedi.
He emphasized:
“This admission constitutes a major turning point: it reduces denial, clarifies responsibilities, and compels action through international law, UN resolutions, and political commitments. No narrative, cause, or security justification can legitimize de facto occupation, parallel administrations, forced displacements, or plundering of resources against a UN member state.”
For the first time, Rwanda officially acknowledged its coordination with AFC/M23 in eastern DRC. Kigali claims this is a defensive measure aimed at protecting the Tutsi population and preventing a resurgence of genocidal violence.
In her statement to the US Congress on January 22, Mathilde Mukantabana explained that this coordination allowed the AFC/M23 to withdraw from Uvira, signaling commitment to de-escalation.
She further stated:
“Rwanda is engaging in security coordination with the AFC/M23 to build trust through transparency. The AFC/M23 has legitimate grievances against Kinshasa. Rwanda and the AFC/M23 share a common interest in protecting Tutsis from the FDLR and other extremist militias. Rwanda’s interest is also to prevent a cross-border genocidal insurgency threatening its existence.”
Kigali stresses that the coordination is strictly defensive, conditional, time-limited, linked to disarmament and neutralization of the FDLR, and does not seek to influence internal DRC politics.

title: FARDC Shoots Down 8 Drones Targeting Bangboka Airport, Authorities Blame AFC/M23
excerpt: Kisangani, February 2, 2026 — Bangboka Airport, located 17 kilometers from downtown Kisangani, was targeted in an armed attack using kamikaze drones between 5:00 a.m. on Saturday, January 31 and 2:00 a.m. on Sunday, February 1, according to the Tshopo provincial government. Autho
title_en: FARDC Shoots Down 8 Drones Targeting Bangboka Airport, Authorities Blame AFC/M23
excerpt_en: Kisangani, February 2, 2026 — Bangboka Airport, located 17 kilometers from downtown Kisangani, was targeted in an armed attack using kamikaze drones between 5:00 a.m. on Saturday, January 31 and 2:00 a.m. on Sunday, February 1, according to the Tshopo provincial government. Autho
body_en:
Kisangani, February 2, 2026 — Bangboka Airport, located 17 kilometers from downtown Kisangani, was targeted in an armed attack using kamikaze drones between 5:00 a.m. on Saturday, January 31 and 2:00 a.m. on Sunday, February 1, according to the Tshopo provincial government.
Authorities reported that the drones carried unconventional munitions composed of submunitions, and attributed the attack to Rwanda and its allies in the AFC/M23, describing it as a "barbaric, unjust, and persistent aggression" against the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Thanks to the vigilance and professionalism of the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) and their security partners, eight drones were neutralized before reaching the airport. No casualties or major damage were reported.
Provincial authorities stated:
“This attack demonstrates once again Rwanda’s intention to undermine the Washington peace agreement.”
They also called on the international community “to move beyond mere condemnations and take concrete, deterrent measures to end an aggression lasting more than three decades, and to ensure the withdrawal of foreign forces and their proxies from occupied areas of the DRC.”
Residents near Bangboka Airport, who had begun to flee in fear, were urged to return home, as no evacuation is currently necessary.

title: Implementation Struggles Seven Months After Signing, Overall Rate Stagnates at 23.3%
excerpt: Washington Agreement February 2, 2026 — Seven months after the signing of the Washington Agreement between the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and Rwanda, implementation continues to face serious challenges, with an overall implementation rate remaining unchanged at 23.3%, acc
title_en: Implementation Struggles Seven Months After Signing, Overall Rate Stagnates at 23.3%
excerpt_en: Washington Agreement February 2, 2026 — Seven months after the signing of the Washington Agreement between the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and Rwanda, implementation continues to face serious challenges, with an overall implementation rate remaining unchanged at 23.3%, acc
body_en:
Washington Agreement February 2, 2026 — Seven months after the signing of the Washington Agreement between the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and Rwanda, implementation continues to face serious challenges, with an overall implementation rate remaining unchanged at 23.3%, according to a recent report by the African Peace Agreements Barometer.
The agreement, signed under the auspices of the Trump administration, was intended to address the ongoing conflict in eastern DRC and the activities of the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebellion, which continues territorial operations in North Kivu and South Kivu.
The report highlights that the main positive developments between January 1 and 31, 2026, include:
High-level meeting in Lomé (January 16-17) to consolidate peace processes in the DRC and the Great Lakes region and adopt a new AU mediation architecture.
Regional tour of the AU Mediator and the Panel of Facilitators, operationalizing the new mediation framework.
Extraordinary meeting of ICGLR defense experts in Livingstone (January 8-10) to review the deteriorating security situation in eastern DRC.
President João Lourenço’s consultations with Congolese political, military, and religious actors to relaunch inclusive political dialogue.
U.S. Congressional hearings (January 22) to assess the Washington Agreement’s implementation.
Withdrawal of AFC/M23 from Uvira.
Despite these steps, the report identifies persistent challenges, including:

body_en:
Butembo, February 2, 2026 — A passenger convoy traveling from Rutshuru territory to the city of Butembo was targeted in an armed attack on Sunday, February 1, along the Rwindi-Kanyabayonga road.
According to local sources, the incident occurred around 3:00 PM, when several vehicles and motorcycles were ambushed by unidentified armed men in an area under AFC/M23 rebel control.
The attackers opened fire and used bladed weapons against the passengers, causing several injuries, though no fatalities were reported. Victims were transported to medical facilities in Kanyabayonga for treatment.
In addition to the physical assault, all passengers’ valuables were looted, including money, cell phones, and merchandise, leaving many stripped of personal belongings.
Civil society actors in Rutshuru noted that such incidents are becoming increasingly frequent on this strategic route. They called on the authorities and security forces to strengthen protection, secure the road, and ensure the free movement of people and goods.
This attack highlights the persistent insecurity in parts of North Kivu, despite repeated warnings and calls for urgent intervention to safeguard civilians.

title: Police Arrest 39 Suspected Armed Bandits, Including Those Who Murdered a Security Agent
excerpt: Lubumbashi DRC February 2, 2026 — The Congolese National Police (PNC) conducted a major security operation in Haut-Katanga province. In Lubumbashi, thirty-nine (39) suspected criminals were presented on Monday, including individuals believed responsible for the murder of an agent
title_en: Police Arrest 39 Suspected Armed Bandits, Including Those Who Murdered a Security Agent
excerpt_en: Lubumbashi DRC February 2, 2026 — The Congolese National Police (PNC) conducted a major security operation in Haut-Katanga province. In Lubumbashi, thirty-nine (39) suspected criminals were presented on Monday, including individuals believed responsible for the murder of an agent
body_en:
Lubumbashi DRC February 2, 2026 — The Congolese National Police (PNC) conducted a major security operation in Haut-Katanga province. In Lubumbashi, thirty-nine (39) suspected criminals were presented on Monday, including individuals believed responsible for the murder of an agent of the National Intelligence Agency (ANR).
According to Deputy Divisional Commissioner Blaise Kilimbalimba, provincial commissioner of the PNC in Haut-Katanga, this operation was possible due to close collaboration between the police and the public. The suspects were presented at the provincial police headquarters.
“They were carrying a loaded AK-47 assault rifle, ammunition, bladed weapons, and dozens of stolen cell phones,” stated Deputy Divisional Commissioner Kilimbalimba.
These arrests are the result of operations conducted in several sensitive neighborhoods, including the Mzee market on Sendwe Avenue, Usines Avenue, Mama Yemo, and the Likasi road.
“The group apprehended is heterogeneous but considered particularly dangerous. Thirteen (13) of them are believed to specialize in armed robbery, and the network involved in the recent assassination of an ANR agent has been dismantled,” said police intelligence services in Haut-Katanga.
Deputy Divisional Commissioner Kilimbalimba commended the public for their role in reporting criminals:
“I commend the courage of the population in reporting criminals. We reiterate our unwavering commitment to apprehending all these criminals who disturb the peace. Vigilance must remain paramount,” he declared.
All suspected criminals will be transferred to the competent judicial authorities to face legal proceedings.

title_en: Kinshasa and the AFC/M23 Sign ICGLR-Backed Mechanism Mandate
excerpt_en: Doha QATAR, February 2, 2026 — The government of the DRC and the Congo River Alliance/March 23 Movement (AFC/M23) signed the mandate of the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region (ICGLR) in Doha on Monday. The signing followed a meeting of the ceasefire monitoring and
body_en:
Doha QATAR, February 2, 2026 — The government of the DRC and the Congo River Alliance/March 23 Movement (AFC/M23) signed the mandate of the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region (ICGLR) in Doha on Monday.
The signing followed a meeting of the ceasefire monitoring and verification mechanism, organized by Qatar as part of its mediation efforts to resolve the conflict in eastern DRC.
Both parties reaffirmed their commitment to the ceasefire and the Doha Peace Framework, signed on November 15, 2025, and expressed their determination to implement all provisions in good faith to support the peace process.
The meeting included members of the mechanism, with the United States and the African Union as observers, as well as Togo, the AU-appointed mediator, MONUSCO, and the ICGLR.
Discussions focused on the evolving situation and current challenges, emphasizing the need to implement concrete measures to strengthen monitoring, verification, and information sharing in support of the peace process.
Plans for implementing the mechanism by MONUSCO and the ICGLR were reviewed, and both parties reaffirmed their commitment to supporting these efforts. MONUSCO will deploy an initial mission to Uvira in the coming days to monitor the ceasefire, with communication channels established to facilitate operations.
Members also agreed on next steps to strengthen the effectiveness of the mechanism and ensure regular meetings within its framework.

title_en: A Month Without Fighting Between FARDC and AFC/M23 in Osso Banyungu Sector
excerpt_en: February 3, 2026 — The Osso Banyungu sector (Masisi territory, North Kivu) has experienced a lull for nearly a month, with no clashes reported between government forces (FARDC) and AFC/M23 rebels. Local sources report that both sides are holding their positions. The rebels have n
body_en:
February 3, 2026 — The Osso Banyungu sector (Masisi territory, North Kivu) has experienced a lull for nearly a month, with no clashes reported between government forces (FARDC) and AFC/M23 rebels.
Local sources report that both sides are holding their positions. The rebels have not advanced along any new axes, while the FARDC, supported by the Wazalendo, remain entrenched in their initial lines.
This relative stability has enabled the spontaneous return of people to several villages. Displaced families who fled hostilities are gradually returning, despite a fragile security situation.
A tentative resumption of socio-economic activity is observed, particularly in local markets and small businesses, though progress is limited due to persistent insecurity on certain roads.
From a humanitarian perspective, the situation remains worrying. Needs are immense, while humanitarian access is severely restricted, limiting assistance to affected populations.
Local civil society actors are calling for the consolidation of this lull and advocating for initiatives to restore lasting peace, enabling the return of government administration, basic social services, and humanitarian aid to the Osso Banyungu sector.
The sector had previously been shaken in December 2015 by repeated clashes between AFC/M23 rebels and the FARDC, supported by the Wazalendo.

excerpt: Walikale February 3, 2026 — Calm was restored on Tuesday morning, February 3, in the villages of Rusamambu (Ikobo group), Kalonge, and Kasopo (Kisimba group) in Walikale territory, North Kivu, following a night of violent clashes between AFC/M23 rebels and the Wazalendo of the CM
title_en: Calm Returns to Rusamambu, Kalonge, and Kasopo (Walikale) After Clashes Between AFC/M23 and Wazalendo
excerpt_en: Walikale February 3, 2026 — Calm was restored on Tuesday morning, February 3, in the villages of Rusamambu (Ikobo group), Kalonge, and Kasopo (Kisimba group) in Walikale territory, North Kivu, following a night of violent clashes between AFC/M23 rebels and the Wazalendo of the CM
body_en:
Walikale February 3, 2026 — Calm was restored on Tuesday morning, February 3, in the villages of Rusamambu (Ikobo group), Kalonge, and Kasopo (Kisimba group) in Walikale territory, North Kivu, following a night of violent clashes between AFC/M23 rebels and the Wazalendo of the CMC/APC group.
According to local sources, the fighting began around 1:00 a.m., when the Wazalendo launched attacks on rebel positions. Exchanges of fire, involving heavy and light weapons, continued until approximately 6:00 a.m.
Residents spent a restless night at home, fearing the spread of violence. No official information is available yet regarding casualties or material damage.
Sources indicate that the Wazalendo withdrew from Rusamambu, Kalonge, and Kasopo on Tuesday morning, leaving the villages under AFC/M23 control.

title_en: New Ceasefire Monitoring and Verification Mechanism Explained
excerpt_en: DRC–AFC/M23 February 3, 2026 — The Congolese government and AFC/M23 have adopted the terms of reference for a joint mechanism to monitor and verify the ceasefire agreement, reached on Monday in Doha. The mechanism consists of two complementary components: Ceasefire Monitoring and
body_en:
DRC–AFC/M23 February 3, 2026 — The Congolese government and AFC/M23 have adopted the terms of reference for a joint mechanism to monitor and verify the ceasefire agreement, reached on Monday in Doha.
The mechanism consists of two complementary components:
Ceasefire Monitoring and Verification Mechanism (CMVM) – the supervisory and decision-making body.
Extended Joint Verification Mechanism Plus (EJVM+) – responsible for technical activities and on-the-ground verifications.
The CMVM is composed equally of government and rebel representatives, with observers from the African Union, Qatar, the United States, and the ICGLR. MONUSCO also participates. Monitoring the security and humanitarian situation in affected areas.
Promoting compliance with agreed security measures and building confidence between parties.
Joint verification teams, appointed by the JMVC Commander, include an equal number of representatives from both sides, with observers where possible. body_en:
Peace Process in Jeopardy in Kwamouth, February 3, 2026 — Deaths continue in Kwamouth, despite ongoing efforts to encourage militiamen to surrender. Between January 26 and 27, a mediator and his wife were killed at the Brazza farm, deep in the territory.
The man had been sent to raise awareness among militiamen as part of the peace process recently launched on the Bateke Plateau by Minister Delegate for Defense, in charge of veterans, Eliezer Ntambwe. He was killed by rogue militiamen, who subsequently dismembered his body. His wife, accompanying him, was also murdered by the same armed men.
Chief Stany Libie of Kimomo village supports government efforts to encourage militiamen to surrender, stating that force must be used against those resisting the peace initiative.
“Some militiamen have rejected the message of peace, including the Cobra and American warlords, in Diangele, who have boycotted government actions. For all enemies of peace, measures must be taken to neutralize them. This is yet another sabotage of the peace process by these militiamen,” said Stany Libie.
Several Mobondo militiamen have voluntarily surrendered as part of the awareness campaign led by Minister Eliezer Ntambwe. In Kwamouth and the Maluku commune, some militiamen have joined the defense and security forces.
The Deputy Minister of Defense, responsible for veterans, reported encountering several victims attempting to protect themselves. However, the implementation of government programs has been delayed due to persistent insecurity in this region of Maï-Ndombe.

title_en: New Clashes Between AFC/M23 and Wazalendo in Bukumbirwa (Walikale)
excerpt_en: Bukumbirwa February 3, 2026 — Violent clashes erupted early Tuesday morning, February 3, between AFC/M23 rebels and Wazalendo from the NDC-Rénové group in Bukumbirwa, located in the Ikobo area of Walikale territory, North Kivu. The Wazalendo launched an attack on AFC/M23 position
body_en:
Bukumbirwa February 3, 2026 — Violent clashes erupted early Tuesday morning, February 3, between AFC/M23 rebels and Wazalendo from the NDC-Rénové group in Bukumbirwa, located in the Ikobo area of Walikale territory, North Kivu.
The Wazalendo launched an attack on AFC/M23 positions around 4:00 a.m., causing widespread panic among residents.
The sounds of heavy and light weapons fire continued for several hours, forcing locals to remain indoors.
After approximately three hours of fighting, the Wazalendo retreated into the bush, leaving Bukumbirwa under rebel control. The toll from these clashes is not yet known.
Socio-economic activities have tentatively resumed, according to local sources. Several witnesses report a strengthening of AFC/M23 positions in Bukumbirwa and Rusamambu, with reinforcements from Buleusa reportedly arriving in these towns on Tuesday morning.

excerpt: Walikale February 3, 2026 — The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), supported by the Wazalendo, successfully repelled an attack by AFC/M23 rebels in Kalinga, Banamulema (Kisimba group), Walikale territory, North Kivu, on the morning of Tuesday, February 3. A

excerpt_en: Walikale February 3, 2026 — The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), supported by the Wazalendo, successfully repelled an attack by AFC/M23 rebels in Kalinga, Banamulema (Kisimba group), Walikale territory, North Kivu, on the morning of Tuesday, February 3. A
body_en:
Walikale February 3, 2026 — The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), supported by the Wazalendo, successfully repelled an attack by AFC/M23 rebels in Kalinga, Banamulema (Kisimba group), Walikale territory, North Kivu, on the morning of Tuesday, February 3.
According to the administrative secretary of the Kisimba group, the attackers came from Mpety, considered one of the rebels’ main strongholds, aiming to expand their influence by seizing new positions.
The FARDC, aided by Wazalendo groups, resisted the assault, forcing the rebels to retreat towards Mpombi, in the Balinda area.
In retaliation, the rebels launched bombings in Kalinga, causing panic among civilians and prompting many residents to flee for safety.
Security sources confirm that Kalinga remains under the control of the FARDC and Wazalendo, though the situation remains tense in the combat zone.

excerpt_en: Uvira February 3, 2026 — The Congolese National Police (PNC) officially returned to the city of Uvira on Tuesday, February 3, after nearly two months of absence. This coastal town on Lake Tanganyika had been under the control of the AFC/M23 rebels. The police officers had previou
body_en:
Uvira February 3, 2026 — The Congolese National Police (PNC) officially returned to the city of Uvira on Tuesday, February 3, after nearly two months of absence. This coastal town on Lake Tanganyika had been under the control of the AFC/M23 rebels.
The police officers had previously crossed into Burundi as the rebels advanced. Representing a company of approximately 100 officers, they entered through the Kavimvira border post, between the Burundian town of Gatuma and Uvira, in the presence of numerous onlookers.
A parade was held, attended by the interim mayor of Uvira and his deputy, symbolizing the restoration of state authority following the rebel withdrawal under U.S. pressure.
“This is the return of the State. It was the army that came before; now the police, who ensure public order, are here. This confirms that state authority is returning and being reasserted,” declared Kyky Kifara, the interim mayor of Uvira.
He also urged residents to reflect on past behavior: “What we were before the aggression must not be what we will become. Uvira has suffered greatly; it is being watched. We must be role models,” he added.
Following the AFC/M23 withdrawal, the army immediately began redeploying in Uvira and surrounding areas.
Uvira is the second-largest city in South Kivu after Bukavu, and during the rebel occupation, it had temporarily assumed the role of provincial capital, with provincial institutions transferred to the city.

body_en:
Rutshuru February 3, 2026 — Fighting erupted early Tuesday morning, February 3, between AFC/M23 rebels and Wazalendo forces in Kivuma and Kanyangohe, two locations in the Bwito chiefdom (Rutshuru territory) of North Kivu.
The rebels, coming from the town of Mweso in neighboring Masisi territory, targeted these areas, located about five kilometers from this strategic town.
Reports indicate the AFC/M23 launched simultaneous attacks against Wazalendo positions on the hills overlooking Kivuma and Kanyangohe, aiming to dislodge them, but their offensive was unsuccessful.
After several hours of intense fighting, the rebels retreated to Mweso, their point of origin.
These clashes have caused massive civilian displacements, worsening the already dire humanitarian situation in the region. Many families fled their villages, seeking refuge in Mweso, Muhongozi, and other locations.
Local humanitarian sources report that the number of displaced people is increasing daily, with many families living in classrooms under precarious conditions, lacking adequate food, healthcare, and protection.

title: AFC/M23 Claims Attack on Army Drone Command Center
excerpt: Kisangani Airport February 4, 2026 — The AFC/M23 rebel group claimed responsibility Tuesday for the weekend attack on Bangboka Airport, located 17 kilometers from Kisangani, capital of Tshopo province. This airport, a key site within the national security apparatus and home to th
title_en: AFC/M23 Claims Attack on Army Drone Command Center
excerpt_en: Kisangani Airport February 4, 2026 — The AFC/M23 rebel group claimed responsibility Tuesday for the weekend attack on Bangboka Airport, located 17 kilometers from Kisangani, capital of Tshopo province. This airport, a key site within the national security apparatus and home to th
body_en:
Kisangani Airport February 4, 2026 — The AFC/M23 rebel group claimed responsibility Tuesday for the weekend attack on Bangboka Airport, located 17 kilometers from Kisangani, capital of Tshopo province. This airport, a key site within the national security apparatus and home to the Third Defense Zone headquarters, was targeted between Saturday, January 31, and Sunday, February 1, 2026, using “kamikaze drones.”
The rebel movement claims to have destroyed the drone command center at Kisangani airport, from which the Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC) launch operations in Masisi, Walikale, Rutshuru, Lubero, Kalehe, Mwenga, and Minembwe.
Provincial authorities had previously accused the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebels of the attacks.
Corneille Nangaa, political coordinator of AFC/M23, justified the operation, accusing the Kinshasa government of orchestrating a “surge of violence” using Sukhoi-23 aircraft, combat drones, and coalition forces. He warned:
“The monopoly on technological terror is definitively broken. The air superiority upon which Tshisekedi's strategy was based is now obsolete. From now on, any air force deployed against the populations of the liberated zones will be neutralized at its source.”
Nangaa added that the attack marks the end of Kisangani as a rear base for the FARDC, stating:
“The doctrine of preemptive defense is activated: every threat will be struck at its point of origin… If Tshisekedi wants dialogue, we are open to it, but if he wants war, let him accept all the consequences.”
While the AFC/M23 claims to have destroyed the drone command center, authorities confirmed that, thanks to the vigilance of the FARDC and security partners, eight drones were neutralized before reaching their target. No casualties or major material damage were reported. The Tshopo provincial government reiterated that “this attack demonstrates, once again, Rwanda’s intention to undermine the Washington peace agreement.”
These attacks caused spontaneous displacement of residents near Bangboka Airport.
This escalation coincides with the February 2, 2026 signing in Doha of the ICGLR-backed mandate between the DRC government and AFC/M23, following a meeting of the ceasefire monitoring and verification mechanism, organized by Qatar as part of ongoing mediation efforts to resolve the conflict in eastern DRC.

The rebel movement claims to have destroyed the drone command center at Kisangani airport, from which the Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC) launch operations in Masisi, Walikale, Rutshuru, Lubero, Kalehe, Mwenga, and Minembwe.
Provincial authorities had previously accused the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebels of the attacks.
Corneille Nangaa, political coordinator of AFC/M23, justified the operation, accusing the Kinshasa government of orchestrating a “surge of violence” using Sukhoi-23 aircraft, combat drones, and coalition forces. He warned:
“The monopoly on technological terror is definitively broken. The air superiority upon which Tshisekedi's strategy was based is now obsolete. From now on, any air force deployed against the populations of the liberated zones will be neutralized at its source.”
Nangaa added that the attack marks the end of Kisangani as a rear base for the FARDC, stating:
“The doctrine of preemptive defense is activated: every threat will be struck at its point of origin… If Tshisekedi wants dialogue, we are open to it, but if he wants war, let him accept all the consequences.”
While the AFC/M23 claims to have destroyed the drone command center, authorities confirmed that, thanks to the vigilance of the FARDC and security partners, eight drones were neutralized before reaching their target. No casualties or major material damage were reported. The Tshopo provincial government reiterated that “this attack demonstrates, once again, Rwanda’s intention to undermine the Washington peace agreement.”
These attacks caused spontaneous displacement of residents near Bangboka Airport.
This escalation coincides with the February 2, 2026 signing in Doha of the ICGLR-backed mandate between the DRC government and AFC/M23, following a meeting of the ceasefire monitoring and verification mechanism, organized by Qatar as part of ongoing mediation efforts to resolve the conflict in eastern DRC.
