excerpt: Panu February 16, 2026 – Idiofa, Kwilu Province – The Kikwit Garrison Military Court handed down eight death sentences, including that of Mayor Xénon Mufele of the semi-rural commune of Panu, following deadly clashes on February 3, 2026. Two other defendants were acquitted and re
title_en: Eight Sentenced to Death, Including Mayor, Two Acquitted
excerpt_en: Panu February 16, 2026 – Idiofa, Kwilu Province – The Kikwit Garrison Military Court handed down eight death sentences, including that of Mayor Xénon Mufele of the semi-rural commune of Panu, following deadly clashes on February 3, 2026. Two other defendants were acquitted and re
body_en:
Panu February 16, 2026 – Idiofa, Kwilu Province – The Kikwit Garrison Military Court handed down eight death sentences, including that of Mayor Xénon Mufele of the semi-rural commune of Panu, following deadly clashes on February 3, 2026. Two other defendants were acquitted and released.
The court found the eight convicted individuals guilty of terrorism, rejecting any mitigating circumstances. In addition to the death penalty, each must pay US$25,000 to the eight civil parties, including General Angel Yanbgonga, Deputy Divisional Commissioner of Police for Kwilu, who will receive US$5,000 from each convicted person. A further 100,000 Congolese francs per person must be paid within eight days to cover court costs.
The clashes erupted early on February 3, after police arrested two suspected bandits, prompting gang members to seize them from custody. Four people, including two police officers, were killed during the violence.
The military prosecutor had requested the death penalty for all defendants, while also calling for the acquittal of Kibala Chadrac, a request partially upheld by the court.

title: Washington Warns of Potential Sanctions Against Kigali
excerpt: DRC-Rwanda February 17, 2026 – The United States has indicated that the agreement between Rwanda and the DRC signed in Washington “is only a starting point” and not the ultimate solution, according to Massad Boulos, Africa advisor to former President Donald Trump. His remarks cam
title_en: Washington Warns of Potential Sanctions Against Kigali
excerpt_en: DRC-Rwanda February 17, 2026 – The United States has indicated that the agreement between Rwanda and the DRC signed in Washington “is only a starting point” and not the ultimate solution, according to Massad Boulos, Africa advisor to former President Donald Trump. His remarks cam
body_en:
DRC-Rwanda February 17, 2026 – The United States has indicated that the agreement between Rwanda and the DRC signed in Washington “is only a starting point” and not the ultimate solution, according to Massad Boulos, Africa advisor to former President Donald Trump. His remarks came during a February 16 interview on France 24, amid renewed fighting on the ground.
Boulos stressed that the Washington agreement is complementary to the Doha process, led by Qatar with US and EU support, which focuses specifically on the M23-DRC conflict. He acknowledged a “serious violation” of the Washington agreement following the capture of Uvira by M23 rebels, reportedly backed by Rwanda. While fighters withdrew, some positions around the city remain under rebel control.
Regarding sanctions, the US official indicated that Washington has “a number of tools” available and could implement measures against President Paul Kagame or other actors. Targeted sanctions have previously been applied to individuals, including James Kabarebe, for conflict-related activities.
Speaking in Kigali at the opening of the “Umushyikirano” national dialogue, Kagame blamed tensions on Rwandan Hutu rebels from the FDLR operating in Congolese territory and denied involvement in M23 operations, mineral exploitation, or territorial ambitions.
UN and US reports, however, continue to allege Rwandan military support to M23, with the UN Security Council calling on Kigali to cease all support and withdraw troops from the DRC. Washington continues to engage Kigali, awaiting “concrete measures on the battlefield” to verify compliance with commitments.

title: EU Commissioner Hadja Lahbib Launches Humanitarian Mission in DRC Amid Escalating Crisis
excerpt: Great Lakes Region February 17, 2026 – Kinshasa, DRC – The European Commissioner for Crisis Preparedness, Management, and Equality, Hadja Lahbib, has begun a humanitarian mission to the Great Lakes region, starting in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The visit comes amid persist
title_en: EU Commissioner Hadja Lahbib Launches Humanitarian Mission in DRC Amid Escalating Crisis
excerpt_en: Great Lakes Region February 17, 2026 – Kinshasa, DRC – The European Commissioner for Crisis Preparedness, Management, and Equality, Hadja Lahbib, has begun a humanitarian mission to the Great Lakes region, starting in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The visit comes amid persist
body_en:
Great Lakes Region February 17, 2026 – Kinshasa, DRC – The European Commissioner for Crisis Preparedness, Management, and Equality, Hadja Lahbib, has begun a humanitarian mission to the Great Lakes region, starting in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The visit comes amid persistent violence in eastern DRC, fueled by the activities of Rwandan-backed ADF/M23 rebels, which has caused massive displacement across South Kivu and neighboring countries.
During her mission, Lahbib plans to meet all parties to the conflict to advocate for improved humanitarian access, ensure the opening of safe corridors, and maintain essential services, including health care, even in areas controlled by armed groups. She will also visit refugee camps, including the largest Congolese camp in Bujumbura, Burundi, which hosts over 70,000 people.
“I have just arrived in the Democratic Republic of Congo, the first stop on my mission to the Great Lakes region. My absolute priority is to negotiate access and humanitarian deliveries. In the East, the situation is critical, with a dramatic humanitarian crisis. Lives must be saved,” Lahbib stated on her Twitter account.
The visit highlights a critical funding shortfall for humanitarian operations in DRC, forcing aid agencies to prioritize resources for only 7.3 million people out of nearly 15 million in urgent need. The European Union, alongside its member states, remains a key donor, providing emergency aid to save lives, prevent suffering, and preserve dignity in areas affected by conflict or disaster.
This humanitarian mission follows government-led efforts by Minister of State Ève Bazaiba Masudi, who recently visited Burundi and Tanzania to support Congolese refugees, coordinate aid, and assess conditions in collaboration with UNHCR and other partners. Lahbib’s mission underscores the urgency of international solidarity to address one of the world’s longest-running and most neglected humanitarian crises, exacerbated by continued rebel activity and recent territorial gains by AFC/M23 in Uvira and surrounding towns.

excerpt_en: February 18, 2026 – North Kivu, DRC – The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reported that armed clashes in Masisi, Rutshuru, and Walikale territories in January 2026 claimed nearly 100 civilian lives, left many wounded, and caused large-scale populatio
body_en:
February 18, 2026 – North Kivu, DRC – The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reported that armed clashes in Masisi, Rutshuru, and Walikale territories in January 2026 claimed nearly 100 civilian lives, left many wounded, and caused large-scale population displacement. The violence involved AFC/M23 rebels and Wazalendo militias aligned with the Congolese army.
Between January 12 and 16, fighting engulfed over a dozen villages in the Bukombo, Kihondo, Mutanda, Bambo, and Tongo groups within the Bwito chiefdom (Rutshuru territory), killing approximately 50 civilians. Displaced populations fled to Bukombo-centre, Ihula, Nyanzale, Kikuku-centre, and Katsiru, while others sought refuge in Mweso and Kitchanga (Masisi territory).
OCHA also noted renewed clashes in Nyamaboko 1 and 2 villages in Masisi and Katoyi Health Zones, further displacing civilians. An army airstrike on January 2 in Masisi-Centre reportedly killed 11 people, injured around 40 others, and destroyed the office of an international NGO.
In Walikale, drone strikes between January 19 and 30 targeted hills overlooking Kasopo, Buleusa (Ikobo group), Mpety, Mindjenje, and Chanjikiro (Kisimba group), leading to mass displacement. Residents of Mpombi and Iteya were forced to flee on January 21 due to escalating clashes, while healthcare access deteriorated as several health facilities were looted or damaged. The Pinga General Referral Hospital reported critical shortages of medicines, equipment, and medical staff.
Adding to the humanitarian toll, a landslide in Burutsi killed at least 30 people, buried homes, and severed the Kashebere Mungazi–Kibua road, the only link to central Walikale.
OCHA’s report underscores the ongoing insecurity, displacement, and disruption of essential services in eastern DRC, emphasizing the urgent need for humanitarian assistance and civilian protection in North Kivu.

title: Armed Men Loot Teachers’ Salaries in Shabunda
excerpt: February 18, 2026 – Shabunda, South Kivu, DRC – Armed assailants targeted a convoy transporting teachers’ salaries for multiple schools in the Shabunda 8 subdivision, specifically in the village of Mungole, on the Shabunda–Centre–Makese road, stealing funds and other valuables. L
title_en: Armed Men Loot Teachers’ Salaries in Shabunda

body_en:
February 18, 2026 – Shabunda, South Kivu, DRC – Armed assailants targeted a convoy transporting teachers’ salaries for multiple schools in the Shabunda 8 subdivision, specifically in the village of Mungole, on the Shabunda–Centre–Makese road, stealing funds and other valuables.
Local civil society sources reported that the attack occurred about one kilometer from Shabunda Centre, with a school principal among the victims. Salaries for teachers at Kigulube Primary School, Un Point Primary School, Kamika Primary School, and Kiseku Primary School were taken, totaling approximately 13 million Congolese francs.
In addition to teachers’ salaries, the assailants also seized money belonging to a businessman, as well as cell phones and personal belongings of other residents traveling with the convoy.
The administrator of Shabunda territory, Raphaël Konga Konga, confirmed the incident and called on security services to apprehend the perpetrators and ensure they face justice.
This robbery highlights the ongoing insecurity in South Kivu, disrupting the delivery of essential public services and threatening education in the region.

title: Wazalendo Militiamen Imposing Illegal Taxes on Displaced Populations in Musienene
excerpt: February 19, 2026 – Musienene, Lubero, North Kivu, DRC – Civil society organizations in Musienene, the main town of the Baswagha chiefdom, are sounding the alarm over the harassment of displaced populations by Wazalendo militiamen. Residents report being forced to pay illegal tax
title_en: Wazalendo Militiamen Imposing Illegal Taxes on Displaced Populations in Musienene
excerpt_en: February 19, 2026 – Musienene, Lubero, North Kivu, DRC – Civil society organizations in Musienene, the main town of the Baswagha chiefdom, are sounding the alarm over the harassment of displaced populations by Wazalendo militiamen. Residents report being forced to pay illegal tax
body_en:
February 19, 2026 – Musienene, Lubero, North Kivu, DRC – Civil society organizations in Musienene, the main town of the Baswagha chiefdom, are sounding the alarm over the harassment of displaced populations by Wazalendo militiamen.
Residents report being forced to pay illegal taxes for activities such as charcoal production, with amounts ranging from 5,000 Congolese francs to 10 US dollars per batch. Affected communities include Vikindwe, Vulimira, Kirirya, Mutiri, and surrounding areas.
Kambale Maboko Fanuel, president of Musienene civil society, highlighted that these demands hinder the livelihoods of displaced people and even impact host families. He urged political and administrative authorities to intervene to halt these abusive practices.
Similar illegal taxation reportedly targets sawyers and timber traders, further disrupting local economic activity.
Civil society notes that displaced residents had previously issued a 48-hour ultimatum to Wazalendo fighters to leave their areas of origin, citing the militia’s actions as the main cause of their displacement. The appeal was delivered during a meeting at the ESCO field in Butembo, led by representatives from the Mwenye civil society and the New Congolese Civil Society (NSCC).
Abuses by Wazalendo-affiliated militiamen in the region reportedly include looting, harassment, sexual violence, arbitrary arrests, unauthorized roadblocks, and the illegal collection of taxes, which have become recurrent in the Baswagha chiefdom and Musienene.
Civil society continues to call for exclusive control by the Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC) to restore peace and security in the area.

title: Humanitarian Access Severely Restricted as 78,500 Displaced People Face Multi-Sectoral Needs
excerpt: February 19, 2026 – Djugu, Ituri, DRC – The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reports that humanitarian access remains severely limited in Bule and surrounding villages in the Djugu territory, where repeated armed clashes continue to disrup
title_en: Humanitarian Access Severely Restricted as 78,500 Displaced People Face Multi-Sectoral Needs
excerpt_en: February 19, 2026 – Djugu, Ituri, DRC – The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reports that humanitarian access remains severely limited in Bule and surrounding villages in the Djugu territory, where repeated armed clashes continue to disrup
body_en:
February 19, 2026 – Djugu, Ituri, DRC – The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reports that humanitarian access remains severely limited in Bule and surrounding villages in the Djugu territory, where repeated armed clashes continue to disrupt civilian life.
Over 78,500 displaced persons, along with host communities, face urgent needs across multiple sectors, including food, education, water, sanitation, hygiene, and shelter, according to a rapid multi-sectoral assessment conducted by the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) in January 2026.
The report highlights that the use of school buildings as emergency shelters has left more than 60 schools non-functional since December 2025, depriving over 24,000 children of education.
Many displaced individuals have sought refuge in neighboring territories of Mahagi and Irumu, including the Plaine Savo displacement site, placing significant pressure on already limited social services. Since December 2025, approximately 37,000 displaced people from Djugu have arrived in the Logo, Rimba, and Kambala health zones in Mahagi, primarily hosted by local families.
Protection concerns are mounting, with reports of arbitrary arrests, illegal fines, thefts, and kidnappings. On January 21, at least ten children were abducted in the Rabu health area by members of an armed group.
The humanitarian crisis in Ituri is exacerbated by persistent insecurity, massive population displacement, epidemics such as measles and Mpox, and the impact of natural disasters. Armed groups, including the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) and the Convention for the People’s Revolution (CRP) led by Thomas Lubanga, continue to operate in the region. The ADF, active for nearly three decades and pledged to the Islamic State, has forced thousands to flee despite joint Congolese-Ugandan military operations.
OCHA warns that the combination of armed violence, intercommunal tensions, and displacement has created a protracted humanitarian crisis in Ituri, requiring urgent international and local support to meet the basic needs of affected populations.

title: Ten Young People Arrested by AFC/M23 Rebels in Kalembe and Kalonge
excerpt: February 20, 2026 – North Kivu, DRC – AFC/M23 rebels arrested a dozen young people overnight from February 19 to 20 in Kalembe and Kalonge, towns on the border between the Masisi and Walikale territories, according to local sources. The youths are accused of collaborating with th
title_en: Ten Young People Arrested by AFC/M23 Rebels in Kalembe and Kalonge
excerpt_en: February 20, 2026 – North Kivu, DRC – AFC/M23 rebels arrested a dozen young people overnight from February 19 to 20 in Kalembe and Kalonge, towns on the border between the Masisi and Walikale territories, according to local sources. The youths are accused of collaborating with th
body_en:
February 20, 2026 – North Kivu, DRC – AFC/M23 rebels arrested a dozen young people overnight from February 19 to 20 in Kalembe and Kalonge, towns on the border between the Masisi and Walikale territories, according to local sources.
The youths are accused of collaborating with the Wazalendo groups, which are active in several areas of North Kivu. Sources report that the arrests were carried out through a cordon and search operation, with the young people taken from their homes during the night and transported to an unknown location.
Families of the detainees have reported no news since the arrests, expressing deep concern over the youths’ fate. “We don’t know where they’ve been taken or the precise charges against them,” said a relative of one of the arrested individuals.
Local security and administrative authorities in Walikale confirmed the arrests but provided no details on the exact number of detainees, charges, or detention sites. AFC/M23 officials have yet to comment on the operation.
The arrests occur amid a tense security environment, marked by ongoing clashes between various armed groups in the region. Among residents, the operation has heightened fear, as accusations of collaboration are often difficult to verify and may be used to exert pressure on local youth.
Families and community leaders are calling for transparency and urgent information regarding the fate of those detained, as the region continues to grapple with persistent insecurity and instability.

title: European Commissioner Hadja Lahbib Arrives in Goma Amid Humanitarian Briefings
excerpt: February 20, 2026 – Goma, North Kivu, DRC – The European Commissioner for Equality, Preparedness and Crisis Management, Hadja Lahbib, arrived in Goma today as part of her tour of the Great Lakes region, focusing on humanitarian and protection issues. The morning began with a brie
title_en: European Commissioner Hadja Lahbib Arrives in Goma Amid Humanitarian Briefings
excerpt_en: February 20, 2026 – Goma, North Kivu, DRC – The European Commissioner for Equality, Preparedness and Crisis Management, Hadja Lahbib, arrived in Goma today as part of her tour of the Great Lakes region, focusing on humanitarian and protection issues. The morning began with a brie
body_en:
February 20, 2026 – Goma, North Kivu, DRC – The European Commissioner for Equality, Preparedness and Crisis Management, Hadja Lahbib, arrived in Goma today as part of her tour of the Great Lakes region, focusing on humanitarian and protection issues.
The morning began with a briefing on the humanitarian access situation with INSO and OCHA at the ECHO office, followed by meetings with national organizations addressing protection concerns in the city.
Commissioner Lahbib also visited Ndosho Hospital, supported by the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), where she was briefed on the surgical response, trends in injuries treated, and toured critical care units, including a confidential discussion with two patients.
A working lunch was held with humanitarian partners, including international NGOs and UN representatives, to discuss coordination and operational challenges.
Later in the afternoon, the commissioner is scheduled to meet with AFC/M23 representatives to emphasize humanitarian access concerns and discuss the potential reopening of Goma airport. Lahbib visited Rwanda the previous day as part of her regional mission.
This visit underscores the urgent need for improved humanitarian access in eastern DRC, where ongoing conflict continues to affect civilians and disrupt essential services.

body_en:
February 20, 2026 – Rutshuru, North Kivu, DRC – An MSF (Médecins Sans Frontières) convoy carrying medical supplies was attacked on Wednesday, February 18, by armed men in Matin ya Moto, within Virunga National Park in the Rutshuru territory. title: Divergent Views on the Humanitarian Situation in Eastern DRC
excerpt: February 21, 2026 – Goma, North Kivu, DRC – The humanitarian crisis in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo is being framed in starkly contrasting terms by two key actors. Hadja Lahbib, European Commissioner for Crisis Preparedness, Management, and Equality, described the situati
title_en: Divergent Views on the Humanitarian Situation in Eastern DRC
excerpt_en: February 21, 2026 – Goma, North Kivu, DRC – The humanitarian crisis in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo is being framed in starkly contrasting terms by two key actors. Hadja Lahbib, European Commissioner for Crisis Preparedness, Management, and Equality, described the situati
body_en:
February 21, 2026 – Goma, North Kivu, DRC – The humanitarian crisis in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo is being framed in starkly contrasting terms by two key actors. Hadja Lahbib, European Commissioner for Crisis Preparedness, Management, and Equality, described the situation as “catastrophic” after her regional tour, while Corneille Nangaa, political coordinator of the AFC/M23, portrayed territories under his control as “the most secure area in the country.”
Hadja Lahbib’s Assessment
During her tour of the DRC, Burundi, and Rwanda, Commissioner Lahbib highlighted severe humanitarian challenges:
Over 21 million people in eastern DRC require emergency aid.
Nearly 28 million people face food insecurity.
Violence continues to cause repeated displacement, human rights violations, conflict-related sexual violence, and disease outbreaks.
Refugee flows into neighboring countries, particularly Burundi, strain limited resources.
Lahbib stressed the urgent need to improve humanitarian access, open safe corridors, and ensure the continuation of basic services.
Corneille Nangaa’s Perspective
In contrast, Nangaa claimed that areas controlled by the AFC/M23 constitute the most secure regions of eastern DRC. He cited:
Territories under his control cover 62,000 km², hosting around 20 million Congolese.
He rejects notions of foreign occupation, asserting, “We are not Rwandans, we are in Congo. A territory cannot be occupied by its own citizens.”
Nangaa pledged that humanitarian access will be guaranteed within M23-controlled zones.
He indicated that catastrophic situations are concentrated in Minembwe, Uvira, Beni, and Ituri, highlighting ongoing attacks and massacres outside his areas of influence.
Conflict Data Highlights
Despite Nangaa’s claims, available data shows continued violence across the region:
Uvira and Fizi plateaus: FARDC, supported by Burundi’s FDNB, launched offensives against M23 positions; Twirwaneho-M23-Red Tabara coalition engaged in multiple clashes.
North Kivu: 52 of 113 clashes documented in January occurred here; Rutshuru, Masisi, and Walikale saw heavy fighting.
Civilians targeted: Drone strikes, grenade attacks, and armed sweeps resulted in dozens of deaths, including in Mpombi, Kirumba, Sange, and other villages.
Uvira recapture: January 2026 operations by FARDC and Wazalendo led to at least 151 civilian deaths.
Refugee crisis: Tens of thousands of Congolese fled to Burundi, exacerbating humanitarian needs.
Analysis
The conflicting narratives underscore a diffuse conflict with no clearly demarcated front lines. While the European Commission emphasizes a dire humanitarian emergency, the AFC/M23 stresses relative security within its territories. Ground reports, however, indicate ongoing violence, civilian casualties, and displacement, casting doubt on claims of stability.
The situation highlights the complexity of eastern DRC: a multi-layered conflict involving government forces, local armed groups, and rebel coalitions, with civilians disproportionately affected.

body_en:
South Kivu, February 21, 2026 – Residents of Kavumu and surrounding areas in the Kabare territory are living in fear following exchanges of fire between AFC/M23 rebels and the Wazalendo.
The fighting began in the morning, briefly subsided, and then resumed in the evening. Locals reported hearing gunfire from as far as Katana to Kavumu.
In the evening, clashes reportedly resumed around 6:30 p.m., coinciding with a noticeable reinforcement of Wazalendo forces near the shopping center.
The violence disrupted traffic along the main road linking Bukavu to Kavumu, forcing residents to stay indoors as combatants positioned weapons along key routes.
Authorities have yet to release official statements, but local communities remain on high alert amid the tensions.

body_en:
Kavumu, South Kivu, February 22, 2026 – The security situation in Kavumu, Kabare territory, remains chaotic after new clashes erupted on Sunday morning between AFC/M23 elements and the Wazalendo.
The exchanges of fire, which began around 5:00 a.m., have paralyzed daily activities in the town and surrounding areas. Residents have stayed indoors, churches remain empty, and public transportation has been disrupted.
Markets, shops, and businesses have been closed since the early hours, while local communities continue to live in fear amid the ongoing tensions.
These clashes follow days of violence in the Kabare territory, with confrontations between the warring parties first intensifying on Friday.

title: DRC and South Africa Discuss Revision of 2004 Military Agreement
excerpt: Kinshasa–Pretoria, February 22, 2026 – The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defense and Veterans Affairs of the Democratic Republic of Congo, Guy Kabombo Muadiamvita, is on an official mission to South Africa to strengthen military cooperation between the two countr
title_en: DRC and South Africa Discuss Revision of 2004 Military Agreement
excerpt_en: Kinshasa–Pretoria, February 22, 2026 – The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defense and Veterans Affairs of the Democratic Republic of Congo, Guy Kabombo Muadiamvita, is on an official mission to South Africa to strengthen military cooperation between the two countr
body_en:
Kinshasa–Pretoria, February 22, 2026 – The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defense and Veterans Affairs of the Democratic Republic of Congo, Guy Kabombo Muadiamvita, is on an official mission to South Africa to strengthen military cooperation between the two countries.
During his participation in the 71st anniversary of the South African Army on February 21, 2026, he met with his South African counterpart, Angie Motshekga, to discuss the revision of the 2004 military agreement that governs bilateral defense collaboration. Both ministers agreed to adopt resolutions based on the work of sectoral experts from each country.
This diplomatic engagement follows South Africa's decision to withdraw its troop contribution from the United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUSCO). With over 700 soldiers deployed, South Africa has been among the top ten troop-contributing countries to the mission.
According to the South African Presidency, President Cyril Ramaphosa stated that the withdrawal aims to reorient resources of the South African National Defence Force after 27 years of support for peacekeeping in the DRC. The process of withdrawal is expected to be completed by the end of 2026, in collaboration with the UN.
Bilateral cooperation between Kinshasa and Pretoria has intensified in recent years. In July 2023, Presidents Félix Tshisekedi and Cyril Ramaphosa reaffirmed their commitment to strengthen security, economic development, infrastructure, agriculture, and other sectors. On the military front, South Africa deployed 2,900 troops to the DRC from December 2023 to December 2024 under Operation SAMIDRC, investing over 2 billion rand (≈ US$134 million) to support peace and security in the eastern provinces.
The 2004 General Cooperation Agreement remains the framework guiding bilateral relations, providing a foundation for enhanced military and strategic collaboration along the Kinshasa-Pretoria axis.

title: Fragile Calm After Clashes Between AFC/M23 Rebels and Wazalendo in Buhaya and Fungura
excerpt: Walikale, North Kivu, February 23, 2026 – A relative calm has returned to the Buhaya and Fungura mountains, near Katobi in the Banakindi area of Walikale territory, following two days of intense fighting between AFC/M23 rebels and the Wazalendo. The hostilities erupted despite a

excerpt_en: Walikale, North Kivu, February 23, 2026 – A relative calm has returned to the Buhaya and Fungura mountains, near Katobi in the Banakindi area of Walikale territory, following two days of intense fighting between AFC/M23 rebels and the Wazalendo. The hostilities erupted despite a
body_en:
Walikale, North Kivu, February 23, 2026 – A relative calm has returned to the Buhaya and Fungura mountains, near Katobi in the Banakindi area of Walikale territory, following two days of intense fighting between AFC/M23 rebels and the Wazalendo.
The hostilities erupted despite a ceasefire proposed by Angola as part of regional efforts to curb persistent insecurity in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
The rebels launched simultaneous offensives on the strategic heights of Buhaya and Fungura, which overlook Katobi village and serve as key security positions for Pinga, a town frequently targeted by armed incursions.
After fierce exchanges of fire, the Wazalendo reportedly contained the rebel advance, forcing AFC/M23 fighters to retreat toward Mpety, considered their main stronghold in the area.
Many residents of Katobi fled into surrounding forests for safety. Despite the lull observed on Monday morning, the displaced population has yet to return, fearing a resumption of fighting.
The situation on the ground remains volatile, with local communities living in uncertainty amid a resurgence of armed violence in Walikale territory.

title: Gatumba-Kavimvira Border Crossing Reopens After Two Months
excerpt: Uvira–Gatumba, February 23, 2026 – The border crossing between Uvira in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Gatumba in Burundi officially reopened this Monday, more than two months after being closed due to the AFC/M23 conflict. The closure, imposed by Burundi following the occu
title_en: Gatumba-Kavimvira Border Crossing Reopens After Two Months
excerpt_en: Uvira–Gatumba, February 23, 2026 – The border crossing between Uvira in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Gatumba in Burundi officially reopened this Monday, more than two months after being closed due to the AFC/M23 conflict. The closure, imposed by Burundi following the occu
body_en:
Uvira–Gatumba, February 23, 2026 – The border crossing between Uvira in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Gatumba in Burundi officially reopened this Monday, more than two months after being closed due to the AFC/M23 conflict.
The closure, imposed by Burundi following the occupation of Uvira by AFC/M23 rebels, disrupted trade and travel between the two countries. No official ceremony marked the reopening, but both sides agreed to allow free passage for travelers.
The head of migration services in Kavimvira (DRC), after discussions with the Burundian Commissioner General of Migration, Maurice Mbonimpa, emphasized that standard migration formalities—including visas and necessary documents—remain mandatory. The border will operate daily from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.
The reopening brought relief to residents and traders on both sides. A Congolese trader said, “I do small-scale trading in Uvira, go to Luvumera in Bujumbura to buy goods, and today I can return as usual. We thank our authorities and those of Burundi for listening to our pleas.”
Burundian citizens expressed similar satisfaction. One resident commented, “The reopening of the border is a huge relief for most of us. Our lives depend on our brotherly and friendly countries.”
The reopening was announced in Uvira on Sunday by the Governor of South Kivu, Jean-Jacques Purusi Sadiki, signaling a step toward restoring normalcy after the recent conflict-induced disruptions.

body_en:
Masisi, North Kivu, February 23, 2026 – Violent fighting erupted on Sunday, February 22, between AFC/M23 rebels and Wazalendo fighters in the villages of Kasenyi, Chugi, and Kinigi, located in the Bahunde chiefdom of Masisi territory, near the mining town of Rubaya.
The Wazalendo successfully regained control of the three villages, which had been considered strategic positions for the AFC/M23 rebels due to the economic and security significance of the area. The proximity to Rubaya, known for its mining activities, underscores the importance of these localities in the military strategy of the warring parties.
During the clashes, several rebel fighters were reportedly captured, and weapons and ammunition were recovered by the Wazalendo. In response, the AFC/M23 reinforced their positions on the Sita hill, aiming to contain the advance and attempt to retake Chugi and Kinigi.
The AFC/M23 denounced the government coalition’s violation of the ceasefire and reported drone strikes in several areas of the Masisi territory.
On Monday, February 23, a fragile calm prevailed along the front line, but the situation remains volatile, with residents fearing a resumption of fighting in a region already weakened by months of insecurity.

title: AFC/M23 Reinforces Positions in Mpety and Mindjendje, Raising Concerns Around Pinga
excerpt: Walikale, North Kivu, February 23, 2026 – The security situation in the Walikale territory remains worrying as AFC/M23 rebels reinforced their positions on Sunday, February 22, in the villages of Mpety and Mindjendje, located in the Banakindi area (Kisimba group). According to lo
title_en: AFC/M23 Reinforces Positions in Mpety and Mindjendje, Raising Concerns Around Pinga
excerpt_en: Walikale, North Kivu, February 23, 2026 – The security situation in the Walikale territory remains worrying as AFC/M23 rebels reinforced their positions on Sunday, February 22, in the villages of Mpety and Mindjendje, located in the Banakindi area (Kisimba group). According to lo
body_en:
Walikale, North Kivu, February 23, 2026 – The security situation in the Walikale territory remains worrying as AFC/M23 rebels reinforced their positions on Sunday, February 22, in the villages of Mpety and Mindjendje, located in the Banakindi area (Kisimba group).
According to local authorities, the reinforcements came from the Kitshanga-Kalembe axis, with columns of heavily armed men moving through Kalembe toward Mpety, a development confirmed by security sources in Walikale.
While the exact objective of these movements is unclear, observers suggest that the rebels could be preparing offensives against FARDC and Wazalendo positions, particularly near the strategic town of Pinga.
The situation has alarmed local communities, already strained by recent clashes in the area. Traditional authorities of the Kisimba group denounce what they describe as a violation of the ceasefire and urge the Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC) and Wazalendo fighters to remain vigilant.
Amid a regional context of persistent instability, the civilian population fears a further escalation of violence, which could trigger more displacement and worsen the humanitarian situation in this already fragile part of Walikale territory.
Conclusion
The period from February 8 to 23, 2026, underscores the Democratic Republic of Congo’s position at a critical juncture, marked by a delicate balance between diplomatic engagement, economic ambition, and persistent humanitarian and security challenges.
Diplomatically and politically, the DRC is actively engaging regional and continental partners to stabilize its eastern provinces. President Félix Tshisekedi’s discussions in Luanda with Angolan and African Union leaders, alongside the acceptance of a regional ceasefire scheduled for February 18, signal a commitment to dialogue. Yet, the process remains fragile: the AFC/M23 continues to denounce what it sees as “diplomatic fragmentation” and alleges ongoing government offensives, highlighting the tenuous nature of peace efforts.
Economically, progress is visible in the formalization of the extractive sector. The first legal artisanal gold exports from Haut-Katanga and the inaugural copper and cobalt shipment via the Lobito Atlantic Railway demonstrate tangible steps toward transparency, traceability, and integration into global markets. At the same time, structural challenges persist. The IMF identifies the public wage bill as a major fiscal risk, while institutional weaknesses and entrenched corruption—as reflected in the DRC’s continued low ranking on the Corruption Perceptions Index—threaten to undermine these gains.
Socially and judicially, reforms aim to strengthen the rule of law, notably through the training of 2,500 new magistrates and the prosecution of law enforcement abuses. Nonetheless, systemic deficiencies remain: regions such as Bulungu illustrate the deadly consequences of judicial inaction, with detainees languishing without trial.
On the security and humanitarian fronts, the situation remains acute. Despite the formal ceasefire, attacks by the ADF and clashes involving AFC/M23 and Wazalendo forces perpetuate instability. The resulting humanitarian crisis is severe, with over 21 million people in need of assistance and thousands displaced, facing critical shortages of food, water, and education.
In conclusion, the DRC is laying the foundations for long-term stability through international partnerships, governance reforms, and sectoral modernization. Yet the immediate well-being of its citizens remains precarious, constrained by corruption, fragile institutions, and unresolved conflict. The coming months will be pivotal in determining whether diplomatic, economic, and institutional initiatives can translate into sustainable peace and tangible prosperity for the Congolese people.
By Glad Musema
Jeff Buleli

title_en: Mali and China Strengthen Strategic Partnership for Development Projects
excerpt_en: Bamako, January 23, 2026 — Mali and China have reaffirmed their commitment to deepening bilateral cooperation, with a focus on accelerating key development projects. Mali’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Abdoulaye Diop, held a working meeting on Friday
body_en:
Bamako, January 23, 2026 — Mali and China have reaffirmed their commitment to deepening bilateral cooperation, with a focus on accelerating key development projects.
Mali’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Abdoulaye Diop, held a working meeting on Friday with the Chinese Ambassador to Mali, Li Xiang, as part of ongoing efforts to monitor and advance the bilateral cooperation portfolio.
During the talks, both sides stressed the importance of the rigorous implementation of priority projects under existing economic and technical cooperation agreements, particularly in solar energy, infrastructure and transportation, agricultural mechanization, and healthcare facility construction.
Minister Diop highlighted the Malian government’s strong commitment to economic development, emphasizing measures taken to ensure the secure and effective execution of development initiatives in a spirit of pragmatism and shared interests.
Both officials praised the strategic partnership between Mali and China and reaffirmed their determination to maintain regular monitoring of ongoing projects, in line with the shared vision of the Malian and Chinese presidents.

During the meeting, both officials strongly condemned what they described as the illegal intervention by the United States in Venezuela, which they said resulted in the kidnapping of President Nicolás Maduro, his wife, and caused numerous civilian and military casualties.

title_en: Malian Foreign Ministry Strengthens Staff Awareness
excerpt_en: Bamako, January 22, 2026 — On the occasion of World AIDS Day, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, in partnership with UNAIDS, organized an awareness and information session for its staff to deepen understanding of HIV/AIDS, promote responsible behavior,
body_en:
Bamako, January 22, 2026 — On the occasion of World AIDS Day, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, in partnership with UNAIDS, organized an awareness and information session for its staff to deepen understanding of HIV/AIDS, promote responsible behavior, and help reduce stigma.
The event was held under the chairmanship of Foreign Minister Abdoulaye Diop, with contributions from Dr. Marc Saba, UNAIDS Country Director in Mali, and Dr. Ichiaka Kone, National Executive Secretary for the Fight Against AIDS.
Minister Diop stated that HIV/AIDS remains a major public health challenge, despite progress in prevention, testing, and treatment, particularly affecting vulnerable groups such as youth, women, and children. He emphasized the need for a multisectoral and collective response, supported at the highest political level by President Assimi Goïta and the government.
He also highlighted the role of diplomacy in mobilizing partnerships and international cooperation, welcomed the establishment of a multinational UNAIDS office in Mali serving Burkina Faso and Niger, and urged ministry staff to act as ambassadors for awareness and responsible behavior.
The session featured a short awareness-raising performance, a roundtable discussion, and voluntary HIV testing.

title_en: Leadership Transition at Foreign Ministry General Secretariat
excerpt_en: Bamako, January 22, 2026 — A handover ceremony was held at the General Secretariat of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, marking the transition between Ambassador Moustapha Traoré, the new Secretary General, and Ambassador Seydou Coulibaly, the outgoin
body_en:
Bamako, January 22, 2026 — A handover ceremony was held at the General Secretariat of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, marking the transition between Ambassador Moustapha Traoré, the new Secretary General, and Ambassador Seydou Coulibaly, the outgoing Secretary General.
Following the ceremony, Foreign Minister Abdoulaye Diop received both diplomats in the presence of cabinet members, senior officials, directors, and department heads. The meeting provided an opportunity to express appreciation for their service, congratulate them on the confidence placed in them, and outline expectations for the future of Malian diplomacy amid geopolitical challenges and ongoing governance reforms.
Ambassador Traoré officially assumed his duties as Secretary General, while Ambassador Coulibaly departed for Luanda, Angola, to take up his new post as Head of the Malian Embassy.
Both diplomats reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening Malian diplomacy in the service of peace, security, and sustainable development, under the leadership of Minister Diop.

excerpt: Bamako, January 28, 2026 – Following the presentation of his credentials on January 26, 2026, to the Director-General of the United Nations Office at Geneva, His Excellency Mr. Sékou dit Gaoussou Cissé, Ambassador and Permanent Representative of the Republic of Mali to Geneva, co

body_en:
Bamako, January 28, 2026 – Following the presentation of his credentials on January 26, 2026, to the Director-General of the United Nations Office at Geneva, His Excellency Mr. Sékou dit Gaoussou Cissé, Ambassador and Permanent Representative of the Republic of Mali to Geneva, continued this diplomatic process on Wednesday, January 28, 2026, by presenting his credentials to Ms. Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, Director-General of the World Trade Organization (WTO).
During the meeting that followed the ceremony, Ambassador Cissé conveyed the warm greetings of the highest Malian authorities and reaffirmed his commitment to strengthening relations between Mali and the WTO, notably through active support for efforts to consolidate the multilateral trading system.
Advocating for the cotton sector, he drew attention to the massive subsidies granted by developed countries to their cotton industries, which he said distort competition to the detriment of producers in C4+ countries.
The Ambassador also highlighted the reforms undertaken by Mali under the Mali 2063 strategic vision, emphasizing progress in the structural transformation of the national economy, the digitization of public services, the fight against corruption, and the modernization of agriculture, aimed at developing industrial value chains.
In response, Ms. Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala welcomed the dynamic cooperation between the WTO and Mali, as well as within the broader C4+ framework, and reaffirmed the Organization’s commitment to supporting initiatives for cotton development, economic modernization, and trade facilitation.

title: Head of State Issues Directives to Mali’s Two New Ambassadors
excerpt: Koulouba, January 29, 2026 – The President of the Transition and Head of State, His Excellency General Assimi Goïta, received Mali’s two newly appointed ambassadors on Thursday, January 29, 2026, as they formally assumed their duties. They are Mr. Seydou Coulibaly, Ambassador Ext
title_en: Head of State Issues Directives to Mali’s Two New Ambassadors
excerpt_en: Koulouba, January 29, 2026 – The President of the Transition and Head of State, His Excellency General Assimi Goïta, received Mali’s two newly appointed ambassadors on Thursday, January 29, 2026, as they formally assumed their duties. They are Mr. Seydou Coulibaly, Ambassador Ext
body_en:
Koulouba, January 29, 2026 – The President of the Transition and Head of State, His Excellency General Assimi Goïta, received Mali’s two newly appointed ambassadors on Thursday, January 29, 2026, as they formally assumed their duties. They are Mr. Seydou Coulibaly, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to the Republic of Angola, and Brigadier General Boubacar Diallo, the new Ambassador of Mali to the Republic of Rwanda.
Following the audience, Mr. Seydou Coulibaly expressed his deep gratitude to the Head of State for the confidence placed in him. The discussions reviewed the national situation and explored prospects for strengthening bilateral relations between Mali and Angola, a country with which Mali maintains excellent political ties. The President of the Transition reaffirmed Angola’s strategic importance, recalling Mali’s long-standing commitment to peace, notably illustrated by the sacrifice of Alioune Blondin Bèye, former UN Special Representative.
The Head of State issued clear directives aimed at enhancing bilateral cooperation, while stressing the importance of protecting Malian nationals residing in Angola. He underscored that this diplomatic action must align with the guiding principles of Malian public policy: national sovereignty, respect for strategic choices, and defense of the population’s best interests. The Ambassador also stated that his mission would include informing Angolan authorities about Mali’s ongoing restructuring, the reforms underway, and the role of the Malian diaspora in nation-building.
For his part, Brigadier General Boubacar Diallo, Ambassador to the Republic of Rwanda, welcomed the renewed confidence of the Head of State and received specific instructions on his roadmap, particularly in the areas of security, economy, and diplomacy. The President emphasized Rwanda’s strategic importance on the regional and international stage, especially in security, innovation, and economic development.
Ambassador Diallo highlighted the need to strengthen bilateral cooperation, still in a consolidation phase, notably through the effective implementation of agreements signed under the Joint Cooperation Commission. He also stressed the importance of providing accurate and balanced information on Mali in the face of disinformation, and of promoting economic opportunities for Malian entrepreneurs.
These two meetings underscore the firm commitment of the highest authorities to revitalizing Mali’s diplomacy in the service of peace, development, and the defense of national interests.

Geneva, January 26, 2026 – His Excellency Mr. Sékou dit Gaoussou Cissé, Ambassador and Permanent Representative of the Republic of Mali to Geneva, presented his credentials to Ms. Tatiana Valovaya, Director-General of the United Nations Office at Geneva, at the Palais des Nations on Monday, January 26, 2026.
During the audience, the Malian diplomat conveyed the warm greetings of His Excellency General Assimi Goïta, President of the Transition and Head of State, and briefed the Director-General on the current national situation, highlighting the Government’s major efforts in territorial security and sustainable development, guided by a comprehensive strategic vision and clearly defined governance principles.
Ambassador Cissé also reaffirmed Mali’s firm commitment to multilateralism, the promotion of sovereignty and equality among states, the preservation of international peace and security, and the strengthening of constructive and pragmatic cooperation with the United Nations system.
For her part, Ms. Tatiana Valovaya reiterated the readiness of the United Nations Office at Geneva to support and assist Mali’s efforts, in line with the mandates and principles of the United Nations, of which Mali remains a committed member.

body_en:
Bamako, January 23, 2026 – As part of the operational monitoring of bilateral cooperation, His Excellency Mr. Abdoulaye Diop, Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, held a working meeting on Friday, January 23, 2026, with His Excellency Mr. Li Xiang, Ambassador of the People’s Republic of China to the Republic of Mali.
Reviewing the strategic areas of cooperation, the two officials emphasized the need for the rigorous implementation of priority projects arising from economic and technical cooperation agreements. These include solar energy projects, infrastructure and transportation development, agricultural mechanization, and the construction of healthcare facilities.
Highlighting the importance attached by the highest authorities to economic development, Minister Diop underscored the significant initiatives undertaken by the Government to ensure the secure execution of development projects, in a spirit of pragmatism and mutual interest. Both sides praised the strategic level of the Mali–China partnership and reaffirmed their commitment to the regular and rigorous monitoring of ongoing projects, with a view to the swift realization of shared ambitions of the Malian and Chinese Heads of State.

title_en: ANASER, Police, and Gendarmerie Join Forces for 2026

body_en:
Bamako, January 30, 2026 – The National Road Safety Agency (ANASER), the National Police, the National Gendarmerie, and Civil Protection have established a new partnership to enhance road safety across Mali.
During a ceremony on Friday afternoon, presided over by the Minister of Transport and Infrastructure and the Minister of Security and Civil Protection, the technical services signed three agreements to formalize the collaboration.
The agreements, approved by Ministers Madina Sissoko Dembélé and Daoud Aly Mohammedine, focus on the organization of joint roadside checks and the provision of first aid training for road users.
Under the joint road control operations, 110 combined ANASER/National Police operations are planned in the cities of Bamako, Kayes, Koulikoro, Kati, Sikasso, Ségou, San, Mopti, Dioila, Nioro, Nara, Bougouni, Gao, Koutiala, Kita, Bandiagara, Fana, and Kenieba.

Bamako, January 30, 2026 – The Minister of Handicrafts, Culture, Hospitality, and Tourism, Mr. Mamou Daffé, held a press conference to present a review of the Year of Culture in Mali, proclaimed by His Excellency General Assimi Goïta, President of the Transition and Head of State.
In his address, Minister Daffé thanked the President for his historic decision and vision to make culture the cornerstone of building a new Mali. He also extended gratitude to the Prime Minister, Head of Government, and all members of the government for their support of initiatives undertaken during this special year.
He further commended the commitment and participation of all stakeholders in the culture, handicrafts, and tourism sectors, whose efforts contributed to the success of this memorable Year of Culture.

title_en: Mali’s Ministry of Agriculture and HELVETAS Sign Project to Prevent Climate-Related Conflicts

body_en:
Bamako, January 30, 2026 – The Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Daniel Siméon Kelema, received representatives from HELVETAS Mali to discuss the implementation of a project aimed at preventing violence linked to land conflicts and climate change in the San and Koutiala regions.
The project agreement was formally signed during the meeting. Funded by UNOPS, HELVETAS, and Search, the initiative will span two and a half years (30 months) and be implemented in 10 communes, five in San and five in Koutiala.
The project aims to prevent emerging conflicts over the access, use, and governance of natural resources and is expected to benefit 18,000 people, including 42% women and 58% men.

body_en:
Bamako, January 22, 2026 — The Maeva Palace Hotel hosted the opening of a workshop to validate the guide on seizures and confiscations of the Agency for the Recovery and Management of Seized or Confiscated Assets (ARGASC).
The event brought together representatives from judicial institutions, agency officials, and members of ARGASC’s General Directorate. The ceremony was chaired by Ibrahim Berthe, Technical Advisor to the Ministry of Justice, representing the Minister of Justice, alongside the Director General of ARGASC and a UNDP representative.

Bamako, January 21, 2026 — The Ministry of Justice and Human Rights hosted the presentation of the new members of the Malian Bar Association Council to Minister Mamoudou Kassogue on Wednesday.
In his address, the new Bar Association President, Souleymane Soumounthera, paid tribute to the outgoing council, particularly Ousmane Bouba Traoré, for his leadership, and introduced his team, pledging to uphold justice and combat lawlessness. He also highlighted plans for organizing the WAEMU Congress in Bamako.
Minister Kassogue welcomed the new council, congratulated its members, and praised Ms. Soumounthera for her professional and moral qualities. He expressed gratitude to the outgoing council for their tireless work under challenging conditions.
The minister reaffirmed his and the highest authorities’ support for the council, emphasizing that a strong judicial system depends on the active participation of lawyers, highlighting the importance of collaboration between the Bar Association and the Ministry of Justice for an effective judicial system in Mali.

title: Opening of the 2026 CIMERAP Meeting
excerpt: Bamako, January 28, 2026 – Under the chairmanship of His Excellency Mr. Moustapha Traoré, Ambassador and Secretary General of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, the Interministerial Committee for Support to the Preparation of Initial and Periodic Repor
title_en: Opening of the 2026 CIMERAP Meeting
excerpt_en: Bamako, January 28, 2026 – Under the chairmanship of His Excellency Mr. Moustapha Traoré, Ambassador and Secretary General of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, the Interministerial Committee for Support to the Preparation of Initial and Periodic Repor
body_en:
Bamako, January 28, 2026 – Under the chairmanship of His Excellency Mr. Moustapha Traoré, Ambassador and Secretary General of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, the Interministerial Committee for Support to the Preparation of Initial and Periodic Reports on the Implementation of Conventions Ratified by Mali (CIMERAP) opened its 2026 session on Wednesday, January 28, 2026, at the headquarters of the Ministry, in the presence of Ms. Fosca Giulidori, Deputy Representative of UNICEF in Mali.
This first session of 2026 marks a key milestone in the process of monitoring and evaluating Mali’s international commitments, particularly regarding the implementation of the Optional Protocols to the Convention on the Rights of the Child and the follow-up to the recommendations of the Committee on the Rights of the Child, issued during its May 2024 session.
In her address, the UNICEF Deputy Representative praised Mali’s steadfast commitment to children’s rights, noting that it is deeply rooted in the country’s ancestral values and millennia-old civilizations. She cited the Charter of Kurukan Fuga, proclaimed in 1236 by the Mali Empire, as one of the earliest international references to fundamental human rights.
Speaking on behalf of His Excellency Mr. Abdoulaye Diop, Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, the Secretary General reaffirmed Mali’s strong commitment to child protection, describing it as a legal, moral, and strategic imperative for the country’s sustainable development and stability.
He urged members of the Interministerial Committee to carry out a thorough review of the relevant legal instruments and to prepare a draft report on the implementation of the Optional Protocol on the involvement of children in armed conflict, as well as the Optional Protocol on the sale of children, child prostitution, and child pornography.

Kidal, January 23, 2026 – Local sources reported that a joint patrol of the Malian army and mercenaries from the Russian African Corps committed serious abuses against civilians in the Kidal region.
According to reports, the patrol killed a civilian, Matkane Ag Amouman, burned several houses, and sabotaged a water tower along with its solar power system in the locality of Ighchar Sdidane.
The same group also abducted, executed, and beheaded an 84-year-old man, Attaouyoub Ag Iknan, in the Intadayni area, near the city of Kidal.

This follows previous graduations in Timbuktu and Sikasso, signaling an intensification of the group’s training and operational capacity.

In response, the Malian army is accelerating its acquisition of drones and AI-powered weapons, increasingly prioritizing air power over ground combat to counter the threat posed by these newly trained fighters.

body_en:
Bamako/Dakar, January 12–22, 2026 — Friction is emerging between the Senegalese Minister of Transport and his Malian counterpart over Malian containers and equipment abandoned at the Port of Dakar for over two months.
According to Senegalese authorities, the port is operating at full capacity, prompting pressure on Mali to urgently recover its goods. The situation is linked to the de facto closure of the Senegal-Mali border, controlled by armed terrorist groups, which has prevented safe transport.
Mali’s request for Senegalese military escorts to move goods through high-risk areas was reportedly refused, leaving containers stuck and creating growing congestion.
Sources from the Malian Ministry of Transport say discussions are ongoing, with authorities seeking alternative solutions to clear the backlog. Updates are expected as the situation evolves.

excerpt_en: Kayes, January 29, 2026 – The Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (JNIM) claimed responsibility for an ambush on a Malian army convoy escorting fuel tankers between Diboli and Kayes in the Kayes region on Thursday, January 29, 2026. According to JNIM, the attack resulted i
body_en:
Kayes, January 29, 2026 – The Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (JNIM) claimed responsibility for an ambush on a Malian army convoy escorting fuel tankers between Diboli and Kayes in the Kayes region on Thursday, January 29, 2026.
According to JNIM, the attack resulted in the deaths of two Malian soldiers and the seizure of a motorcycle, multiple weapons, and a large quantity of ammunition. The group also claims to have set fire to four military vehicles.
The ambush reportedly caused the burning of approximately fifty fuel tankers, further exacerbating the ongoing energy crisis in the country.
Witnesses and local sources indicate that around ten bodies remain by the roadside between Kayes and Diboli, near the burned tankers, raising serious humanitarian and health concerns.
This incident highlights the human toll of the attack and underscores the deteriorating security situation along this strategic route connecting Mali to Senegal.

body_en:
Menaka, January 29, 2026 – A joint patrol of the Malian army and the Russian Africa Corps was targeted in a complex attack in the Menaka region of northern Mali on January 29, 2026.
According to a statement from the Islamic State in the Sahel (IS-Sahel), a first unit was ambushed near Agarmbaw, followed by an attack on a reinforcement patrol near Tin Fadimata. The jihadist group claims the operation caused at least 20 dead and wounded among the Malian and Russian forces.
Local sources report that the attackers also used suicide drones during the assault. They further indicate that the Islamic State in the Sahel controls nearly 90% of the Menaka region, with all districts in the area under its influence or effective control since 2022.

title_en: Commander of AES Unified Force Receives Audience with President Assimi Goïta
excerpt_en: Koulouba, January 29, 2026 – The President of the Transition and Head of State, General Assimi Goïta, received Brigadier General Daouda Traoré, Commander of the AES Unified Force (FU-AES), in an official audience on Thursday, January 29, 2026. During the meeting, Brigadier Genera
body_en:
Koulouba, January 29, 2026 – The President of the Transition and Head of State, General Assimi Goïta, received Brigadier General Daouda Traoré, Commander of the AES Unified Force (FU-AES), in an official audience on Thursday, January 29, 2026.
During the meeting, Brigadier General Traoré expressed gratitude to the President for the trust placed in him and presented a detailed report on the preparations for the Unified Force, which comprises 6,000 personnel. He also highlighted efforts to establish this new unit, aimed at strengthening security and stability in the Sahel.
The President of the Transition commended the progress made in the formation of the force and provided guidance to ensure the successful achievement of its objectives.
Conclusion
The period from January 18 to February 1, 2026, underscores a Mali navigating a complex duality of proactive diplomacy and intensifying internal security threats. While the Malian government has successfully strengthened strategic international partnerships—notably with China to advance infrastructure and energy projects, and with the WTO to advocate for the national cotton sector—the domestic landscape remains highly volatile.
The security situation is marked by a significant escalation in insurgent activity and mounting human rights concerns:
Insurgent Expansion: The Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (JNIM) and Islamic State in the Sahel (IS-Sahel) have demonstrated increased operational capacity, seizing military posts near key hubs such as Sikasso and Koulikoro. A recent ambush on the Diboli-Kayes axis resulted in the destruction of approximately 50 fuel tankers, exacerbating the national energy crisis.
Military Response: The Malian Armed Forces (FAMa) are increasingly pivoting toward air power and AI-powered weaponry to counter these threats, supported by the operationalization of the 6,000-person AES Unified Force, aimed at stabilizing the broader Sahel region.
Civilian Impact: Amidst ongoing fighting, troubling reports have surfaced of civilian abuses by joint patrols of the army and Russian Africa Corps in Kidal and Mopti. Concurrently, political tensions persist, exemplified by the detention of figures like Moussa Mara and Choguel Maïga.
Ultimately, Mali stands at a critical juncture. The successful realization of the “Mali 2063” strategic vision and the tangible benefits of its new diplomatic alliances hinge on the government’s ability to restore security along vital trade routes and foster national reconciliation, all while confronting persistent extremist violence and growing domestic opposition.
By Maïga Sidi Bonkana
(Boukari Zankey Sidi)
Jeff Buleli

title: Foreign Minister Abdoulaye Diop Bids Farewell to UNAIDS Country Director
excerpt: Bamako Mali, February 5, 2026 – Mali’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Abdoulaye Diop, received Dr. Marc Saba, Country Director of the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS), in a farewell audience marking the end of his mission in Mali. Du
title_en: Foreign Minister Abdoulaye Diop Bids Farewell to UNAIDS Country Director
excerpt_en: Bamako Mali, February 5, 2026 – Mali’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Abdoulaye Diop, received Dr. Marc Saba, Country Director of the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS), in a farewell audience marking the end of his mission in Mali. Du
body_en:
Bamako Mali, February 5, 2026 – Mali’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Abdoulaye Diop, received Dr. Marc Saba, Country Director of the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS), in a farewell audience marking the end of his mission in Mali.
During the meeting in Bamako, Minister Diop praised Dr. Saba’s commitment and contributions to the Malian government, particularly in strengthening the national response to HIV/AIDS. He highlighted the quality of cooperation between Mali and UNAIDS, noting tangible progress in prevention efforts, treatment access, and care for people living with HIV.
For his part, Dr. Marc Saba expressed gratitude for his five years of service in Mali, describing the country as welcoming and thanking the authorities for their sustained support throughout his tenure. He reaffirmed that his mission had been dedicated to expanding access to HIV prevention, care, and treatment services.
The farewell meeting underscored the continued partnership between Mali and UNAIDS in addressing public health challenges and consolidating gains in the fight against HIV/AIDS.

title: U.S. Envoy Raises Conditions for Security Cooperation During Bamako Visit
excerpt: February 3, 2026 – Twenty-four hours after the visit to Bamako by Nick Checker, Director of the Bureau of African Affairs at the U.S. State Department, details have emerged regarding discussions between American officials and Malian authorities. According to diplomatic sources, t
title_en: U.S. Envoy Raises Conditions for Security Cooperation During Bamako Visit
excerpt_en: February 3, 2026 – Twenty-four hours after the visit to Bamako by Nick Checker, Director of the Bureau of African Affairs at the U.S. State Department, details have emerged regarding discussions between American officials and Malian authorities. According to diplomatic sources, t
body_en:
February 3, 2026 – Twenty-four hours after the visit to Bamako by Nick Checker, Director of the Bureau of African Affairs at the U.S. State Department, details have emerged regarding discussions between American officials and Malian authorities.
According to diplomatic sources, the talks focused primarily on security cooperation and intelligence sharing in the Sahel region. In recent months, Mali—alongside Burkina Faso and Niger—has reportedly sought closer engagement with Washington on military and intelligence matters amid persistent insecurity.
During a separate visit to Abuja, a senior official from the U.S. Africa Command (AFRICOM) indicated that intelligence collaboration with Sahelian armed forces could continue under certain conditions.
U.S. Conditions for Cooperation
During his discussions in Bamako, Nick Checker reportedly conveyed that the United States is open to strengthening cooperation with Mali and other Sahelian states. However, American support would be contingent upon specific political and security benchmarks.
Among the key conditions mentioned were:
Progress toward a return to constitutional order
Clarification regarding the presence of foreign military actors in Mali
The visit comes amid evolving geopolitical dynamics in the Sahel, where transitional authorities have diversified partnerships in response to mounting security challenges.
Observers note that intelligence cooperation remains a strategic priority for all parties, as armed groups continue to operate across the region.
The discussions in Bamako highlight the broader recalibration of international partnerships in the Sahel and underscore the linkage between security cooperation, governance reforms, and diplomatic alignment.

Observers note that intelligence cooperation remains a strategic priority for all parties, as armed groups continue to operate across the region.
The discussions in Bamako highlight the broader recalibration of international partnerships in the Sahel and underscore the linkage between security cooperation, governance reforms, and diplomatic alignment.

excerpt_en: Bamako, February 5, 2026 – Mali officially launched the inaugural session of the Steering Committee of the Technical Cooperation Unit with the European Union (CTC-EU) on Thursday in Bamako. The meeting was chaired by Abdoulaye Diop, Minister of Foreign Affairs and International C
body_en:
Bamako, February 5, 2026 – Mali officially launched the inaugural session of the Steering Committee of the Technical Cooperation Unit with the European Union (CTC-EU) on Thursday in Bamako. The meeting was chaired by Abdoulaye Diop, Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, in the presence of the European Union Representative in Mali.
Strengthening National Ownership
Minister Diop emphasized that the establishment of the CTC-EU, financed through the national budget, reflects the commitment of Mali’s highest authorities to ensuring strong national ownership and leadership in the management of cooperation programs with the European Union.
According to the minister, the initiative seeks to enhance coordination, improve oversight of ongoing projects, and maximize the impact of EU-funded programs, particularly in a context requiring greater efficiency in public action.
Reinforcing Institutional Capacity
Diop welcomed the role of the CTC-EU in strengthening the operational capacities of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, enabling it to effectively manage, coordinate, and oversee the full cycle of EU-financed projects and programs in Mali.
He also reaffirmed the Malian government’s commitment to maintaining a constructive and collaborative partnership with the European Union and its Member States, aimed at improving the well-being of the population.
During the session, members of the Steering Committee were tasked with reviewing the draft annual report of the CTC-EU, assessing project implementation, identifying constraints, and outlining prospects to enhance the impact of future interventions.

body_en:
Bamako, February 13, 2026 – Abdoulaye Diop, Malian Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, participated in celebrations marking the 47th anniversary of the Islamic Revolution of the Islamic Republic of Iran in Bamako on Friday, February 13, 2026.
On behalf of Mali’s highest authorities, Minister Diop conveyed congratulations and wishes for peace, prosperity, and progress to the President, Government, and people of Iran.
Speaking on Mali’s current challenges in its pursuit of freedom and dignity, he highlighted the shared commitment of both countries to the inalienable right of peoples to preserve national sovereignty and define their development paths without external interference.
Minister Diop also praised Mali-Iran cooperation on major international issues, including:
Respect for territorial integrity
Rejection of the instrumentalization of human rights for political ends
Defense of non-interference
Promotion of a democratic, inclusive, and multipolar multilateral order
Both sides condemned unilateral coercive measures and economic sanctions, labeling them unjustified and counterproductive, and welcomed the strengthening of bilateral cooperation since the first Mali-Iran Joint Commission in Bamako, August 2022.

body_en:
Bamako, February 12, 2026 – Abdoulaye Diop, Malian Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, participated in celebrations marking the birthday of His Majesty Emperor Naruhito of Japan on Thursday, February 12, 2026, in Bamako, at the invitation of Japanese Ambassador Yukuo Murata. The event was also attended by the President of the Economic, Social, Environmental and Cultural Council.
On behalf of Mali’s highest authorities, Minister Diop conveyed wishes for health, happiness, and prosperity to His Majesty, the Imperial Family, and the Government and People of Japan. He praised the Japanese model, noting its harmonious integration of culture, technology, and modernity, and its focus on human capital development, particularly as Mali marks 2026-2027 as the Years of Education and Culture.
Both countries also highlighted the achievements of Professor Abdoulaye Djimdé, recipient of the Hideyo Noguchi Prize for Africa in medical research, recognizing his contribution to the fight against malaria.
The event further underscored the strengthening of bilateral cooperation between Mali and Japan, with ongoing projects in security, agriculture, health, education, access to drinking water, justice, and infrastructure. Minister Diop concluded by commending the resilience of the Malian people amid ongoing complex challenges.

body_en:
Bamako, February 12, 2026 – Abdoulaye Diop, Malian Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, and Lieutenant General Ismaël Wagué, Minister of State for Reconciliation, Peace, and National Cohesion, co-chaired the National Steering Committee for Peacebuilding Investment Mechanisms in Mali on Thursday, February 12, 2026, in Bamako, with the UN Resident Coordinator in Mali in attendance.
The session reviewed projects under the Peacebuilding Fund and the Women’s Peace and Humanitarian Action Fund, bringing together technical and financial partners, including the Chargé d’affaires of Canada, representatives of UN Women, the United Nations Population Fund, and members of civil society.
Minister Diop highlighted the importance of aligning all projects with national priorities and the country’s strategic development vision, in line with new principles guiding public action. The UN Resident Coordinator praised the government’s leadership in peacebuilding, noting the structured and inclusive nature of Mali’s framework.
Minister Wagué welcomed progress in project implementation, while Committee members recommended intensifying government-led interventions, with strengthened operational monitoring and field visits, to sustainably improve the living conditions of the population.

title_en: Assimi Goïta Reaffirms Mali’s Sovereign Diplomacy During New Year’s Diplomatic Ceremony
excerpt_en: Koulouba, February 10, 2026 – President of the Transition, General Assimi Goïta, received the Diplomatic Corps accredited to Mali on Tuesday, February 10, 2026, at the Koulouba Palace for the traditional New Year’s greetings ceremony. In his address, President Goïta reaffirmed th
body_en:
Koulouba, February 10, 2026 – President of the Transition, General Assimi Goïta, received the Diplomatic Corps accredited to Mali on Tuesday, February 10, 2026, at the Koulouba Palace for the traditional New Year’s greetings ceremony.
In his address, President Goïta reaffirmed the principles of sovereign diplomacy, emphasizing mutual respect, freedom of strategic choice, and responsibility. He declared 2026 a year of constructive dialogue and sincere partnerships, welcoming the strengthening of political dialogue and new diplomatic accreditations, which highlight growing interest in Mali and the Confederation of Sahel States (CESA).
On security, the Head of State commended the Defense and Security Forces for confronting the asymmetric threat, stressing that territorial security is essential for the restoration of state authority and essential social services. He also denounced disinformation targeting the countries of the Economic and Social Affairs Group (ESA) and reaffirmed Mali’s adherence to UN principles, including non-interference and respect for territorial integrity.
Domestically, President Goïta reiterated ongoing state reforms under the Vision “Mali Kura ɲɛtaasira ka bɛn san 2063 ma” and the National Strategy for Emergence and Sustainable Development 2024-2033. He announced that 2026-2027 would focus on education and culture, while emphasizing endogenous solutions, energy sovereignty, and structuring investments to support sustainable development and shared progress.

body_en:
Bamako, February 12, 2026 – In a special news bulletin broadcast on #ORTM, the Secretary General of the Presidency announced the results of a cabinet reshuffle under Decree No. 062/PT-RM 2026, appointing the members of the Government of the President of the Transition, Head of State.
The reshuffle saw the appointment of three Ministers of State for Defense, Economy and Finance, and Reconciliation, while four ministries experienced changes in leadership: Territorial Administration, State Reform, Agriculture, and Energy and Water.
The move signals a reorganization of the transitional government as Mali continues to address national priorities and ongoing challenges.

Dakar, February 10, 2026 – The Malian Minister of Transport and Infrastructure, at the invitation of the Minister of Fisheries and Maritime Economy of Senegal, participated in the opening ceremony of the Port of Dakar 2026 in the Senegalese capital.
