title: Ugandan Troops May End 19-Year Peacekeeping Mission in Somalia
excerpt: Kampala, January 27, 2026 — Uganda’s military is considering ending its 19-year peacekeeping mission in Somalia, according to Maj Gen Felix Kulayigye, spokesperson for the Ugandan Armed Forces. The announcement follows remarks by Chief of Staff Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who said:
title_en: Ugandan Troops May End 19-Year Peacekeeping Mission in Somalia
excerpt_en: Kampala, January 27, 2026 — Uganda’s military is considering ending its 19-year peacekeeping mission in Somalia, according to Maj Gen Felix Kulayigye, spokesperson for the Ugandan Armed Forces. The announcement follows remarks by Chief of Staff Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who said:
body_en:
Kampala, January 27, 2026 — Uganda’s military is considering ending its 19-year peacekeeping mission in Somalia, according to Maj Gen Felix Kulayigye, spokesperson for the Ugandan Armed Forces.
The announcement follows remarks by Chief of Staff Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who said:
"After 19 years in Somalia, very soon we plan to leave the country completely."
Maj Gen Kulayigye highlighted Uganda’s contributions since its deployment in 2007, emphasizing efforts to facilitate dialogue among Somali factions and reduce ongoing fighting. He explained that peace talks previously held abroad in countries such as Kenya, Ethiopia, and Egypt had failed, but Uganda helped organize successful talks on Somali soil, fostering local ownership of the peace process.
He also noted Uganda’s role in supporting Somali elections, ensuring leadership transitions were conducted peacefully rather than through violence. Since 2006, Somalia has held four elections under Uganda’s facilitation.
Despite Uganda’s efforts, Al-Shabaab continues to carry out terrorist attacks, indicating that the security situation remains fragile even as Uganda evaluates the conclusion of its long-term mission.
This potential withdrawal marks a significant shift in the Horn of Africa’s security landscape, as Ugandan forces have been a central component of stabilizing Somalia for nearly two decades.

title: Nangaa Warns DRC Forces Against Violence in Uvira
excerpt: Uvira, January 28, 2026 — AFC/M23 leader Corneille Nangaa has warned the DRC government-backed military alliance that if violence continues in Uvira, his fighters will take responsibility for protecting civilians. Nangaa said that AFC/M23 voluntarily withdrew from Uvira at the re
title_en: Nangaa Warns DRC Forces Against Violence in Uvira
excerpt_en: Uvira, January 28, 2026 — AFC/M23 leader Corneille Nangaa has warned the DRC government-backed military alliance that if violence continues in Uvira, his fighters will take responsibility for protecting civilians. Nangaa said that AFC/M23 voluntarily withdrew from Uvira at the re
body_en:
Uvira, January 28, 2026 — AFC/M23 leader Corneille Nangaa has warned the DRC government-backed military alliance that if violence continues in Uvira, his fighters will take responsibility for protecting civilians.
Nangaa said that AFC/M23 voluntarily withdrew from Uvira at the request of the United States to allow peace talks to continue. He noted that similar withdrawals had previously occurred in Bunagana, Masisi, and Walikale.
“This is not the first time we have done this… In Walikale, we left so that the Doha talks could take place. Now, too, we have been asked to leave Uvira,” he said.
Before leaving the city, Nangaa warned the international community that civilians could be killed, accused of collaborating with AFC/M23, and that Banyamulenge communities in South Kivu Province could be targeted. He said that requests for neutral forces to protect civilians were not respected.
He added that following their withdrawal, there were lootings, extrajudicial killings, arbitrary arrests, and targeted attacks, particularly against the Banyamulenge, with about 900 families displaced to areas such as Luvungi, Sange, and especially Kamanyola.
Nangaa stated that AFC/M23 had learned it could reclaim territory quickly if necessary. He accused DRC soldiers of criminal behavior and warned: “If they continue, we will take responsibility for rescuing the population.”
This warning comes amid discussions in Kinshasa about launching a rapid campaign to retake areas controlled by AFC/M23, after government forces cleared the group from Uvira on January 17, 2026.

He added that following their withdrawal, there were lootings, extrajudicial killings, arbitrary arrests, and targeted attacks, particularly against the Banyamulenge, with about 900 families displaced to areas such as Luvungi, Sange, and especially Kamanyola.

body_en:
Doha, January 28, 2026 — Peace talks between the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government and the AFC/M23 coalition could resume this weekend, following a suspension since early December 2025 when AFC/M23 captured Uvira after a week of fighting in the Ruzizi Valley, South Kivu Province.

title_en: RED Tabara Denies Ties to Rwanda, AFC/M23, and 2015 Burundi Coup Plot
excerpt_en: January 29, 2026 — The armed group RED Tabara has rejected accusations of collaborating with Rwanda, the AFC/M23 alliance, and the attempted coup in Burundi in May 2015. The denial follows statements by Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye, who said in a January 17 interview
body_en:
January 29, 2026 — The armed group RED Tabara has rejected accusations of collaborating with Rwanda, the AFC/M23 alliance, and the attempted coup in Burundi in May 2015.
The denial follows statements by Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye, who said in a January 17 interview that RED Tabara was being used by Rwanda to destabilize Burundi and reinforce AFC/M23 in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
In response, RED Tabara spokesperson Patrick Nahimana said the group has never cooperated with Rwanda, citing the 2021 handover of 19 RED Tabara fighters by Rwandan authorities to Burundi as evidence. He also dismissed any link to the 2015 coup attempt, stating that those responsible were Burundian soldiers and not RED Tabara, which he said was already active prior to the events.
The group further denied any collaboration with AFC/M23, past or present, and accused the Burundian government of attempting to divert attention from the root causes of its opposition, particularly the dismantling of the Arusha Peace Accords.
RED Tabara reaffirmed that its struggle is aimed at promoting democratic governance in Burundi.

title: Ethiopian Airlines Suspends Flights to Tigray Amid Rising Tensions
excerpt: January 29, 2026 — Ethiopian Airlines has suspended passenger flights between Addis Ababa and towns in Tigray, citing unforeseen circumstances, amid fears of renewed fighting between government forces and the TPLF. Neither the airline nor the government has officially commented.
title_en: Ethiopian Airlines Suspends Flights to Tigray Amid Rising Tensions
excerpt_en: January 29, 2026 — Ethiopian Airlines has suspended passenger flights between Addis Ababa and towns in Tigray, citing unforeseen circumstances, amid fears of renewed fighting between government forces and the TPLF. Neither the airline nor the government has officially commented.
body_en:
January 29, 2026 — Ethiopian Airlines has suspended passenger flights between Addis Ababa and towns in Tigray, citing unforeseen circumstances, amid fears of renewed fighting between government forces and the TPLF.
Neither the airline nor the government has officially commented. Tigray’s transport chief, Tadele Mengistu, confirmed the suspension, while BBC reporters in Mekelle said airport staff were told not to report to work. Bus transport between Addis Ababa and Tigray continues.
The 2022 peace deal remains unimplemented, as land disputes, June 2026 elections, and reports of clashes in Mai Degusha fuel tensions. The conflict centers on the Amhara region’s control of land in western Tigray, which the government says will be resolved by referendum, though up to one million displaced people may be unable to vote.
The war that began in November 2020 between the government and the TPLF caused massive destruction, with the African Union reporting over 600,000 deaths.

title_en: FARDC, Allies Recapture Point Zero from Twirwaneho in South Kivu
excerpt_en: South Kivu, January 30, 2026 — The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), alongside Burundian forces and Wazalendo fighters, have recaptured Point Zero from the MRDP-Twirwaneho group following intense fighting supported by drone strikes. The area had been seize
body_en:
South Kivu, January 30, 2026 — The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), alongside Burundian forces and Wazalendo fighters, have recaptured Point Zero from the MRDP-Twirwaneho group following intense fighting supported by drone strikes.
The area had been seized by Twirwaneho on January 17, 2026. Its recapture is considered a major victory, as government forces had been preparing operations in zones inhabited by the Banyamulenge community in the Minembwe commune.
According to reports, in the early hours of January 29, FARDC forces — reportedly accompanied by FDLR fighters and mercenaries — deployed large numbers of troops and heavy weapons to retake the strategic position.
“They were supported in the air by six drones, in groups of three,” said Moïse Nyarugabo, a politician from Minembwe. “When one group of three drones was shot down, the other returned and bombed the compound. These drones fired 34 bombs in one day.”
Following the operation, Twirwaneho fighters were forced to withdraw from Point Zero and Bikyaka, retreating toward the Tuwetuwe area.
The fighting triggered the displacement of thousands of residents, many of whom had previously fled to the area when Twirwaneho first captured it.
The recapture of Point Zero has restored freedom of movement along key routes in Fizi Territory, including access to Baraka and areas leading to Uvira, where the location serves as a critical crossroads.

Sange, South Kivu, January 30, 2026 — Five civilians were killed in a bomb attack at a market in Sange center, South Kivu Province, the AFC/M23 coalition reported. The coalition claimed that the attack was carried out by armed groups supported by the DRC government.
According to AFC/M23 spokesman Lawrence Kanyuka, the attack occurred on the evening of January 29, 2026, at 6:30 p.m., when a grenade was deliberately thrown into the crowded market, killing five innocent civilians, including women, and injuring several others.

title: Burundi Maintains Closed Borders with DRC, Refuses Return of Congolese Refugees
excerpt: Bujumbura, January 30, 2026 — Burundi has announced that it will not reopen its land border with the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) or allow the return of Congolese refugees, citing ongoing security concerns, according to Foreign Affairs Minister Dr. Edouard Bizimana. The Gat
title_en: Burundi Maintains Closed Borders with DRC, Refuses Return of Congolese Refugees
excerpt_en: Bujumbura, January 30, 2026 — Burundi has announced that it will not reopen its land border with the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) or allow the return of Congolese refugees, citing ongoing security concerns, according to Foreign Affairs Minister Dr. Edouard Bizimana. The Gat
body_en:
Bujumbura, January 30, 2026 — Burundi has announced that it will not reopen its land border with the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) or allow the return of Congolese refugees, citing ongoing security concerns, according to Foreign Affairs Minister Dr. Edouard Bizimana.
The Gatumba and Vugizo border posts were closed on December 9, 2025, following the entry of AFC/M23 fighters into Uvira. Although the group withdrew on January 17, 2026, and DRC and Wazalendo forces, alongside the Burundian army, regained control the next day, the border remains closed due to continued security risks, including attempted crossings of the Ruzizi River.
Minister Bizimana explained at a press conference on January 29 that reopening the border requires ensuring that all security conditions are met. “Opening them today, and then closing them tomorrow because you are not well prepared, without making sure that the requirements are met, no one will do anything,” he said.
Since early December 2025, Burundi has hosted over 100,000 Congolese refugees fleeing fighting in the Ruzizi Valley. Many have expressed the desire to return home but have been turned away. Minister Bizimana acknowledged the difficult living conditions in refugee camps but assured that refugees continue to receive support, including financial assistance from the DRC government.
“We want those Congolese to return home, to their properties, but there are still issues that prevent the borders from being safely opened,” he stated, adding that the situation will be communicated when it is resolved.
Mercenaries Fuel Insecurity in South Kivu, Threatening Regional Stability
Kinshasa, 31 January 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC)’s eastern province of South Kivu is facing a new wave of instability as reports indicate a growing reliance on foreign mercenaries, raising alarm across the Great Lakes region.
Sources from international and regional media suggest that mercenaries from Eastern Europe and Colombia—countries known for deploying former soldiers abroad—are actively operating alongside both the DRC army and armed groups such as the FDLR, a terrorist organization formed by perpetrators of the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi. Rwanda has repeatedly warned that such alliances pose a serious threat to its own security and that of the broader region.
Observers note that President Félix Tshisekedi appears to have prioritized a military strategy over ongoing peace initiatives, sidelining regional and international efforts aimed at dialogue and reconciliation. The deployment of foreign fighters violates previous agreements reached in Luanda, Nairobi, Washington, and Doha, as well as other regional mechanisms designed to dismantle armed groups and restore peace.
Reports also suggest that mercenaries have obstructed the operations of the East African Community Regional Force (EACRF), even intimidating regional soldiers deployed to stabilize South Kivu—a move seen as Kinshasa’s reluctance to implement regional resolutions.
Analysts warn that the use of mercenaries often exacerbates conflict rather than resolving it. “History shows that foreign fighters rarely restore peace,” said one expert. “Their presence tends to fuel human rights violations, resource plundering, and further instability.” The DRC’s increasing reliance on Colombian mercenaries highlights persistent weaknesses within its national army.
The consequences extend beyond Congo’s borders. Regional security across Rwanda, Burundi, and Uganda is threatened, and ethnic tensions are exacerbated, placing civilians—particularly Tutsi communities—at risk outside zones controlled by the AFC/M23.
The international community has faced criticism for its muted response to mercenary activity and collaboration with armed groups. Experts argue that continued inaction could prolong the conflict, rather than promote resolution.
Observers are calling for urgent condemnation of mercenary use, renewed diplomatic pressure on Kinshasa to return to negotiations, and a commitment to dismantling terrorist organizations. Without decisive action, South Kivu—and the wider Great Lakes region—risks remaining trapped in a cycle of violence.

title: Ibalanky Signals Willingness to Work with AFC/M23 After Years of Serving Tshisekedi
excerpt: Kinshasa, January 31, 2026 — Claude Ibalanky Ekolomba, a senior Congolese politician who previously worked closely with President Félix Tshisekedi, has announced his willingness to collaborate with the AFC/M23 alliance, marking a significant political shift. Ibalanky was appointe
title_en: Ibalanky Signals Willingness to Work with AFC/M23 After Years of Serving Tshisekedi
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, January 31, 2026 — Claude Ibalanky Ekolomba, a senior Congolese politician who previously worked closely with President Félix Tshisekedi, has announced his willingness to collaborate with the AFC/M23 alliance, marking a significant political shift. Ibalanky was appointe
body_en:
Kinshasa, January 31, 2026 — Claude Ibalanky Ekolomba, a senior Congolese politician who previously worked closely with President Félix Tshisekedi, has announced his willingness to collaborate with the AFC/M23 alliance, marking a significant political shift.
Ibalanky was appointed by Tshisekedi as coordinator of the body monitoring the implementation of the Addis Ababa Peace Agreement, a key framework for restoring stability in the Democratic Republic of Congo. In 2023, he was also named the country’s special ambassador.
After nearly a year outside the country, Ibalanky resurfaced in Goma on January 31, 2025, where he was seen alongside senior AFC/M23 leaders, including Corneille Nangaa and Bertrand Bisimwa.
He stated that he has not formally joined the AFC/M23 but traveled to Goma to hold consultations with its leadership on how dialogue could help restore peace. Ibalanky emphasized that he does not intend to oppose President Tshisekedi, but rather seeks to serve as an advisor to the alliance, pending approval from its leader, Corneille Nangaa.
“I came to consult. I have not betrayed anyone; I am only on one side, which is Congo,” Ibalanky said. “If they accept my help and show me how we can work together, I will consider it. What matters is not being in Goma or Kinshasa, but working for peace.”
In 2023, Ibalanky founded the REPOP political party, which initially supported Tshisekedi’s bid for a second term. However, in January 2024, the party announced it would not recognize the election results, signaling a break with the ruling camp.

title: Tshisekedi Rejects AFC/M23 Participation in National Peace Talks
excerpt: Kinshasa, January 31, 2026 — President Félix Tshisekedi has signaled that members of the AFC/M23 alliance will not be allowed to participate in planned national peace talks aimed at uniting the Congolese people. Since December 2025, the Congolese government, with support from Ang
title_en: Tshisekedi Rejects AFC/M23 Participation in National Peace Talks
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, January 31, 2026 — President Félix Tshisekedi has signaled that members of the AFC/M23 alliance will not be allowed to participate in planned national peace talks aimed at uniting the Congolese people. Since December 2025, the Congolese government, with support from Ang
body_en:
Kinshasa, January 31, 2026 — President Félix Tshisekedi has signaled that members of the AFC/M23 alliance will not be allowed to participate in planned national peace talks aimed at uniting the Congolese people.
Since December 2025, the Congolese government, with support from Angolan President and African Union Chair João Lourenço, has been preparing a dialogue process initially expected to take place in Kinshasa. Early reports suggested that opposition groups, including AFC/M23, could be invited. However, the venue is now reportedly under consideration in Luanda, Angola, or Lomé, Togo.
AFC/M23 leader Corneille Nangaa confirmed that Angolan authorities had invited him to attend the talks, but he questioned how this forum would differ from the ongoing Doha process, warning that achievements made there should not be undermined.
In an interview conducted in Goma on January 26, Nangaa stated that the Doha talks should continue, as they are, in his view, the only framework capable of resolving differences between AFC/M23 and the Congolese government, before broader national dialogue can take place.
On January 31, Tshisekedi briefed diplomatic representatives in Kinshasa on the security situation in eastern DRC, insisting that any Congolese dialogue must be held on national territory and led by state institutions.
“If these talks take place, they will take place on national territory, led and organized by national institutions, based on the Constitution, national laws and democratic principles,” Tshisekedi said.
He further stressed that dialogue would not include those he accuses of committing crimes against civilians. “Talks, yes. But we will not do it with those who committed crimes against our population,” he added.
The DRC government has long accused the AFC/M23 of serious abuses, including killings, in areas under its control in North Kivu and South Kivu, particularly Goma and Bukavu, a matter discussed during a cabinet meeting on January 30.
AFC/M23 rejects these accusations, instead blaming government forces for most abuses and claiming that security has improved and living conditions are better in areas it controls.

title: Rubavu Honors Heroes, Praises Resistance Against FDLR
excerpt: Rubavu, February 1, 2026 — The courage and resilience of the people of Rubavu District were celebrated during the Heroes of Rwanda ceremony, honoring their decades-long resistance against the FDLR armed group. Speaking at the event, Rubavu Mayor Mulindwa Prosper said the values o

excerpt_en: Rubavu, February 1, 2026 — The courage and resilience of the people of Rubavu District were celebrated during the Heroes of Rwanda ceremony, honoring their decades-long resistance against the FDLR armed group. Speaking at the event, Rubavu Mayor Mulindwa Prosper said the values o
body_en:
Rubavu, February 1, 2026 — The courage and resilience of the people of Rubavu District were celebrated during the Heroes of Rwanda ceremony, honoring their decades-long resistance against the FDLR armed group.
Speaking at the event, Rubavu Mayor Mulindwa Prosper said the values of courage that define Rwandans prevented the district from being defeated, despite its proximity to hostile forces.“These values made Rwanda endure and resist those who carried out repeated attacks,” he said.
He recalled that hostile forces crossed from neighboring countries between 1994 and early 2025, settling in the area but ultimately being defeated. He praised local heroes and criticized those who joined the FDLR instead of contributing to national development.
Western Province Governor Ntibitura Jean Bosco echoed this message, expressing regret that some residents were deceived into joining the group, which he described as cowardly.
He warned that any attempt to undermine Rwanda’s security would fail, urging citizens to encourage those still in armed groups to return home, stressing that the country is now safe and liberated.
Governor Ntibitura also highlighted that Heroes’ Day serves as a reminder of the sacrifices made for Rwanda’s survival and development, while emphasizing the country’s current focus on fighting poverty.
In support of reintegration efforts, the Rwanda Demobilization and Reintegration Commission (RDRC) announced in October 2025 that it has rehabilitated 12,602 former combatants from armed groups operating in eastern DRC since 2001.

title: AFC/M23 Accuses DRC Government of Politicizing Rubaya Mining Tragedy
excerpt: February 2, 2026 — The AFC/M23 coalition has condemned the DRC government, accusing it of exploiting the deaths of more than 200 people in the Rubaya mining area for political purposes. The coalition said the tragedy, which occurred on January 28, 2026, was caused by landslides t
title_en: AFC/M23 Accuses DRC Government of Politicizing Rubaya Mining Tragedy
excerpt_en: February 2, 2026 — The AFC/M23 coalition has condemned the DRC government, accusing it of exploiting the deaths of more than 200 people in the Rubaya mining area for political purposes. The coalition said the tragedy, which occurred on January 28, 2026, was caused by landslides t
body_en:
February 2, 2026 — The AFC/M23 coalition has condemned the DRC government, accusing it of exploiting the deaths of more than 200 people in the Rubaya mining area for political purposes.
The coalition said the tragedy, which occurred on January 28, 2026, was caused by landslides triggered by heavy rains and unstable soil, not by issues related to territorial control. The victims reportedly included numerous miners.
On January 31, the DRC Ministry of Mineral Resources stated that most of the victims were engaged in illegal mining under AFC/M23 control. This claim was strongly rejected by the group.
AFC/M23 spokesperson Lawrence Kanyuka criticized the government’s response, saying:“Instead of acknowledging the long-standing failure of the government to regulate the mining sector, it is trying to exploit the disaster caused by heavy rains in the Rubaya mines for political gain.”
The coalition emphasized that mining accidents have occurred repeatedly in areas under government control, citing more than 800 deaths across multiple sites over the years.
Among the examples cited were Nyamukubi and Bushushu in South Kivu, where more than 500 people died on May 4, 2023. AFC/M23 also recalled previous disasters, including:
37 deaths in Fizi in October 2018,
43 deaths at the KOV mine in Lualaba in June 2019, and
50 deaths near Kamituga, South Kivu, in September 2020 — all in areas under state control.
AFC/M23 concluded that the Rubaya tragedy reflects systemic failures in mining regulation, rather than the actions of any single group.

title: DRC Army Accused of Drone Strikes Targeting Civilians
excerpt: Minembwe, DRC — February 2, 2026 — The armed group MRDP-Twirwaneho has accused the Congolese army (FARDC) of conducting intensive drone operations over Minembwe, claiming that more than 18 military drones were deployed in the area over a three-day period. According to Colonel Kam

excerpt_en: Minembwe, DRC — February 2, 2026 — The armed group MRDP-Twirwaneho has accused the Congolese army (FARDC) of conducting intensive drone operations over Minembwe, claiming that more than 18 military drones were deployed in the area over a three-day period. According to Colonel Kam
body_en:
Minembwe, DRC — February 2, 2026 — The armed group MRDP-Twirwaneho has accused the Congolese army (FARDC) of conducting intensive drone operations over Minembwe, claiming that more than 18 military drones were deployed in the area over a three-day period.
According to Colonel Kamasa Ndakize Welcome, spokesperson for Twirwaneho, the drone flights occurred between January 30 and February 1, 2026, and allegedly resulted in the deaths of numerous civilians, as well as the destruction of civilian infrastructure, including homes, hospitals, and churches.
“These attacks were carried out in densely populated areas, particularly in the Minembwe center, where many people had sought refuge after fleeing earlier violence involving a coalition of forces including the DRC army, Burundi, Wazalendo militias, and the FDLR,” Kamasa said.
He further claimed that the air operations intensified in January 2026, following the withdrawal of AFC forces from Uvira, and alleged that the campaign forms part of a broader strategy by the Kinshasa government to target the Banyamulenge community.
MRDP-Twirwaneho stated that it remains ready to resist what it described as actions aimed at the extermination of civilians by government forces.

title: MONUSCO Requested to Deploy Troops to Uvira After Qatar Talks
excerpt: Uvira DRC February 3, 2026 — At a meeting held in Qatar, participants requested that MONUSCO (UN peacekeeping mission in the DRC) deploy troops to the city of Uvira, the Qatari Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced. The request was made at the conclusion of a meeting monitoring t
title_en: MONUSCO Requested to Deploy Troops to Uvira After Qatar Talks
excerpt_en: Uvira DRC February 3, 2026 — At a meeting held in Qatar, participants requested that MONUSCO (UN peacekeeping mission in the DRC) deploy troops to the city of Uvira, the Qatari Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced. The request was made at the conclusion of a meeting monitoring t
body_en:
Uvira DRC February 3, 2026 — At a meeting held in Qatar, participants requested that MONUSCO (UN peacekeeping mission in the DRC) deploy troops to the city of Uvira, the Qatari Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced.
The request was made at the conclusion of a meeting monitoring the implementation of the ceasefire between the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and the AFC/M23 alliance, under the Ceasefire Oversight and Verification Mechanism facilitated by Qatar.
The meeting brought together both parties as part of ongoing efforts to resolve the conflict in eastern DRC.
It was also announced that the DRC government and AFC/M23 signed a document outlining broad guidelines on the issues to be discussed and the modalities for negotiations, approved by the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region (ICGLR).
In a statement issued on the night of February 2, 2026, Qatar’s Foreign Ministry said both sides renewed their commitment to the ceasefire and the principles signed on November 15, 2025, in Doha.
“Both sides confirmed their commitment to implementing all agreed conditions in support of the peace agreement,” the ministry stated.
The meeting was attended by representatives of the United States, the African Union (AU) as observers, and Togo as the AU-appointed mediator, alongside officials from MONUSCO and the ICGLR.
Participants reviewed the security situation in the DRC and the ongoing challenges to peace, stressing the need for concrete measures to improve monitoring and information-sharing.
MONUSCO and ICGLR strategies for ceasefire monitoring were also examined, with participants reaffirming their support for both institutions.
MONUSCO was specifically asked to deploy troops to Uvira to monitor compliance with the ceasefire and to establish communication channels to ensure the effectiveness of monitoring operations.
On December 10, AFC/M23 announced it had captured Uvira in South Kivu. However, the group’s last fighters were reportedly killed in the city on January 17, 2026.
AFC/M23 stated that it withdrew from Uvira at the request of the international community, emphasizing that its priority is peace, unlike what it describes as the DRC government’s preference for renewed conflict.

title_en: Gen Muhoozi Orders Sacking of Officials Blocking Rwandans’ Documents
excerpt_en: Kampala Uganda, 4 February 2026 – Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, Chief of Staff of the Ugandan Armed Forces and son of President Yoweri Museveni, announced he will sack immigration officials obstructing Rwandans in Uganda from obtaining official documents. In a statement on 3 February
body_en:
Kampala Uganda, 4 February 2026 – Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, Chief of Staff of the Ugandan Armed Forces and son of President Yoweri Museveni, announced he will sack immigration officials obstructing Rwandans in Uganda from obtaining official documents.
In a statement on 3 February 2026, Gen Muhoozi declared:
“I have decided to immediately sack all immigration officials who are making it difficult for our Rwandans in Uganda to obtain documents. Others will be deployed soon.”
Rwandans in Uganda are recognized under the 1995 Constitution as a legal ethnic group, tracing their presence in the country to before February 1926. Some have long complained that officials withheld passports and identity papers over doubts about ancestry.
Previously, President Museveni emphasized that citizenship applies to those born in Uganda, those of Ugandan descent, and eligible foreigners, calling for grassroots reviews to ensure proper documentation. Despite this, some Rwandans are still waiting for their papers.

title: Boulos: Peace Will Take Time
excerpt: Great Lakes Region, 4 February 2026 – Massad Boulos, Special Advisor to the US President for African Affairs, stated that achieving peace in the Great Lakes region will be a long-term process. He emphasized that stability will not come immediately, noting that the region faces on
title_en: Boulos: Peace Will Take Time
excerpt_en: Great Lakes Region, 4 February 2026 – Massad Boulos, Special Advisor to the US President for African Affairs, stated that achieving peace in the Great Lakes region will be a long-term process. He emphasized that stability will not come immediately, noting that the region faces on
body_en:
Great Lakes Region, 4 February 2026 – Massad Boulos, Special Advisor to the US President for African Affairs, stated that achieving peace in the Great Lakes region will be a long-term process. He emphasized that stability will not come immediately, noting that the region faces ongoing challenges and obstacles.
Boulos recalled that on 4 December 2025, Rwanda and the DRC signed a peace agreement with US support, backing the Doha talks aimed at ending the war in North Kivu and South Kivu.
He noted that when AFC/M23 captured Uvira on 9 December 2025, the US condemned the action, although the group explained it was intended to stop attacks by DRC, Burundian, Wazalendo, FDLR forces, and mercenaries against civilians in Minembwe.
During a briefing on humanitarian operations in the DRC and Sudan on 3 February 2026, Boulos said the US remains concerned about Uvira and that AFC/M23 was asked to withdraw its fighters, which they did.
He highlighted the Doha peace talks and the ceasefire monitoring agreement with MONUSCO, signed on 2 February 2026 with Qatar’s support, as major steps toward stability.
Boulos stated, “Peace is a journey and it will take time. Here and there we will encounter obstacles. There will be challenges, but we must be firm and we are very firm. President Trump is firm. He signed as a witness, he is firm.”
Meanwhile, AFC/M23 continues to accuse the DRC government of violating the ceasefire and targeting civilians, pledging on 3 February to combat these violations directly.

title: UK and DRC Reach Agreement on Repatriation of Illegal Migrants
excerpt: London / Kinshasa – 06/02/2026 – The United Kingdom and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) have reached an agreement to repatriate Congolese nationals who entered the UK illegally or have criminal convictions. The accord also allows Congolese citizens to legally enter the UK.
title_en: UK and DRC Reach Agreement on Repatriation of Illegal Migrants
excerpt_en: London / Kinshasa – 06/02/2026 – The United Kingdom and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) have reached an agreement to repatriate Congolese nationals who entered the UK illegally or have criminal convictions. The accord also allows Congolese citizens to legally enter the UK.
body_en:
London / Kinshasa – 06/02/2026 – The United Kingdom and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) have reached an agreement to repatriate Congolese nationals who entered the UK illegally or have criminal convictions. The accord also allows Congolese citizens to legally enter the UK.
UK Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood welcomed the partnership, stating that illegal entrants and criminals from the DRC will be repatriated swiftly. She added that similar arrangements are expected for citizens of Namibia and Angola.
The agreement follows Britain’s warning to countries that refuse to accept their citizens, which could face consequences under UK immigration policy.
“My message is clear. If governments in these countries refuse to take in their citizens, they will bear the consequences,” Mahmood said.
The UK continues to grapple with illegal immigration, with the Home Office reporting 41,472 illegal arrivals by boat in 2025, the second-highest number since 2018, following 45,774 arrivals in 2022.
AFC/M23 Accuses African Union Commission of Supporting Crimes in DRC
Kisangani, Tshopo February 6, 2026 – The AFC/M23 alliance has accused the African Union (AU) Commission of supporting crimes committed by the FARDC. Between the night of 31 January and 1 February 2026, the alliance carried out a drone attack against a military facility at Bangoka Airport in Kisangani, Tshopo province.
The AFC/M23 said the attack targeted the installation because the FARDC allegedly use it to strike their bases and civilian populations in North Kivu and South Kivu.
On 6 February, AU Commission President Mahmoud Ali Youssouf condemned the operation, expressing concern that the attack on a facility in a major city could endanger civilians and violate international law. Mahmoud noted that, despite no evidence of the airport’s military use, the attack was considered an assault on a civilian base, labeling it an act of terrorism.
In response, AFC/M23 Secretary General Benjamin Mbonimpa reminded the AU that DRC government forces have conducted drone strikes against their positions and civilians in areas including Minembwe, Kalehe, Masisi, and Rutshuru.
“The drone operation was strictly military, no civilians were involved, and it aimed to protect innocent civilians, in line with the Doha ceasefire,’’ Mbonimpa said.
The alliance criticized the AU for condemning the security operation without investigation, arguing that this shows bias and raises questions about its ability to conduct peace talks in the DRC.
“By siding with a government that has committed serious violations against its population, rather than supporting the victims, the AU undermines its credibility. Labeling an operation that saved lives as terrorism represents a step back for the African Union,” the AFC/M23 statement said.
According to sources, the AFC/M23 deployed eight drones against Bangoka Airport, while the DRC government claims to have destroyed most of them.

title: FBI Investigates 2024 Coup Attempt in Kinshasa
excerpt: Kinshasa, DRC – February 7, 2026 – The United States Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is investigating a failed coup attempt that occurred in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) in 2024. On the morning of 19 May 2024, armed men led by Congolese-American Christian Malanga
title_en: FBI Investigates 2024 Coup Attempt in Kinshasa
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, DRC – February 7, 2026 – The United States Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is investigating a failed coup attempt that occurred in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) in 2024. On the morning of 19 May 2024, armed men led by Congolese-American Christian Malanga
body_en:
Kinshasa, DRC – February 7, 2026 – The United States Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is investigating a failed coup attempt that occurred in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) in 2024.
On the morning of 19 May 2024, armed men led by Congolese-American Christian Malanga stormed the presidential palace, claiming to have overthrown President Félix Tshisekedi. They also attacked the homes of senior officials, including former Economy Minister Vital Kamerhe, killing several of his bodyguards, and former Defense Minister Jean-Pierre Bemba.
Tshisekedi’s security forces engaged the assailants in a violent battle at the palace, killing Malanga and arresting several individuals, including his son Marcel and other Americans: Tyler Thomson, Benjamin Zalman-Polun, and Joseph Peter.
Those arrested at the presidential palace were sentenced to death, but American nationals were extradited to the U.S. in April 2025 for trial in their country of origin.
The U.S. Department of Justice announced charges including conspiracy to support terrorist acts, use of weapons of mass destruction, attacks on state infrastructure, and conspiracy to commit murder or kidnapping.
According to Radio France Internationale (RFI), prior to their trial in Utah in March 2026, two FBI agents traveled to Kinshasa to investigate the crimes and assess the damage caused by the coup attempt.
Officials expected to be questioned include investigators, prosecutors, defense attorneys, and judges involved at all levels in the case.
Conclusion
In summary, the report highlights a period of significant diplomatic tension and internal reform in Rwanda and the broader Great Lakes region from late January to early February 2026. Domestically, Rwanda is advancing its digital governance and export goals while addressing social security and tax compliance. Regionally, however, the situation remains fragile, characterized by escalating friction with Burundi and the DRC, ongoing conflict in eastern Congo, and the controversial use of foreign mercenaries. These developments underscore a complex landscape where Rwanda continues to strive for economic progress and international recognition while navigating deep-rooted regional security challenges.
By Jeff Buleli

title: Nyarugabo Warns Tshisekedi and Ndayishimiye Over Civilian Deaths in Minembwe
excerpt: February 9, 2026 – Lawyer and former Minister of Economy and Senator Moïse Nyarugabo has issued a stark warning to President Félix Tshisekedi of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and his Burundian counterpart Evariste Ndayishimiye, declaring that they will be held accountable
title_en: Nyarugabo Warns Tshisekedi and Ndayishimiye Over Civilian Deaths in Minembwe
excerpt_en: February 9, 2026 – Lawyer and former Minister of Economy and Senator Moïse Nyarugabo has issued a stark warning to President Félix Tshisekedi of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and his Burundian counterpart Evariste Ndayishimiye, declaring that they will be held accountable
body_en:
February 9, 2026 – Lawyer and former Minister of Economy and Senator Moïse Nyarugabo has issued a stark warning to President Félix Tshisekedi of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and his Burundian counterpart Evariste Ndayishimiye, declaring that they will be held accountable for the blood of innocent civilians.
According to Nyarugabo, since the early hours of February 8, 2026, multiple drones deployed by the DRC and Burundi have targeted villages of the Banyamulenge in the Minembwe commune while residents were asleep, causing deaths and injuries.
“These drones have returned repeatedly, firing during both day and night. Their bombs and long-range gunfire have caused casualties in villages including Bicumbi, Mutunda, Ruhemba, and Karongi,” Nyarugabo said.
He added that these attacks are part of a series of assaults by the DRC-Burundi military alliance, which have occurred in areas such as Rugezi, Rwitsankuku, Baruta, Point-Zéro, Mukoko, Gakenke, Biziba, and Runundu over the past days.
“I condemn these acts of genocide in Minembwe and against the Banyamulenge, carried out by Mr. Tshisekedi and the Kinshasa government, alongside his accomplice Mr. Evariste Ndayishimiye and the Burundian government. You will be held accountable for the blood of these innocents, one way or another,” he warned.

title: Nduhungirehe Questions UN and AU Over Alleged Use of Mercenaries in DRC
excerpt: Kigali February 11, 2026 - Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, Olivier Nduhungirehe, has called on the United Nations Security Council and the African Union to clarify whether they will continue to remain silent over what he described as the unlawful use of merc
title_en: Nduhungirehe Questions UN and AU Over Alleged Use of Mercenaries in DRC
excerpt_en: Kigali February 11, 2026 - Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, Olivier Nduhungirehe, has called on the United Nations Security Council and the African Union to clarify whether they will continue to remain silent over what he described as the unlawful use of merc
body_en:
Kigali February 11, 2026 - Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, Olivier Nduhungirehe, has called on the United Nations Security Council and the African Union to clarify whether they will continue to remain silent over what he described as the unlawful use of mercenaries by the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
His remarks follow reports that American security contractor Erik Prince deployed personnel to South Kivu to assist Congolese forces in efforts to retake Uvira from the M23/AFC coalition. The contractors were reportedly involved in operating drone systems during military operations.
In a statement released by his ministry, Nduhungirehe argued that the recruitment and use of mercenaries constitute a violation of international law. He cited the 1977 OAU Convention for the Elimination of Mercenarism in Africa, adopted in Libreville, and the 1989 International Convention against the Recruitment, Use, Financing and Training of Mercenaries, adopted by the UN General Assembly, both of which prohibit such practices.
“Through the repeated use of foreign mercenaries, the DRC government is violating the norms of the international community,” the minister said, accusing Kinshasa of disregarding binding continental and international legal frameworks.
He further questioned whether international institutions would continue to observe what he described as ongoing violations. “Will the UN Security Council, the African Union and the international community in general continue to remain silent while these international laws are being violated?” he asked.
The Congolese government has previously faced allegations of relying on foreign fighters in its conflict with the AFC/M23. Such accusations intensified after the armed group captured Goma, where European contractors — reportedly including Romanian nationals — were seen withdrawing before returning to their home countries.
Following those developments, Kinshasa is said to have turned to Erik Prince for additional security support, a move that has further heightened regional diplomatic tensions amid the ongoing crisis in eastern Congo.

title: U.S. Lawmakers Urge DRC to Dismantle FDLR as Condition for Rwanda Security Withdrawal
excerpt: WASHINGTON, February 11, 2026 — Members of the U.S. House of Representatives Africa Subcommittee have reminded the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo that Rwanda is expected to lift its security measures only after the dismantling of the FDLR. In a statement issue
title_en: U.S. Lawmakers Urge DRC to Dismantle FDLR as Condition for Rwanda Security Withdrawal
excerpt_en: WASHINGTON, February 11, 2026 — Members of the U.S. House of Representatives Africa Subcommittee have reminded the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo that Rwanda is expected to lift its security measures only after the dismantling of the FDLR. In a statement issue
body_en:
WASHINGTON, February 11, 2026 — Members of the U.S. House of Representatives Africa Subcommittee have reminded the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo that Rwanda is expected to lift its security measures only after the dismantling of the FDLR.
In a statement issued on February 10, Congresswoman Sara Jacobs said that despite a U.S.-brokered peace arrangement between Kigali and Kinshasa, reports indicate elements of the Congolese army continue cooperating with the armed group.
“On the part of the DRC military, in violation of the peace agreement, it is said to continue working with the FDLR, a group founded by leaders who organized the 1994 genocide in Rwanda,” she said.
Subcommittee chairman Chris Smith emphasized that Rwanda’s commitment to remove defensive measures depends on full implementation of the agreement’s provisions, particularly the neutralization of the militia.
“The Washington Peace Agreement includes a four-stage action plan agreed to by both parties. This is essential for Rwanda to withdraw its forces, but only if the DRC follows through on a comprehensive plan to dismantle the FDLR,” he said.
Lawmakers also warned that the genocidal ideology associated with the group remains a security concern for Rwanda and areas under control of the AFC/M23, urging efforts to mobilize combatants to disarm.
Kigali has already launched reintegration initiatives through the Rwanda Demobilization and Reintegration Commission, including the Isange mu Banyu program encouraging Rwandan fighters in eastern Congo to return home.
Authorities, local residents and former rebels have continued awareness campaigns in the forests of eastern Congo, particularly targeting fighters originating from Rubavu District, which officials say accounts for a majority of returnees.
In November 2025, the commission’s vice president Jacques Nziza noted that about 70 percent of former FDLR members who repatriated came from that region, explaining why the area remains central to demobilization efforts.

title: Rwanda Grants Citizenship to 1,500 Foreigners Since 2009
excerpt: KIGALI, February 12, 2026 — The Rwanda Immigration Service announced that since 2009, Rwanda has granted citizenship to 1,500 foreigners, drawn to the country for its security, peace, cleanliness, and ease of investment. Rusanganwa Jean Damascène, Director of Citizenship Services
title_en: Rwanda Grants Citizenship to 1,500 Foreigners Since 2009
excerpt_en: KIGALI, February 12, 2026 — The Rwanda Immigration Service announced that since 2009, Rwanda has granted citizenship to 1,500 foreigners, drawn to the country for its security, peace, cleanliness, and ease of investment. Rusanganwa Jean Damascène, Director of Citizenship Services
body_en:
KIGALI, February 12, 2026 — The Rwanda Immigration Service announced that since 2009, Rwanda has granted citizenship to 1,500 foreigners, drawn to the country for its security, peace, cleanliness, and ease of investment.
Rusanganwa Jean Damascène, Director of Citizenship Services, told RBA that the latest round included 101 individuals, with 80 residing in Rwanda and 21 in Rwandan embassies abroad, who will gradually receive their citizenship.
Citizenship is granted based on criteria such as birth in Rwanda, adoption on Rwandan soil, marriage, national interests, special knowledge or talents, large investments, residence in Rwanda, or honorary recognition. Rusanganwa emphasized that naturalized citizens have the same rights and obligations as all Rwandans, without distinctions by ethnic group, noting that the previous categories of Hutu, Tutsi, Twa, and Naturalized no longer apply.
Regarding revocation, Organic Law No. 002/2021.OL of July 16, 2021, allows citizenship to be revoked under four circumstances: use of fraudulent documents, betrayal of the Republic, marriages intended solely to gain citizenship, or behavior contrary to Rwandan values. To date, no naturalized citizen has had their Rwandan citizenship revoked.
The authority to grant Rwandan citizenship lies with the Cabinet, while citizenship granted on the basis of merit is under the discretion of the President of the Republic of Rwanda.

body_en:
ADDIS ABABA, February 13, 2026 — Justin Nsengiyumva represented Paul Kagame at the Africa–Italy Summit held in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, ahead of the 39th Ordinary Session of the African Union Heads of State and Government.
Arriving on the afternoon of February 13, the Prime Minister immediately joined the high-level proceedings, which focused on sustainable access to clean water, sanitation, and hygiene, in line with Africa’s long-term development framework, Agenda 2063. Participants also assessed progress in political and economic cooperation between Italy and African nations under the Mattei Plan.
The summit marked the second edition of the Africa–Italy meeting, following the inaugural gathering in Rome in 2024. Rwanda and Italy maintain longstanding diplomatic relations, further strengthened in 2024 through a €50 million agreement supporting environmental protection projects in Rwanda.
The Addis Ababa engagement highlights Kigali’s sustained multilateral diplomacy, reinforcing partnerships aimed at economic growth, sustainable development, and continental integration.

title: EU Parliament Calls on Uganda to Release Opposition Members
excerpt: BRUSSELS, February 13, 2026 — The European Union Parliament has adopted a resolution condemning violence and the detention of opposition members before and after the January 15, 2026 elections in Uganda. The resolution highlights human rights violations, including internet shutdo
title_en: EU Parliament Calls on Uganda to Release Opposition Members
excerpt_en: BRUSSELS, February 13, 2026 — The European Union Parliament has adopted a resolution condemning violence and the detention of opposition members before and after the January 15, 2026 elections in Uganda. The resolution highlights human rights violations, including internet shutdo
body_en:
BRUSSELS, February 13, 2026 — The European Union Parliament has adopted a resolution condemning violence and the detention of opposition members before and after the January 15, 2026 elections in Uganda.
The resolution highlights human rights violations, including internet shutdowns, political violence, and the detention of members of the National Unity Platform, led by Robert Kyagulanyi. Following the elections, President Yoweri Museveni secured 71.6% of the vote, while Kyagulanyi went into exile, alleging that the Ugandan military besieged his home and attempted to arrest him.
In its February 12, 2026 resolution, the EU Parliament called for the release of all unlawfully detained individuals and urged Uganda to stop trying civilians in military courts and reveal the whereabouts of missing persons.
The resolution notes that detained opposition figures include Dr. Kiiza Besigye, held for over a year, and Robert Kyagulanyi, who fled into exile in January 2026.

title: Tshisekedi ‘Agrees’ to Respect Angola-Requested Ceasefire, But Violations Continue
excerpt: KINSHASA, February 13, 2026 — President Félix Tshisekedi has announced that DRC government forces will respect a ceasefire called for by his João Lourenço, in coordination with the African Union. According to the Presidential Office, the ceasefire requires both the government and
title_en: Tshisekedi ‘Agrees’ to Respect Angola-Requested Ceasefire, But Violations Continue
excerpt_en: KINSHASA, February 13, 2026 — President Félix Tshisekedi has announced that DRC government forces will respect a ceasefire called for by his João Lourenço, in coordination with the African Union. According to the Presidential Office, the ceasefire requires both the government and
body_en:
KINSHASA, February 13, 2026 — President Félix Tshisekedi has announced that DRC government forces will respect a ceasefire called for by his João Lourenço, in coordination with the African Union. According to the Presidential Office, the ceasefire requires both the government and the AFC/M23 coalition to remain in current positions, stop reinforcing fighting areas, refrain from repositioning to launch attacks, and halt external assistance.
The agreement, based on the Doha peace process signed on October 15, 2025, also establishes a monitoring body to track compliance. The Angolan government had requested the ceasefire to begin on February 18, following consultations with Tshisekedi and mediators including Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé and Olusegun Obasanjo.
Despite Tshisekedi’s announcement, ceasefire violations by the DRC government have persisted. AFC/M23 forces have repeatedly responded, citing the principle of “destroying evil at its source”, and have seized key areas including Goma and Bukavu.
On February 12, Olivier Nduhungirehe, Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, expressed skepticism over the DRC’s commitment, saying:
“We can always negotiate peace agreements or ceasefire declarations, but as long as Kinshasa does not stop airstrikes and heavy artillery, and President Tshisekedi insists on a military solution, while the international community overlooks these violations, it will be futile.”
On February 13, Benjamin Mbonimpa, Permanent Secretary of AFC/M23, stated that Angola had not formally informed the alliance of the ceasefire request, reaffirming that AFC/M23 continues to respect the Doha process. He added:
“We were not invited, we do not know its contents. We have always respected the ceasefire and many times announced it ourselves.”
Mbonimpa also accused the DRC government of further violating the ceasefire on February 13 and expressed confidence that MONUSCO troops will properly monitor compliance.
body_fr:
KINSHASA, February 13, 2026 — President Félix Tshisekedi has announced that DRC government forces will respect a ceasefire called for by his João Lourenço, in coordination with the African Union. According to the Presidential Office, the ceasefire requires both the government and the AFC/M23 coalition to remain in current positions, stop reinforcing fighting areas, refrain from repositioning to launch attacks, and halt external assistance.
The agreement, based on the Doha peace process signed on October 15, 2025, also establishes a monitoring body to track compliance. The Angolan government had requested the ceasefire to begin on February 18, following consultations with Tshisekedi and mediators including Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé and Olusegun Obasanjo.
Despite Tshisekedi’s announcement, ceasefire violations by the DRC government have persisted. AFC/M23 forces have repeatedly responded, citing the principle of “destroying evil at its source”, and have seized key areas including Goma and Bukavu.
On February 12, Olivier Nduhungirehe, Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, expressed skepticism over the DRC’s commitment, saying:
“We can always negotiate peace agreements or ceasefire declarations, but as long as Kinshasa does not stop airstrikes and heavy artillery, and President Tshisekedi insists on a military solution, while the international community overlooks these violations, it will be futile.”
On February 13, Benjamin Mbonimpa, Permanent Secretary of AFC/M23, stated that Angola had not formally informed the alliance of the ceasefire request, reaffirming that AFC/M23 continues to respect the Doha process. He added:
“We were not invited, we do not know its contents. We have always respected the ceasefire and many times announced it ourselves.”
Mbonimpa also accused the DRC government of further violating the ceasefire on February 13 and expressed confidence that MONUSCO troops will properly monitor compliance.

MUNICH, February 14, 2026 — A Rwandan government delegation led by Vincent Biruta, Minister of Security, and Juvenal Marizamunda, Minister of Defence, is participating in the Munich Security Conference 2026 (MSC 2026), which opened on February 13 and runs through February 15 in Munich, Germany.
According to Rwanda’s Ministry of Defence, the delegation took part in a series of high-level discussions, presenting Rwanda’s perspective on the current international political and security landscape. The meetings brought together heads of state and government, senior policymakers, and global security experts from multiple continents.
The delegation also held bilateral talks with representatives of friendly nations, focusing on advancing shared interests and strategic cooperation.
The Munich Security Conference, now in its 62nd edition, is being hosted at the Hotel Bayerischer Hof and Rosewood Munich. Approximately 50 heads of state and government, alongside key international decision-makers, are expected to attend.
The annual gathering serves as a major platform for debating global security challenges, including geopolitical tensions, armed conflicts, and emerging threats to international stability.

title_en: Mia Amor Mottley Reaffirms Commitment to Rwanda After Re-Election
excerpt_en: BRIDGETOWN, February 15, 2026 — Mia Amor Mottley, re-elected for a third term as Prime Minister of Barbados, has reaffirmed her commitment to strengthening bilateral ties with Rwanda following her decisive electoral victory. After securing a landslide win in the parliamentary ele
body_en:
BRIDGETOWN, February 15, 2026 — Mia Amor Mottley, re-elected for a third term as Prime Minister of Barbados, has reaffirmed her commitment to strengthening bilateral ties with Rwanda following her decisive electoral victory.
After securing a landslide win in the parliamentary elections — with her party, the Barbados Labour Party, winning all 30 seats — Mottley thanked Paul Kagame for his congratulatory message and underscored the importance of continued cooperation between the two nations.
President Kagame had earlier congratulated her, calling the victory well deserved.
In response, Mottley expressed appreciation for what she described as a friendship rooted in mutual respect and shared development goals. She emphasized that Barbados places great value on its relationship with Rwanda and looks forward to deepening collaboration aimed at protecting dignity, expanding opportunities, and advancing prosperity for their respective populations.
Growing Strategic Partnership
Relations between Rwanda and Barbados have strengthened in recent years through agreements in areas including air transport and sports cooperation. A key component of this partnership has involved collaboration with RwandAir to enhance air connectivity.
In November 2022, Prime Minister Mottley inaugurated Barbados’ embassy in Kigali during an official working visit — a move that followed President Kagame’s visit to Barbados earlier the same year. Those engagements led to the signing of multiple cooperation agreements.
Barbados, a Caribbean island known for its thriving tourism sector and investor-friendly climate, has increasingly sought to expand its diplomatic and economic partnerships beyond the region.
The renewed mandate for Prime Minister Mottley is expected to further consolidate ties between Bridgetown and Kigali as both countries pursue expanded South–South cooperation.

title: United States Urges DRC to Respect Upcoming Ceasefire
excerpt: KINSHASA, February 15, 2026 — Massad Boulos, Senior Advisor on African Affairs to the U.S. President, has called on the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo to fully respect the ceasefire agreed on February 13 and expected to take effect on February 18. The presiden
title_en: United States Urges DRC to Respect Upcoming Ceasefire
excerpt_en: KINSHASA, February 15, 2026 — Massad Boulos, Senior Advisor on African Affairs to the U.S. President, has called on the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo to fully respect the ceasefire agreed on February 13 and expected to take effect on February 18. The presiden
body_en:
KINSHASA, February 15, 2026 — Massad Boulos, Senior Advisor on African Affairs to the U.S. President, has called on the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo to fully respect the ceasefire agreed on February 13 and expected to take effect on February 18.
The presidency confirmed that Félix Tshisekedi accepted the truce proposed by Angola, current chair of the African Union (AU). Authorities, however, stressed that the government would not allow the rebel coalition AFC/M23 to expand positions, reinforce fighters, or receive foreign support during the ceasefire period.
Rebels Dispute Government Position
AFC/M23 leader Corneille Nangaa accused government forces of continuing attacks on civilians and rebel positions, describing the ceasefire announcement as an attempt to mislead the international community.
The group stated it had not been invited to the negotiations that preceded the Angolan proposal but said it supports the peace process and would respect the truce framework emerging from the Doha talks in Qatar.
Washington Calls for Concrete Action
Boulos welcomed Kinshasa’s acceptance of the ceasefire but emphasized that it must translate into real actions on the ground.
He urged all parties to immediately halt hostilities, including drone strikes, warning that civilians continue to be killed despite diplomatic commitments.
Implementation on the Ground
The Angolan initiative comes as the MONUSCO peacekeeping mission prepares to implement additional arrangements linked to the Doha discussions, particularly in Uvira territory in eastern DRC.
Diplomatic efforts are ongoing to stabilize the region amid persistent fighting and humanitarian concerns, with international actors pushing for the ceasefire to become a first step toward broader negotiations.

excerpt: KIGALI, February 12, 2026 — Ambassador Olivier Nduhungirehe, Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, expressed doubt over the Democratic Republic of Congo’s willingness to respect a new ceasefire proposed by João Lourenço. He cited the lack of political will demonstrated by
title_en: Rwanda’s Nduhungirehe Questions DRC’s Commitment to Angola-Proposed Ceasefire
excerpt_en: KIGALI, February 12, 2026 — Ambassador Olivier Nduhungirehe, Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, expressed doubt over the Democratic Republic of Congo’s willingness to respect a new ceasefire proposed by João Lourenço. He cited the lack of political will demonstrated by
body_en:
KIGALI, February 12, 2026 — Ambassador Olivier Nduhungirehe, Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, expressed doubt over the Democratic Republic of Congo’s willingness to respect a new ceasefire proposed by João Lourenço. He cited the lack of political will demonstrated by Kinshasa since previous agreements.
The Angolan government, acting on Lourenço’s authority as Chairperson of the African Union, requested that the ceasefire begin on February 18, 2026, while inter-Congolese peace talks are being prepared. Nduhungirehe recalled that in 2024, two ceasefires were declared, and in 2025, six peace or ceasefire agreements were signed, none of which the DRC government fully respected.
He stated:
“We can always negotiate peace agreements or ceasefires, but as long as Kinshasa does not stop airstrikes and heavy artillery, and President Tshisekedi insists on an impossible military solution, while the international community ignores these violations, it will be futile.”
The ceasefire request followed a meeting on February 9, 2026, between President Félix Tshisekedi, AU-appointed mediator Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé, and Olusegun Obasanjo, appointed by the East African Community (EAC) and Southern African Development Community (SADC).
The mediators emphasized that an AU-led inter-Congolese dialogue remains the only way to address the root causes of DRC’s conflict.

title: DRC Signals It Could Seek New Mining Partner if U.S. Deal Falters
excerpt: CAPE TOWN, February 11, 2026 — Louis Watum Kabamba, Minister of Mineral Resources of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, said Kinshasa may look for another mining partner if its agreement with the United States fails to deliver benefits. He made the remarks at the Mining Indaba
title_en: DRC Signals It Could Seek New Mining Partner if U.S. Deal Falters
excerpt_en: CAPE TOWN, February 11, 2026 — Louis Watum Kabamba, Minister of Mineral Resources of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, said Kinshasa may look for another mining partner if its agreement with the United States fails to deliver benefits. He made the remarks at the Mining Indaba
body_en:
CAPE TOWN, February 11, 2026 — Louis Watum Kabamba, Minister of Mineral Resources of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, said Kinshasa may look for another mining partner if its agreement with the United States fails to deliver benefits. He made the remarks at the Mining Indaba in Cape Town.
The agreement, signed on December 4, 2025, allows American investors access to several mining sites in exchange for U.S. support in strengthening the DRC’s security systems. Kabamba stressed the deal remains at a preliminary stage and has not transferred ownership of resources.
“It could result in a good and big project, or another that is not very profitable. We will continue because there are many partners to discuss,” he said, adding:“We have not sold anything and we will not sell anything if we do not profit.”
Despite its vast resources, the minister noted that only about 10% of the country’s minerals are currently exploited. He also downplayed the geopolitical competition between Washington and Beijing, saying the DRC would prioritize its own national interests.
Earlier in January 2026, Kinshasa reportedly sent Washington a list of targeted resources including manganese, gold, lithium, copper, and cobalt, key materials for electric vehicle batteries and electronics manufacturing. Potential sites include Kisenge and Mutoshi (Lualaba), Moto (Haut-Uélé), Kilo (Ituri), as well as deposits in North Kivu, South Kivu, and Maniema.

title: Before U.S. Congress, Byamungu Says DRC Must Address Internal Failures Instead of Blaming Rwanda

title_en: Before U.S. Congress, Byamungu Says DRC Must Address Internal Failures Instead of Blaming Rwanda
excerpt_en: WASHINGTON, D.C., February 11, 2026 — Appearing before members of the U.S. Congress, Umunye-Congo researcher Christian-Géraud Neema Byamungu argued that the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) should not place primary blame on Rwanda for its persistent instability, warning that su
body_en:
WASHINGTON, D.C., February 11, 2026 — Appearing before members of the U.S. Congress, Umunye-Congo researcher Christian-Géraud Neema Byamungu argued that the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) should not place primary blame on Rwanda for its persistent instability, warning that such an approach risks overlooking the country’s deeper structural problems.
Byamungu told lawmakers that focusing solely on Kigali would be “like treating a disease with the wrong medicine.” While acknowledging accusations that Rwanda has undermined security in eastern Congo, he stressed that multiple armed groups operating within the DRC are major drivers of violence.
“Stopping Rwanda alone will not solve the problem of armed groups in the DRC such as the ADF,” he said, referring to the Allied Democratic Forces, which has been blamed for deadly attacks in the east. “The ADF kills hundreds of people almost every week, but there is little mention of CODECO, Red Tabara, the Wazalendo, or the Mobondo militia near Kinshasa.”
Byamungu further emphasized that externalizing responsibility would not address what he described as chronic poor governance, misappropriation of resources, and weak state institutions. According to him, these longstanding deficiencies have enabled armed groups to flourish for more than two decades.
“It will not solve the problem of poor governance, incompetent institutions, and the systemic weaknesses that allow these groups to grow,” he stated. “If these root causes remain unaddressed, insecurity will return, as it has repeatedly over the past 20 years.”
The researcher also challenged the widely held assumption that precious minerals are the principal driver of violence in the DRC. While acknowledging their role in criminal networks, he argued that many conflicts stem from communal tensions, disputes over traditional leadership, and the rise of self-defense groups formed in response to state failures.
“For many years, insecurity in the DRC has been caused by reasons other than precious metals,” Byamungu said. “Resources are sometimes used for criminal activities, but they are not the primary cause of the crisis.”
He concluded by urging U.S. policymakers to adopt a more comprehensive approach to the Congolese crisis—one that not only seeks to end current conflicts but also prevents future ones. Key stakeholders, he noted, must include civil society organizations, religious institutions, and church leaders, whose involvement he described as essential for sustainable peace.
Byamungu’s remarks come amid heightened diplomatic attention on the Great Lakes region, as Washington reassesses its engagement strategy in Central Africa.

WASHINGTON, D.C., February 11, 2026 — Appearing before members of the U.S. Congress, Umunye-Congo researcher Christian-Géraud Neema Byamungu argued that the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) should not place primary blame on Rwanda for its persistent instability, warning that such an approach risks overlooking the country’s deeper structural problems.
Byamungu told lawmakers that focusing solely on Kigali would be “like treating a disease with the wrong medicine.” While acknowledging accusations that Rwanda has undermined security in eastern Congo, he stressed that multiple armed groups operating within the DRC are major drivers of violence.
“Stopping Rwanda alone will not solve the problem of armed groups in the DRC such as the ADF,” he said, referring to the Allied Democratic Forces, which has been blamed for deadly attacks in the east. “The ADF kills hundreds of people almost every week, but there is little mention of CODECO, Red Tabara, the Wazalendo, or the Mobondo militia near Kinshasa.”
Byamungu further emphasized that externalizing responsibility would not address what he described as chronic poor governance, misappropriation of resources, and weak state institutions. According to him, these longstanding deficiencies have enabled armed groups to flourish for more than two decades.
“It will not solve the problem of poor governance, incompetent institutions, and the systemic weaknesses that allow these groups to grow,” he stated. “If these root causes remain unaddressed, insecurity will return, as it has repeatedly over the past 20 years.”
The researcher also challenged the widely held assumption that precious minerals are the principal driver of violence in the DRC. While acknowledging their role in criminal networks, he argued that many conflicts stem from communal tensions, disputes over traditional leadership, and the rise of self-defense groups formed in response to state failures.
“For many years, insecurity in the DRC has been caused by reasons other than precious metals,” Byamungu said. “Resources are sometimes used for criminal activities, but they are not the primary cause of the crisis.”
He concluded by urging U.S. policymakers to adopt a more comprehensive approach to the Congolese crisis—one that not only seeks to end current conflicts but also prevents future ones. Key stakeholders, he noted, must include civil society organizations, religious institutions, and church leaders, whose involvement he described as essential for sustainable peace.
Byamungu’s remarks come amid heightened diplomatic attention on the Great Lakes region, as Washington reassesses its engagement strategy in Central Africa.

title: Rwanda Criticizes Belgian MP Over Meeting With Paul Rusesabagina
excerpt: Kigali Rwanda February 10, 2026 - Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, Olivier Nduhungirehe, has condemned Belgian lawmaker Lydia Mutyebele Ngoi after she publicly expressed support for Paul Rusesabagina, who was convicted in Rwanda on terrorism-related charges.
title_en: Rwanda Criticizes Belgian MP Over Meeting With Paul Rusesabagina
excerpt_en: Kigali Rwanda February 10, 2026 - Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, Olivier Nduhungirehe, has condemned Belgian lawmaker Lydia Mutyebele Ngoi after she publicly expressed support for Paul Rusesabagina, who was convicted in Rwanda on terrorism-related charges.
body_en:
Kigali Rwanda February 10, 2026 - Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, Olivier Nduhungirehe, has condemned Belgian lawmaker Lydia Mutyebele Ngoi after she publicly expressed support for Paul Rusesabagina, who was convicted in Rwanda on terrorism-related charges.
On February 9, Mutyebele announced she had received Rusesabagina at the Belgian Parliament in Brussels, describing him as “a powerful voice for human rights” and thanking him for supporting the Democratic Republic of the Congo in its fight against the M23/AFC alliance, which she accused of seeking control of mineral resources.
In response, Nduhungirehe posted a list of civilians killed by the FLN, the armed group linked to Rusesabagina, arguing that praising him disregards victims of attacks carried out in southwestern Rwanda.
“Fighting for dignity clearly means supporting criminals convicted of terrorism,” the minister wrote, criticizing what he described as indifference toward victims of the FLN’s violence.
Rusesabagina — a former head of the MRCD coalition — was arrested in Kigali in August 2020 and later convicted by Rwanda’s High Court chamber for international crimes for terrorism-related offenses, including backing attacks in 2018 and 2019. He was sentenced to 25 years in prison.
On March 24, 2023, he was released following a presidential pardon granted by President Paul Kagame, after requesting specialized medical treatment. He currently resides in San Antonio, Texas, and holds permanent U.S. residency as well as Belgian citizenship.
The exchange underscores ongoing diplomatic tensions surrounding Rusesabagina’s case, which continues to draw sharply divided reactions among political figures internationally.

title: Ruto and Nsengiyumva Agree to Strengthen Rwanda–Kenya Ties
excerpt: Addis Ababa February 15, 2026 — Kenyan President William Ruto and Rwandan Prime Minister Justin Nsengiyumva have agreed to further reinforce diplomatic and economic relations between their two countries. The talks took place on the sidelines of the 39th Ordinary Session of the Af
title_en: Ruto and Nsengiyumva Agree to Strengthen Rwanda–Kenya Ties
excerpt_en: Addis Ababa February 15, 2026 — Kenyan President William Ruto and Rwandan Prime Minister Justin Nsengiyumva have agreed to further reinforce diplomatic and economic relations between their two countries. The talks took place on the sidelines of the 39th Ordinary Session of the Af
body_en:
Addis Ababa February 15, 2026 — Kenyan President William Ruto and Rwandan Prime Minister Justin Nsengiyumva have agreed to further reinforce diplomatic and economic relations between their two countries.
The talks took place on the sidelines of the 39th Ordinary Session of the African Union Summit in Addis Ababa, where Nsengiyumva represented President Paul Kagame.
In a message posted on X, President Ruto said the discussions focused on strengthening bilateral cooperation.
“I met with the Prime Minister of Rwanda, Mr. Justin Nsengiyumva, following the 39th Ordinary Summit of the Heads of State and Government of the African Union in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. We agreed to strengthen our diplomatic relations and partnerships with other countries, in our common interest, to contribute to the development of Africa and the world,” Ruto stated.
The Prime Minister’s Office also confirmed that Nsengiyumva held talks with Namibian President Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah during the summit.
Strong and Expanding Economic Links
Rwanda and Kenya maintain long-standing and robust ties, particularly in trade and investment.
Kenyan banks — including Equity Bank, KCB Bank, I&M Bank, and NCBA Bank — have established a strong presence in Rwanda’s financial sector.
In higher education, Kenyan institutions such as Mount Kigali University operate in Rwanda.
Air connectivity also remains strong, with Kenya Airways and Jambojet serving the Rwandan market.
The renewed commitment announced in Addis Ababa signals continued momentum in Rwanda–Kenya cooperation, with both governments positioning their partnership as a driver of regional integration and African development.
