title: Burundian Team Poised to Support Ndayishimiye’s AU Leadership
excerpt: Addis Ababa February 16, 2026 — Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye is assembling a team of trusted officials and diplomats to support his one-year tenure at the helm of the African Union (AU), with a focus on advancing the bloc’s economic and security agenda. Ndayishimiye
title_en: Burundian Team Poised to Support Ndayishimiye’s AU Leadership
excerpt_en: Addis Ababa February 16, 2026 — Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye is assembling a team of trusted officials and diplomats to support his one-year tenure at the helm of the African Union (AU), with a focus on advancing the bloc’s economic and security agenda. Ndayishimiye
body_en:
Addis Ababa February 16, 2026 — Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye is assembling a team of trusted officials and diplomats to support his one-year tenure at the helm of the African Union (AU), with a focus on advancing the bloc’s economic and security agenda.
Ndayishimiye officially assumed the rotating presidency of the AU on February 14, 2026, succeeding Angolan President João Lourenço. In line with the organization’s rotational principles, he is expected to hand over leadership next year to the President of Ghana.
Key Figures in the Inner Circle
Among the prominent figures expected to play a central role is Burundi’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Dr. Édouard Bizimana. A seasoned diplomat, Bizimana previously served under former President Pierre Nkurunziza before being appointed special advisor to Ndayishimiye in August 2022. In August 2025, he was named Foreign Minister, replacing Albert Shingiro, who had held the post since June 2020.
Ndayishimiye and Bizimana share longstanding ties, having both originated from Gitega province and studied at the University of Burundi — a relationship seen as reinforcing political trust at the highest level of government.
Diplomatic and Security Support
Burundi’s Ambassador to Ethiopia and the AU, Willy Nyamitwe, is also viewed as a key asset, given his experience in Addis Ababa, where the AU is headquartered. Though he is nearing the end of his current posting, he is expected to remain influential in supporting the AU presidency.
Other diplomats who may join the presidential support team include Ambassador Ferdinand Bashikako, former Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs; Gaudence Sindayigaya, former Ambassador to the United States; Ambassador Thérence Ntahiraja in Belgium; and Jean Bosco Bare in Washington.
On security matters, former customs chief Joseph Ndarishikanye and Adolphe Hasabindero, known for his expertise in reintegration and rehabilitation of former soldiers, are among those being considered to provide technical backing.
Formation of a Strategic Taskforce
President Ndayishimiye is reportedly preparing to establish a core team of around ten members to coordinate his AU leadership, with five already confirmed. In parallel, a national committee dubbed “Cap2026” is set to be formed in Burundi to support strategic planning efforts tied to his continental mandate. Among those expected to contribute is Ambassador Adolphe Nahayo, Director-General for Cooperation in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
With a trusted circle of diplomats and technocrats, Ndayishimiye appears intent on consolidating Burundi’s diplomatic footprint while steering the African Union through a year marked by pressing economic and security challenges.

title: Danish Foreign Minister Visits Rwanda to Officially Open Embassy in Kigali
excerpt: Kigali, 16 February 2026 – Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen is in Rwanda for an official visit marked by the formal inauguration of Denmark’s embassy in Kigali, underscoring Copenhagen’s growing engagement with African countries. Lars Løkke Rasmussen arrived in Rwanda
title_en: Danish Foreign Minister Visits Rwanda to Officially Open Embassy in Kigali
excerpt_en: Kigali, 16 February 2026 – Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen is in Rwanda for an official visit marked by the formal inauguration of Denmark’s embassy in Kigali, underscoring Copenhagen’s growing engagement with African countries. Lars Løkke Rasmussen arrived in Rwanda
body_en:
Kigali, 16 February 2026 – Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen is in Rwanda for an official visit marked by the formal inauguration of Denmark’s embassy in Kigali, underscoring Copenhagen’s growing engagement with African countries.
Lars Løkke Rasmussen arrived in Rwanda on Sunday, 15 February 2026, as part of Denmark’s broader strategy to strengthen bilateral cooperation and deepen diplomatic and economic ties across the continent.
On Monday, the Danish minister and his delegation visited the Kigali Genocide Memorial in Gisozi, Gasabo District, where they were briefed on the history of the Genocide against the Tutsi. The delegation paid tribute to the victims laid to rest at the memorial site.
During his stay, the Danish top diplomat is expected to hold talks with his Rwandan counterpart, Amb. Olivier Nduhungirehe, focusing on enhancing partnerships, expanding economic cooperation, and exploring new avenues of collaboration between the two countries.
The minister will also engage with Danish entrepreneurs operating in Rwanda, discussing both the investment opportunities and challenges facing European businesses in the country. In addition, he is scheduled to visit the University of Rwanda, where he will meet with students to discuss opportunities for pursuing further studies in Europe.
Ahead of the visit, Lars Løkke Rasmussen described the opening of the embassy as part of Denmark’s expanding focus on Africa and its commitment to strengthening engagement with African nations. He highlighted Rwanda’s rapid development, particularly its ambitions in innovation, technology, and green solutions, noting that Danish expertise could contribute meaningfully to these sectors.
A key milestone of the visit is the official opening of the Danish Embassy in Rwanda, which began operations in August 2025. Denmark appointed Casper Stenger Jensen as its first resident ambassador to Rwanda. Based in Kigali, Ambassador Jensen has emphasized Denmark’s intention to further broaden and deepen its relations with Rwanda and other countries in the region.
The visit signals a new chapter in Denmark–Rwanda relations, anchored in diplomacy, trade, education, and sustainable development cooperation.

Speaking on February 17, 2026, Nduhungirehe reacted to an interview published on social media in which Marc Perelman of France 24 questioned Boulos on issues concerning Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).
“You will remember me to tell you how I feel when there is an impartial interview by a France 24 journalist. I am not interested in the way journalists or evaluators try to present themselves who always think about Rwanda,” Nduhungirehe said.
Debate Over the Washington Peace Agreement
The remarks come amid renewed debate over the Washington peace agreement signed on December 4, 2025, between Rwanda and Democratic Republic of the Congo with facilitation from the United States. The accord reinforced a previous agreement reached on June 27, 2025, but tensions have persisted since its signing.
In the February 16 interview, Perelman asked Boulos whether the agreement had failed to deliver tangible results. Boulos responded that the deal marked the beginning of a longer process toward regional stability.
“From the beginning, we said that the Washington peace agreement is not the end but the beginning. Eventually, there will be complete peace and security in the region. But that is a journey that will take time,” Boulos said.
He added that the agreement’s strength lies in its multi-track approach to addressing different aspects of the conflict. According to Boulos, the Washington accord—focused specifically on relations between Rwanda and the DRC—will be complemented by the Doha process, which seeks to facilitate dialogue between the Congolese government and the AFC/M23 rebellion, with backing from the United States and the African Union.
Tensions After Uvira’s Capture
The peace deal came under strain after AFC/M23 fighters captured the city of Uvira on December 9, 2025. Following the takeover, the Congolese government accused Rwanda of violating the Washington agreement and called on Washington to impose sanctions.
When asked whether the United States still had confidence in President Paul Kagame, Boulos replied, “We believe we do. We are talking.”
Allegations of Selective Questioning
Rwandan officials argue that the interview sought to portray Rwanda as the primary source of instability in eastern DRC, and that the journalist pressed Boulos on potential sanctions against Kigali while refraining from addressing other contentious issues.
Among them is the presence of the FDLR (Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda), an armed group operating in eastern DRC. The Congolese government has maintained that dismantling the group is complicated because many of its fighters are allegedly in areas controlled by AFC/M23.
However, Minister Nduhungirehe recently reiterated Rwanda’s position that numerous FDLR fighters have been integrated into the Congolese army and are operating in government-controlled zones.
The latest exchange highlights the ongoing diplomatic friction surrounding implementation of the Washington peace agreement, as regional and international actors continue efforts to stabilize eastern DRC.

title: Rwanda Holds Talks with Russian Nuclear Watchdog on Future Cooperation
excerpt: Moscow, February 18, 2026 – The Government of Rwanda is in discussions with the Russian nuclear regulatory agency, Rostekhnadzor, exploring potential cooperation on nuclear energy development. The talks took place on February 16, 2026, between Rwandan Ambassador to Russia Maj. Ge
title_en: Rwanda Holds Talks with Russian Nuclear Watchdog on Future Cooperation
excerpt_en: Moscow, February 18, 2026 – The Government of Rwanda is in discussions with the Russian nuclear regulatory agency, Rostekhnadzor, exploring potential cooperation on nuclear energy development. The talks took place on February 16, 2026, between Rwandan Ambassador to Russia Maj. Ge
body_en:
Moscow, February 18, 2026 – The Government of Rwanda is in discussions with the Russian nuclear regulatory agency, Rostekhnadzor, exploring potential cooperation on nuclear energy development.
The talks took place on February 16, 2026, between Rwandan Ambassador to Russia Maj. Gen. Joseph Nzabamwita and Rostekhnadzor Director Alexander Trembitsky in Moscow. During the meeting, Trembitsky explained the agency’s functions and expressed readiness to collaborate with Rwanda on nuclear facility supervision, technology transfer, and related areas.
Maj. Gen. Nzabamwita thanked Russia and President Vladimir Putin for supporting Rwanda and other African countries, while also acknowledging Rostekhnadzor’s willingness to cooperate. The discussions led to preparations for a cooperation agreement between Rostekhnadzor and Rwanda’s Public Utilities Regulatory Authority (RURA).
Rwanda’s Nuclear Ambitions
Rwanda aims to increase its electricity generation from the current 447 megawatts to over 3,000 megawatts, with plans to construct small nuclear power plants. These plants are designed to produce high energy output while minimizing environmental impact compared to conventional power facilities.
In November 2025, Rwanda’s Minister of Infrastructure Dr. Gasore Jimmy informed the Senate that the first feasibility study had been completed, approved, and site selection was underway. A second impact assessment is currently ongoing.
“The goal is that between 2030 and 2032 we will have our first nuclear power plant. We have chosen small nuclear plants because they require less land, reduce accident risks, and are suitable for our country, which has limited space,” Minister Gasore explained.
Rwanda is also engaging with other international partners, including the United States and several European countries, to advance its nuclear energy program, signaling a strategic push toward sustainable and high-capacity electricity generation.

title: Rwanda Urges UN to Act Against Rising Hate Speech
excerpt: New York, February 19, 2026 – Rwanda has called on the United Nations to take urgent action against the growing spread of hate speech, warning that inaction amounts to complicity. Speaking at the UN Special Committee on Peacekeeping Operations on February 18, 2026, Col. Deo Mutab
title_en: Rwanda Urges UN to Act Against Rising Hate Speech
excerpt_en: New York, February 19, 2026 – Rwanda has called on the United Nations to take urgent action against the growing spread of hate speech, warning that inaction amounts to complicity. Speaking at the UN Special Committee on Peacekeeping Operations on February 18, 2026, Col. Deo Mutab
body_en:
New York, February 19, 2026 – Rwanda has called on the United Nations to take urgent action against the growing spread of hate speech, warning that inaction amounts to complicity.
Speaking at the UN Special Committee on Peacekeeping Operations on February 18, 2026, Col. Deo Mutabazi, Military Adviser at the Rwandan Embassy to the UN, described hate speech as a deliberate, government-led project that often precedes mass atrocities and genocide.
“Hate speech is a government project, and it precedes mass atrocities, crimes of genocide and stems from a genocide ideology that has been planted in a well-planned manner,” Col. Mutabazi said.
Hate Speech as a Precursor to Genocide
Col. Mutabazi reminded UN member states that hate speech was a key factor leading to the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi, where acts of dehumanization were used to justify mass killings. He emphasized that such rhetoric should not be mistaken for freedom of expression, and silence in the face of it can be seen as support or complicity.
“I would like to emphasize that hate speech should not be confused with freedom of speech, and the UN’s continued silence on these increasing crimes is seen as supporting and complicity in the violation of the rights of a group of people and the deprivation of their identity,” he said.
Current Situation in the DRC
Col. Mutabazi’s warning comes amid escalating hate speech targeting Kinyarwanda-speaking Congolese, particularly the Tutsi ethnic group, reportedly spread by elements within the DRC government.
Politicians and former military officials have made inflammatory statements, including MP Justin Bitakwira, who referred to the Tutsi as “the worst creature that ever lived,” and former military spokesman Gen. Maj. Sylvain Ekenge, who claimed on national television that Tutsi women cannot have children with spouses from other ethnic groups.
These statements coincide with airstrikes and drone attacks in areas predominantly inhabited by Tutsi-Congolese, including Minembwe Commune in South Kivu Province.
Call to Action
Rwanda reiterated its commitment to combating hate speech and called on UN member states to protect fundamental rights and the right to life, urging the international community to act before the situation escalates further.
“Rwanda is committed to combating hate speech and calls on member states to not tolerate those who deny others their fundamental right to life,” Col. Mutabazi said.
The appeal highlights the urgent need for international intervention as rising hate speech continues to fuel violence and ethnic targeting in the eastern DRC.

title: Rwandans in Europe to Gather for Dialogue on Unity and Solidarity
excerpt: Paris, February 19, 2026 – The Rwandan Ministry of National Unity and Civic Engagement (MINUC) has announced a dialogue aimed at strengthening unity and solidarity among Rwandans living in Europe. The event is scheduled for February 21, 2026, in Paris, France. The dialogue will b
title_en: Rwandans in Europe to Gather for Dialogue on Unity and Solidarity
excerpt_en: Paris, February 19, 2026 – The Rwandan Ministry of National Unity and Civic Engagement (MINUC) has announced a dialogue aimed at strengthening unity and solidarity among Rwandans living in Europe. The event is scheduled for February 21, 2026, in Paris, France. The dialogue will b
body_en:
Paris, February 19, 2026 – The Rwandan Ministry of National Unity and Civic Engagement (MINUC) has announced a dialogue aimed at strengthening unity and solidarity among Rwandans living in Europe. The event is scheduled for February 21, 2026, in Paris, France.
The dialogue will bring together Rwandans, particularly young people born abroad or who left the country during the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi, as well as representatives of Rwandan communities from across Europe.
Purpose and Focus
The event is designed as a platform for sharing ideas and experiences, providing participants with a better understanding of Rwanda’s journey toward national unity and the challenges that have arisen over the years. It will also highlight opportunities for those living abroad to engage with and contribute to their homeland.
Topics of discussion will include:
The role of youth in preserving Rwandan culture
How various community forums maintain unity
The community’s role in sharing accurate information and promoting social cohesion
Event Format
The dialogue will feature a combination of speeches, expert panels, testimonies, and interactive discussions, aiming to strengthen connections among Rwandans abroad.
Officials expect the event to:
Foster a stronger sense of community and shared values
Promote a culture of support, respect, and non-violence
Encourage young Rwandans abroad to uphold Rwandan traditions and cultural identity
The initiative reflects Rwanda’s ongoing commitment to unity, reconciliation, and the active participation of its diaspora in national development.

title: Rwandan Embassy in UK Launches ‘Nshuti’ Online Platform for Citizens Abroad
excerpt: London, February 19, 2026 – The Rwandan Embassy in the United Kingdom has launched a new digital platform called ‘Nshuti’, designed to provide 24/7 services and support to Rwandans living abroad and others seeking information about Rwanda. The platform, part of the Embassy’s broa
title_en: Rwandan Embassy in UK Launches ‘Nshuti’ Online Platform for Citizens Abroad
excerpt_en: London, February 19, 2026 – The Rwandan Embassy in the United Kingdom has launched a new digital platform called ‘Nshuti’, designed to provide 24/7 services and support to Rwandans living abroad and others seeking information about Rwanda. The platform, part of the Embassy’s broa
body_en:
London, February 19, 2026 – The Rwandan Embassy in the United Kingdom has launched a new digital platform called ‘Nshuti’, designed to provide 24/7 services and support to Rwandans living abroad and others seeking information about Rwanda.
The platform, part of the Embassy’s broader digital innovation strategy, allows users to access a wide range of services instantly via WhatsApp or the embassy’s website.
Key Features of Nshuti
Immediate assistance and answers to frequently asked questions
Support for passport applications, identity card registration, document authentication, and appointment requests
Guidance for accessing other consular services
Information on embassy activities, national holidays, and Rwandan organizations abroad
Contact details for Rwandan representatives in countries served by the embassy
Users can interact with the platform by sending a WhatsApp message to +44 7427 941212 or starting a chat via the embassy website.
Ambassador Emphasizes Innovation
In a statement, Rwanda’s Ambassador to the UK, Johnston Busingye, highlighted that Nshuti reflects the embassy’s commitment to leveraging technology to simplify processes, reduce waiting times, and provide reliable, up-to-date information to Rwandans abroad.
The launch of Nshuti marks a significant step toward modernizing consular services, improving accessibility, and enhancing engagement with Rwanda’s diaspora community in the UK and beyond.

title: Goma Connected to High-Speed Fiber Network via Kenya, Uganda and Rwanda
excerpt: GOMA, February 10, 2026 — The city of Goma in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo has begun receiving high-speed fiber optic internet through a new regional network linking Kenya, Uganda, and Rwanda, according to the Paratus Group. The company announced the launch of a 2
title_en: Goma Connected to High-Speed Fiber Network via Kenya, Uganda and Rwanda
excerpt_en: GOMA, February 10, 2026 — The city of Goma in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo has begun receiving high-speed fiber optic internet through a new regional network linking Kenya, Uganda, and Rwanda, according to the Paratus Group. The company announced the launch of a 2
body_en:
GOMA, February 10, 2026 — The city of Goma in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo has begun receiving high-speed fiber optic internet through a new regional network linking Kenya, Uganda, and Rwanda, according to the Paratus Group.
The company announced the launch of a 2,000-kilometer fiber optic corridor stretching from the Port of Mombasa in Kenya to Goma, passing through major hubs in East Africa. The infrastructure includes data centers in Kigali, Kampala, and Nairobi, aimed at strengthening regional connectivity.
Paratus said the network will provide high-speed and secure internet access to traditional internet service providers as well as corporate clients operating across multiple locations.
The company’s Chief Commercial Officer, Martin Cox, stated that the new connection is expected to boost the digital economy in the region.
“The establishment of a secure network from the port to Goma is an opportunity for internet service providers and businesses to access the international market. It will enhance stability and efficiency and open up new business opportunities in Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda and the DRC,” he said.
Cox added that the project strengthens Paratus Group’s presence within the East African Community (EAC) and complements another major fiber optic backbone connecting eastern and western Africa, stretching from Maputo in Mozambique to Swakopmund in Namibia.
Paratus operates across EAC member states through subsidiaries including Paratus Rwanda, Paratus Kenya, and Paratus Uganda, and maintains partnerships with regional telecommunications firms such as Roke Telecom Uganda and MoveOn Telecoms Kenya.
In addition to terrestrial fiber infrastructure, the company also delivers connectivity solutions via satellite internet, expanding broadband access to remote and underserved areas.
The new link is expected to significantly improve connectivity in eastern Congo, a region that has long faced infrastructure and security challenges affecting digital access.

title: Belgium Declines to Share Colonial-Era DRC Mineral Records with U.S. Firm
excerpt: February 16, 2026 — The Belgian government has refused to grant U.S.-based mining company KoBold Metals access to colonial-era archives detailing mineral deposits in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Belgium, which ruled the DRC from 1885 to 1960, gathered extensive geologica
title_en: Belgium Declines to Share Colonial-Era DRC Mineral Records with U.S. Firm
excerpt_en: February 16, 2026 — The Belgian government has refused to grant U.S.-based mining company KoBold Metals access to colonial-era archives detailing mineral deposits in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Belgium, which ruled the DRC from 1885 to 1960, gathered extensive geologica
body_en:
February 16, 2026 — The Belgian government has refused to grant U.S.-based mining company KoBold Metals access to colonial-era archives detailing mineral deposits in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Belgium, which ruled the DRC from 1885 to 1960, gathered extensive geological data during the colonial period to support mining operations. Much of that information has since been preserved in museums and state archives.
Two years ago, following an agreement with the European Union, Belgian authorities began compiling these historical records into a digital platform intended to be accessible, under certain conditions, to researchers, private entities, and the Congolese government.
Agreements with Kinshasa
In July 2025, KoBold’s DRC representative, Benjamin Katabuka, and Congo’s Minister of Mineral Resources, Kizito Pakabomba, signed an agreement authorizing a company delegation to travel to Brussels to request copies of the documents.
A month later, in August 2025, the DRC government and KoBold concluded another agreement granting the company rights to explore and mine lithium, cobalt, and copper across a 1,600-square-kilometer area.
Seeking to better pinpoint mineral locations, KoBold requested participation in Belgium’s digitization process. However, Belgian authorities rejected the request.
Legal and Policy Constraints
Officials at the Royal Museum for Central Africa in Tervuren — which houses many Africa-related archives — stated that private companies cannot be granted privileged access to the records.
“We cannot give all the ancient documents to a private sector,” said museum director Bart Ouvry.
Belgium’s Minister for Science Policy, Vanessa Matz, argued that granting exclusive access to a foreign company would contravene Belgian and European legal frameworks.
Strategic Minerals at Stake
KoBold Metals is pursuing mining operations in the DRC under broader U.S.–Congo cooperation initiatives. The targeted minerals — particularly lithium, cobalt, and copper — are critical components in the production of electric vehicle batteries and advanced electronic devices, placing the dispute within the wider geopolitical competition over strategic resources.
Social and Health

title: First Epilepsy Surgery Successfully Performed in Rwanda
excerpt: KIGALI, February 9, 2026 — Doctors at Kigali University Teaching Hospital have carried out Rwanda’s first epilepsy surgery, marking a major step forward in specialized neurological care in the country. The procedure began on Monday with the operation of a 39-year-old patient who
title_en: First Epilepsy Surgery Successfully Performed in Rwanda
excerpt_en: KIGALI, February 9, 2026 — Doctors at Kigali University Teaching Hospital have carried out Rwanda’s first epilepsy surgery, marking a major step forward in specialized neurological care in the country. The procedure began on Monday with the operation of a 39-year-old patient who
body_en:
KIGALI, February 9, 2026 — Doctors at Kigali University Teaching Hospital have carried out Rwanda’s first epilepsy surgery, marking a major step forward in specialized neurological care in the country.
The procedure began on Monday with the operation of a 39-year-old patient who had suffered from epilepsy for 15 years despite continuous medication. The intervention was performed by a local medical team working alongside visiting foreign specialists.
Until now, patients requiring this type of treatment were often referred abroad — mainly to India — due to the lack of local surgical capacity.
The operation was led by neurosurgeon Sylvie Musoni Inyange, who explained that scans showed the seizures originated from a specific area on the left side of the brain.
“We removed a small part of the brain where the MRI indicated the source of the epilepsy,” she said.
Doctors reported the patient had been collapsing about twice a week and had become physically weakened. Following surgery, the treatment offers roughly an 85% chance of recovery, with the possibility of reducing or completely stopping medication.
Medical specialists describe epilepsy as abnormal brain activity causing symptoms such as loss of consciousness, repeated falls, involuntary movements, temporary paralysis and sometimes loss of bladder control.
Health professionals say the new capability represents a significant breakthrough for Rwanda’s healthcare system, as some patients could not be effectively treated with medication alone and traveling abroad was financially and logistically difficult.
Family members welcomed the development, saying the condition had affected the patient since childhood and required frequent travel to Kigali for care.
The hospital indicated that expanding specialized surgery locally will reduce medical evacuation costs and improve long-term treatment access for patients across the country.

title_en: Prime Minister Nsengiyumva Meets CEPI Chief to Strengthen Pandemic Preparedness
excerpt_en: ADDIS ABABA, February 14, 2026 — Justin Nsengiyumva held high-level talks with Richard Hatchett, Director-General of the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI), focusing on strengthening pandemic preparedness and response capacity in Rwanda and across Africa. The
body_en:
ADDIS ABABA, February 14, 2026 — Justin Nsengiyumva held high-level talks with Richard Hatchett, Director-General of the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI), focusing on strengthening pandemic preparedness and response capacity in Rwanda and across Africa.
The meeting took place on the sidelines of the Ordinary Session of the Assembly of Heads of State and Government of the African Union, held on February 14–15, 2026, in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.
Discussions centered on deepening cooperation to enhance the continent’s ability to anticipate and respond to health emergencies, including boosting medical research, strengthening legislative frameworks, and accelerating the production and equitable distribution of vaccines in the event of unexpected outbreaks.
Rwanda has positioned itself as an emerging hub for biomedical innovation and vaccine manufacturing, aligning with broader continental efforts to reduce reliance on external supply chains during global health crises.
On February 15, Prime Minister Nsengiyumva is also expected to participate in a session of the African Union High-Level Ad Hoc Committee on South Sudan, a body established to promote political dialogue, unity, and lasting peace in South Sudan.
The Prime Minister’s engagements in Addis Ababa reflect Rwanda’s continued commitment to continental solidarity, health security, and regional stability.

title: Rwanda Signs Firm to Develop Nationwide Housing Plans Aligned with 2050 Vision
excerpt: Kigali, February 17, 2026 – The Rwandan Ministry of Infrastructure has signed a long-term contract with Dar Al-Handasah Consultants (Shair & Partners) S.A.L to develop and prepare housing plans across the country, in line with the Kigali City Master Plan and other regional land-u
title_en: Rwanda Signs Firm to Develop Nationwide Housing Plans Aligned with 2050 Vision
excerpt_en: Kigali, February 17, 2026 – The Rwandan Ministry of Infrastructure has signed a long-term contract with Dar Al-Handasah Consultants (Shair & Partners) S.A.L to develop and prepare housing plans across the country, in line with the Kigali City Master Plan and other regional land-u
body_en:
Kigali, February 17, 2026 – The Rwandan Ministry of Infrastructure has signed a long-term contract with Dar Al-Handasah Consultants (Shair & Partners) S.A.L to develop and prepare housing plans across the country, in line with the Kigali City Master Plan and other regional land-use plans extending to 2050.
The agreement aims to produce comprehensive urban designs covering housing sites, infrastructure, government service centers, stormwater drainage, roads, commercial areas, recreational facilities, and other public amenities. Without an approved physical plan, developers cannot obtain building permits.
The contract, signed at the national level, allows government agencies and regional authorities to collaborate directly with Dar Al-Handasah Consultants (Shair & Partners) S.A.L without issuing separate tenders, reducing both time and cost in preparing urban studies.
Dar Al-Handasah Consultants (Shair & Partners) S.A.L is an international firm specializing in construction, civil engineering, and environmental project management. In Rwanda, it has contributed to major infrastructure projects, including the new Kigali International Airport in Bugesera and updates to the national transport master plan.
Streamlining Urban Development
Jack Ngarambe, Director General of Urban Development and Housing at MININFRA, explained that using ministerial-level contracts will accelerate the procurement process for housing projects and ensure high-quality designs tailored to each area.
“The biggest challenge has been integrating accurate information into the design and aligning it with the local planning system,” Ngarambe said. He emphasized that housing projects must reflect a comprehensive vision, including stormwater and sewage systems, domestic water supply, transportation links, and public infrastructure such as schools, sports facilities, and conservation areas.
The initiative is intended to allow different institutions to carry out high-level urban planning whenever capacity is available. Ngarambe noted that the main obstacle has been the high cost of preparing housing designs, which limits the simultaneous development of multiple projects, especially when incorporating community preferences.
The national land-use master plan remains aligned with Rwanda’s 2050 vision, and authorities believe that contracting a single firm for nationwide planning will improve quality, even if it may raise service costs and affect opportunities for local surveyors and planners.
This move reflects Rwanda’s commitment to systematic, long-term urban development, balancing population growth, infrastructure needs, and sustainable land use across the country.

title: 46% of People with Disabilities in Rwanda Lack Access to Bank Loans
excerpt: Kigali, February 20, 2026 – A recent consultative meeting organized by Access to Finance Rwanda (AFR) revealed that 46% of people with disabilities in Rwanda do not have access to bank and financial services, highlighting persistent barriers to financial inclusion. The meeting, h
title_en: 46% of People with Disabilities in Rwanda Lack Access to Bank Loans
excerpt_en: Kigali, February 20, 2026 – A recent consultative meeting organized by Access to Finance Rwanda (AFR) revealed that 46% of people with disabilities in Rwanda do not have access to bank and financial services, highlighting persistent barriers to financial inclusion. The meeting, h
body_en:
Kigali, February 20, 2026 – A recent consultative meeting organized by Access to Finance Rwanda (AFR) revealed that 46% of people with disabilities in Rwanda do not have access to bank and financial services, highlighting persistent barriers to financial inclusion.
The meeting, held on February 19, 2026, brought together government agencies, financial institutions, development partners, non-profits, civil society, and disability associations to discuss findings from an AFR survey on financial accessibility for people with disabilities.
Key Findings
The proportion of people with disabilities unable to apply for bank loans rose from 36.3% in 2020 to 46.6% in 2024.
Overall access to financial services has decreased, despite 92.9% of those surveyed reportedly being reached by some services.
Key obstacles include lack of collateral, limited trust from banks, and insufficient staff trained to communicate with people with hearing or visual impairments.
Voices from the Community
Ingabire Mukamurenzi Francine, a blind entrepreneur, shared her experience:
“Banks generally do not trust people with disabilities, and there are no special programs for us like there are for youth or women. I had to approach Urwego Finance to secure a loan to expand my business, and they have supported me ever since.”
Dr. Mukarwego Beth Nasiforo, head of the Rwandan Network of People with Disabilities (NUDOR), emphasized that perceptions and lack of awareness among financial institution employees hinder access for people with disabilities.
Emmanuel Ndayisaba, Executive Secretary of the National Council for Persons with Disabilities (NCPD), highlighted the broader impact:

Kigali, February 20, 2026 – A recent consultative meeting organized by Access to Finance Rwanda (AFR) revealed that 46% of people with disabilities in Rwanda do not have access to bank and financial services, highlighting persistent barriers to financial inclusion.
The meeting, held on February 19, 2026, brought together government agencies, financial institutions, development partners, non-profits, civil society, and disability associations to discuss findings from an AFR survey on financial accessibility for people with disabilities.
Key Findings
The proportion of people with disabilities unable to apply for bank loans rose from 36.3% in 2020 to 46.6% in 2024.
Overall access to financial services has decreased, despite 92.9% of those surveyed reportedly being reached by some services.
Key obstacles include lack of collateral, limited trust from banks, and insufficient staff trained to communicate with people with hearing or visual impairments.
Voices from the Community
Ingabire Mukamurenzi Francine, a blind entrepreneur, shared her experience:
“Banks generally do not trust people with disabilities, and there are no special programs for us like there are for youth or women. I had to approach Urwego Finance to secure a loan to expand my business, and they have supported me ever since.”

Emmanuel Ndayisaba, Executive Secretary of the National Council for Persons with Disabilities (NCPD), highlighted the broader impact:
“When people with disabilities are given access to financial services, they contribute to business development, employment creation, innovation, and national development.”
The meeting underscored the urgent need for targeted financial programs and inclusive policies to ensure that people with disabilities can fully participate in Rwanda’s economic growth.

title: Rwanda Seeks Extradition of “Prince Kid” From the United States
excerpt: KIGALI, February 9, 2026 — Rwanda’s prosecution authorities say they are working with the United States to extradite Ishimwe Dieudonne, widely known as Prince Kid, to face justice after his conviction in a high-profile sexual assault case linked to the Miss Rwanda beauty pageant.
title_en: Rwanda Seeks Extradition of “Prince Kid” From the United States
excerpt_en: KIGALI, February 9, 2026 — Rwanda’s prosecution authorities say they are working with the United States to extradite Ishimwe Dieudonne, widely known as Prince Kid, to face justice after his conviction in a high-profile sexual assault case linked to the Miss Rwanda beauty pageant.
body_en:
KIGALI, February 9, 2026 — Rwanda’s prosecution authorities say they are working with the United States to extradite Ishimwe Dieudonne, widely known as Prince Kid, to face justice after his conviction in a high-profile sexual assault case linked to the Miss Rwanda beauty pageant.
Prosecutor General Angelique Habyarimana announced that Kigali issued an international arrest warrant after confirming he was in the United States and submitted the necessary legal documents for his return.
Prince Kid rose to national prominence as the organizer of the pageant through his company Rwanda Inspiration Backup. In October 2023, Rwanda’s High Court sentenced him to five years in prison for sexual assault and solicitation of sexual favors involving contestants.
Court proceedings were held in his absence, as he had already fled the country.
On March 3, 2025, the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested him in Fort Worth, Texas. Authorities stated he had entered the United States legally but later violated immigration rules and now faces separate legal proceedings there.
Speaking during Anti-Corruption Week activities, Habyarimana said Rwanda formally transmitted the conviction record and requested extradition.
“The verdict is final and without further appeal. We submitted arrest warrants and his full profile to the relevant authorities and cooperation is ongoing,” she said.
She added that extradition could occur once U.S. proceedings conclude.
The charges against Prince Kid stem from allegations that he abused participants in the pageant over several years, prompting a major public scandal in Rwanda’s entertainment industry.
Rwandan officials say they will continue legal cooperation with U.S. authorities until the case is resolved and the sentence enforced.

title: “We Are Beginning to See Changes” — Minister Bizimana Highlights Impact of Reintegration Training for Genocide Convicts
excerpt: NYAMASHEKE, February 13, 2026 — Jean-Damascene Bizimana, Rwanda’s Minister of National Unity and Civic Engagement, says authorities are observing positive behavioral changes among prisoners convicted for their role in the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi who underwent pre-release
title_en: “We Are Beginning to See Changes” — Minister Bizimana Highlights Impact of Reintegration Training for Genocide Convicts
excerpt_en: NYAMASHEKE, February 13, 2026 — Jean-Damascene Bizimana, Rwanda’s Minister of National Unity and Civic Engagement, says authorities are observing positive behavioral changes among prisoners convicted for their role in the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi who underwent pre-release
body_en:
NYAMASHEKE, February 13, 2026 — Jean-Damascene Bizimana, Rwanda’s Minister of National Unity and Civic Engagement, says authorities are observing positive behavioral changes among prisoners convicted for their role in the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi who underwent pre-release civic training.
He made the remarks in Nyamasheke District during the closing ceremony of the sixth phase of a reintegration program targeting inmates with less than six months remaining on their sentences for genocide-related crimes.
According to Minister Bizimana, individuals who received the training demonstrated improved reintegration outcomes upon returning to their families, while some who did not participate showed signs of social isolation, divisionism, and adherence to genocide ideology.
Call for Accountability and Unity
Addressing the participants, Minister Bizimana emphasized the importance of acknowledging responsibility for past crimes committed during the Genocide against the Tutsi. He reminded them that their convictions stemmed from choices made under a regime that promoted persecution and mass violence against the Tutsi population.
“The message we give them,” he said, “is to accept that they have completed their sentence, that they have received the lessons provided, and that they are rejoining the Rwandan community to build ‘Ndi Umunyarwanda’ — a Rwanda free from ethnic division, discrimination, and genocide ideology.”
He stressed the importance of telling the truth about history, underscoring that national unity depends on confronting the realities of the past.
Low Recidivism Among Trained Inmates
Minister Bizimana noted that cases of reoffending remain rare among those who completed the training. In contrast, some individuals who did not undergo the program have reportedly exhibited signs associated with genocide ideology.
Also speaking at the ceremony, the Commissioner General of the National Service for the Prevention of Crime, CG Evariste Murenzi, urged participants to avoid reoffending and to become responsible members of society.
Families Participate in Reintegration
For the first time, families attended the closing ceremony, which included the awarding of completion certificates. Officials say the move aims to strengthen family reconciliation and community reintegration.
Iyakaremye Pacifique, a resident of Nyamasheke whose father was sentenced to 19 years for genocide crimes, shared the emotional toll of growing up with that legacy. He said he once felt ashamed but now hopes for positive change and responsible parental guidance moving forward.
Twagiramungu Jean Baptiste, who completed a 30-year sentence, thanked the government for establishing the program and pledged to uphold national unity. “The days we have spent here will not be in vain,” he said, adding that the rebuilding of unity under the ‘Ndi Umunyarwanda’ framework must be preserved.
Another participant, Musabyimana Jean, said he intends to promote what he described as historical truth and defend Rwanda’s leadership, including Paul Kagame.
654 Participants in Sixth Cohort
The sixth phase of the program brought together 654 inmates, including 165 individuals who were released immediately after completing both their sentences and the training.
Rwandan authorities say the initiative forms part of broader efforts to reinforce national reconciliation, civic responsibility, and long-term social cohesion more than three decades after the 1994 genocide.

title: Banyamulenge Organizations Sue Burundi at EAC Court Over Alleged Atrocities in South Kivu
excerpt: ARUSHA, February 14, 2026 — Two organizations representing Banyamulenge communities in South Kivu Province have filed a lawsuit against the Burundi before the East African Court of Justice (EACJ), accusing Burundian forces of committing war crimes and crimes against humanity in e
title_en: Banyamulenge Organizations Sue Burundi at EAC Court Over Alleged Atrocities in South Kivu
excerpt_en: ARUSHA, February 14, 2026 — Two organizations representing Banyamulenge communities in South Kivu Province have filed a lawsuit against the Burundi before the East African Court of Justice (EACJ), accusing Burundian forces of committing war crimes and crimes against humanity in e
body_en:
ARUSHA, February 14, 2026 — Two organizations representing Banyamulenge communities in South Kivu Province have filed a lawsuit against the Burundi before the East African Court of Justice (EACJ), accusing Burundian forces of committing war crimes and crimes against humanity in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo.
The groups — ADEPAE and Mutualité Shikama — allege that since October 2025, Burundian troops deployed in South Kivu have blocked all major roads linking the Banyamulenge population in Minembwe commune to surrounding areas, including access to markets, health centers, and humanitarian assistance.
According to the complaint, the road closures were allegedly intended to isolate the community and expose it to life-threatening conditions.
Allegations of Abuses
One of the lawyers representing the plaintiffs, Me Innocent Nteziryayo, stated that beyond restricting movement, Burundian troops are accused of abductions, torture, destruction of property, and undermining the community’s livelihoods.
On November 11, 2025, the spokesperson of the Burundian army, Brig. Gen. Gaspard Baratuza, confirmed that troops had sealed off roads leading to Minembwe. He said the measure was aimed at protecting the town of Uvira, which Burundian forces continue to control.
Baratuza argued that securing Uvira required broader territorial control, adding that individuals suspected of collaborating with armed groups would not be allowed to cross.
Humanitarian Concerns Raised
On November 24, 2025, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reported that humanitarian access to Minembwe and surrounding border areas had become impossible due to the road closures.
OCHA warned that the restrictions had contributed to a sharp rise in deaths, particularly among children under five, and had triggered significant price increases for basic goods as supply routes remained cut off.
Burundi Rejects Allegations
While Brig. Gen. Baratuza acknowledged the closure of the roads, Burundi’s Minister of Justice reportedly told the regional court that the government does not accept responsibility for the full range of alleged crimes in South Kivu.
The complainants maintain that they possess documented evidence and witness testimonies to substantiate their claims and say they are prepared to present their case before the EACJ in pursuit of justice.
The case is expected to test regional legal mechanisms at a time of heightened tensions in eastern DRC, where multiple armed actors and foreign forces remain active.

title: Rwandan Woman Testifies to Being Raped by FARDC Soldiers in DRC
excerpt: RUBAVU, February 12, 2026 — Nyiramana, 36, is one of 161 Rwandans recently repatriated from the Democratic Republic of Congo, who has spoken out about being raped twice by FARDC soldiers because she is Rwandan. Nyiramana returned on February 10 from the Masisi area, describing ye
title_en: Rwandan Woman Testifies to Being Raped by FARDC Soldiers in DRC
excerpt_en: RUBAVU, February 12, 2026 — Nyiramana, 36, is one of 161 Rwandans recently repatriated from the Democratic Republic of Congo, who has spoken out about being raped twice by FARDC soldiers because she is Rwandan. Nyiramana returned on February 10 from the Masisi area, describing ye
body_en:
RUBAVU, February 12, 2026 — Nyiramana, 36, is one of 161 Rwandans recently repatriated from the Democratic Republic of Congo, who has spoken out about being raped twice by FARDC soldiers because she is Rwandan. Nyiramana returned on February 10 from the Masisi area, describing years of persecution since her parents fled in 1994 from the former Rutongo commune.
She recounted her first assault in 2020:
“My parents separated me, we became Gatoyi, later I married Kamuronzi. Life was not good because when they found out that you are a refugee, they treat you like someone who came to rob them… I went to collect firewood in the forest and met men dressed badly like shepherds but wearing FARDC military uniforms. They raped me and I kept quiet to protect my home.”
Nyiramana explained that the soldiers targeted her for being Rwandan and even tried to coerce her into marriage:
“I saw that they could even kill me, so I decided to agree by force. I kept quiet because I had a husband and did not want the family to fall apart. Now I can speak because he has returned.”
Her second assault occurred in 2024 after leaving the market:
“I came back late and found them waiting near my house, not in military uniforms. They said we asked you many times and you refused, so we decided to rape you. It was dark, and I decided to accept. I kept quiet to avoid being hurt, but now I am happy to have returned to Rwanda.”
Nyiramana returned to Rwanda with her seven children, the survivors of her late husband, and expressed her readiness to work and rebuild her life. She also encouraged others still in the Congolese jungle to return, highlighting the opportunities and development available in Rwanda.
The repatriation was based on resolutions adopted at a meeting between Rwanda, the DRC, and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees in Addis Ababa on July 24, 2025.
Mulindwa Prosper, Mayor of Rubavu District, addressed the returning Rwandans, saying:
“There is no reason for any Rwandan to still be called a refugee. You were misled in the forest. You are now witnessing the truth… You are in the hands of a country that loves you, and you must call those left behind to return home.”

Nyiramana returned on February 10 from the Masisi area, describing years of persecution since her parents fled in 1994 from the former Rutongo commune.
She recounted her first assault in 2020:
“My parents separated me, we became Gatoyi, later I married Kamuronzi. Life was not good because when they found out that you are a refugee, they treat you like someone who came to rob them… I went to collect firewood in the forest and met men dressed badly like shepherds but wearing FARDC military uniforms. The repatriation was based on resolutions adopted at a meeting between Rwanda, the DRC, and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees in Addis Ababa on July 24, 2025.

“There is no reason for any Rwandan to still be called a refugee. You were misled in the forest. You are now witnessing the truth… You are in the hands of a country that loves you, and you must call those left behind to return home.”

title: Family of Former President Edgar Lungu Denies Poisoning Claims

title_en: Family of Former President Edgar Lungu Denies Poisoning Claims
excerpt_en: Lusaka, February 18, 2026 – Lawyers representing the family of former Zambian President Edgar Lungu have dismissed claims that his death was the result of poisoning. Edgar Lungu passed away in South Africa in June 2025, but his body has yet to be buried. South African authorities
body_en:
Lusaka, February 18, 2026 – Lawyers representing the family of former Zambian President Edgar Lungu have dismissed claims that his death was the result of poisoning.
Edgar Lungu passed away in South Africa in June 2025, but his body has yet to be buried. South African authorities have stated that his remains are still needed for an autopsy.
According to legal representatives, including Neo Mashele, the allegations of poisoning are unfounded. Lungu’s family is reportedly cooperating with security agencies to investigate the circumstances of his death.
His body remains in a South African morgue while legal disputes continue over the location of his burial. The African Union described the situation as “a serious matter that cannot be discussed publicly.”
Lungu’s family has expressed a desire for him to be buried in South Africa, in part to ensure that President Hakainde Hichilema would not miss the funeral.
This ongoing situation continues to attract attention in Zambia and across the region, as legal and diplomatic considerations surrounding the former president’s burial remain unresolved.

title: Witness Accuses Muhayimana’s Lawyer of Attempting to Mislead Judges
excerpt: Paris, February 18, 2026 – A witness convicted of involvement in the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi testified before the Appeals Chamber of the Paris People’s Court, alleging that Claude Muhayimana’s representative attempted to influence him to give misleading testimony to prote
title_en: Witness Accuses Muhayimana’s Lawyer of Attempting to Mislead Judges
excerpt_en: Paris, February 18, 2026 – A witness convicted of involvement in the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi testified before the Appeals Chamber of the Paris People’s Court, alleging that Claude Muhayimana’s representative attempted to influence him to give misleading testimony to prote
body_en:
Paris, February 18, 2026 – A witness convicted of involvement in the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi testified before the Appeals Chamber of the Paris People’s Court, alleging that Claude Muhayimana’s representative attempted to influence him to give misleading testimony to protect Muhayimana from conviction.
The witness, a former teacher who admitted participating in Interahamwe patrols and attacks against Tutsi, explained that he was sentenced by a Gacaca Court in 2006 or 2007 to 12 years in prison for his role in the killings.
Witness Details Muhayimana’s Involvement
The witness recounted seeing Muhayimana drive a blue Daihatsu transporting Interahamwe members, armed men, and gendarmes to the Bisesero hills in Kibuye Prefecture, where Tutsi civilians were attacked.
“From April, when the genocide began, until July, the vehicles were used across all communes of Kibuye Prefecture, hunting Tutsi in the mountains,” the witness told the court.
During the investigation, Muhayimana, through his lawyer, contacted the witness asking about life in Rwanda and the progress of the case. The witness provided information but later said the lawyer instructed him to give less incriminating testimony, claiming foreign judges would not distinguish truth from falsehood.
“He asked me to give a less incriminating testimony so that the judges would not be able to understand the truth,” the witness said, describing how he provided a confusing statement on October 16, 2013.
Document Controversy
The witness also testified about a search of Muhayimana’s home, where authorities found a document listing witnesses, their families, and staff of the French Office for the Fight against Crimes against Humanity (OCLCH). The witness denied providing the names of French personnel and said Muhayimana had lied about his access to this information.
When Muhayimana claimed that the Rwandan government had trained witnesses to lie against him, the witness rejected the allegation, stating that his testimony was truthful and based on firsthand knowledge of the events.
Conviction and Appeal
In December 2021, the Paris International Criminal Court convicted Muhayimana of genocide and crimes against humanity, sentencing him to 14 years in prison. The court determined that he had led the Interahamwe militia responsible for killing Tutsi, a charge Muhayimana has consistently denied.
The appeal hearing, which began on February 3, 2026, is focused on Muhayimana’s efforts to overturn his convictions and secure release. The testimony presented by the witness highlights allegations of witness tampering and attempts to mislead the court, central to the appeal proceedings.

title: DRC and AS Monaco Face French Court Over Alleged Embezzlement
excerpt: Paris, February 19, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and French football club AS Monaco have been taken to court in France over allegations of embezzlement and corruption related to a cooperation agreement signed in June 2025. The agreement aimed to promote the DRC i
title_en: DRC and AS Monaco Face French Court Over Alleged Embezzlement
excerpt_en: Paris, February 19, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and French football club AS Monaco have been taken to court in France over allegations of embezzlement and corruption related to a cooperation agreement signed in June 2025. The agreement aimed to promote the DRC i
body_en:
Paris, February 19, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and French football club AS Monaco have been taken to court in France over allegations of embezzlement and corruption related to a cooperation agreement signed in June 2025.
The agreement aimed to promote the DRC internationally, develop football talent, and advance the sport in the country. However, concerns quickly arose among Congolese citizens over the legality and transparency of the deal.
Legal Action Initiated by Congolese Residents in France
Two Congolese residents in France, requesting anonymity, filed a lawsuit with the help of lawyer Hervé Diakiese, prompting the French Public Prosecutor’s Office (PNF) to review the case. The complaint alleges that the agreement involved corruption, misuse of public funds, and bribery.
The complaint specifically cites irregularities linked to the DRC Minister of Sports and Recreation, Didier Budimbu, in relation to the payment of €4.8 million (≈8.3 billion Rwandan francs) over three years.
Although the complaint was initially addressed to the Attorney General of Monaco, Stéphane Thibault, the PNF noted that it lacks jurisdiction to prosecute certain international crimes, prompting Diakiese to consider escalating the case to other courts.
AS Monaco and Other Clubs Respond
AS Monaco has stated that it will defend itself vigorously, emphasizing that due diligence and legal compliance were followed before signing the contract. Other European clubs involved in similar agreements with the DRC, including FC Barcelona and AC Milan, are also part of the investigation.
The case has drawn attention to the governance and oversight of public funds in international sports partnerships, raising questions about accountability in agreements involving government and private entities.
The proceedings are ongoing, and the next steps could set a precedent for cross-border accountability in sports and public funding.

title: Gen Mbala to Testify in Trial of Lt Gen Yav Over Alleged Rwanda Collaboration
excerpt: Kinshasa, February 21, 2026 – Gen Célestin Mbala Munsense, former Commander-in-Chief of the FARDC (2018–2022), is set to testify in the trial of Lt Gen Philemon Yav Irung, who faces accusations of collaborating with the Rwandan government while commanding the 3rd Military Region.
title_en: Gen Mbala to Testify in Trial of Lt Gen Yav Over Alleged Rwanda Collaboration
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, February 21, 2026 – Gen Célestin Mbala Munsense, former Commander-in-Chief of the FARDC (2018–2022), is set to testify in the trial of Lt Gen Philemon Yav Irung, who faces accusations of collaborating with the Rwandan government while commanding the 3rd Military Region.
body_en:
Kinshasa, February 21, 2026 – Gen Célestin Mbala Munsense, former Commander-in-Chief of the FARDC (2018–2022), is set to testify in the trial of Lt Gen Philemon Yav Irung, who faces accusations of collaborating with the Rwandan government while commanding the 3rd Military Region.
The Military High Court heard that Lt Gen Yav allegedly communicated with Rwandan officials to undermine FARDC troops. The general denied the accusations, stating that he had never engaged with Rwandan authorities, and that he only received a phone message from an unknown sender alleging FARDC collusion with the FDLR.
The prosecution acknowledged the difficulty in accessing the phone messages. The court subsequently requested the National Cyber Security Agency (CNC) to investigate any potential communications.
Lt Gen Yav requested that Gen Mbala be summoned to clarify the issues and testify on his conduct while serving in the national army. The judges approved this request, scheduling Gen Mbala to appear at the next hearing on March 2, 2026.
Additionally, Lt Gen Yav asked for the re-summoning of other military officials, including Lt Gen Constant Ndima (former Governor of North Kivu Province), Brig Gen Mwehu Lumbu (former FARDC Spokesperson), and Gen Maj Sylvain Ekenge (former National Army Spokesperson), to provide further testimony. Previous statements from these officials had been contradictory regarding messages allegedly received from Rwandan authorities.
Lt Gen Yav was arrested in September 2022 following the capture of Rutshuru territory, including Bunagana, by the M23 armed group. His trial began in January 2026, amid growing scrutiny of alleged military collusion with neighboring countries.

title: Rwanda Police Wins Bronze at Dubai Counter-Terrorism Competition
excerpt: DUBAI, February 11, 2026 — The Rwanda National Police SWAT Team I secured a bronze medal at the UAE SWAT Challenge, an international counter-terrorism competition held in Dubai, bringing together 109 police and military teams from around the world. The event tested tactical skill
title_en: Rwanda Police Wins Bronze at Dubai Counter-Terrorism Competition
excerpt_en: DUBAI, February 11, 2026 — The Rwanda National Police SWAT Team I secured a bronze medal at the UAE SWAT Challenge, an international counter-terrorism competition held in Dubai, bringing together 109 police and military teams from around the world. The event tested tactical skill
body_en:
DUBAI, February 11, 2026 — The Rwanda National Police SWAT Team I secured a bronze medal at the UAE SWAT Challenge, an international counter-terrorism competition held in Dubai, bringing together 109 police and military teams from around the world.
The event tested tactical skills across five categories, including obstacle courses requiring strength, teamwork, wall-climbing, and navigation through complex terrain. During the final on February 11, teams from 48 countries tackled 19 demanding obstacles in coordinated five-member formations.
RNP SWAT Team I completed the course in 3 minutes 40 seconds, earning third place in the final challenge and ultimately finishing sixth overall with 484 points.
Rwanda fielded two additional teams:
RNP SWAT Team II placed 14th in the final and 29th overall with 386 points.
The Rwanda Defence Force SOF Team finished 15th in the final and 37th overall with 361 points.
In the overall standings, Kazakhstan Police Team C won the gold medal with 536 points, followed by Kazakhstan A with silver, while China Police Team C also placed on the podium.
The competition showcased Rwanda’s growing capacity in specialized counter-terrorism operations and its expanding presence in international security exercises.

title: MONUSCO Chief Urges Reopening of Goma Airport
excerpt: GOMA, February 12, 2026 — Vivian van de Perre, Acting Head of the United Nations Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, visited Goma for the first time in over a year to call for the reopening of Goma airport. She arrived by helicopter on the morning of February 12, mar
title_en: MONUSCO Chief Urges Reopening of Goma Airport
excerpt_en: GOMA, February 12, 2026 — Vivian van de Perre, Acting Head of the United Nations Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, visited Goma for the first time in over a year to call for the reopening of Goma airport. She arrived by helicopter on the morning of February 12, mar
body_en:
GOMA, February 12, 2026 — Vivian van de Perre, Acting Head of the United Nations Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, visited Goma for the first time in over a year to call for the reopening of Goma airport. She arrived by helicopter on the morning of February 12, marking the first use of the airport since the AFC/M23 coalition took control of the city in late January 2025.
The visit aimed to coordinate with stakeholders, including members of the Great Lakes region community, in preparation for ceasefire monitoring operations in Uvira Territory. The UN Security Council has mandated MONUSCO to monitor the ceasefire between the DRC Government and AFC/M23, in collaboration with the regional EJVM.
Van de Perre said:
“I would like to remind you that more than a year ago, on January 26, 2025, I was on the last plane to land at Goma airport. Today, I was on the first helicopter to land here. I hope this marks the gradual reopening of the airport for the benefit of the population.”
On February 10, 2026, Jean-Pierre Lacroix, UN Under-Secretary-General for Peacekeeping Operations, announced that MONUSCO would use Goma airport for ceasefire monitoring operations, adding that surveillance drones would first be deployed from the airport to assess the security situation in Uvira before troops arrive.

KIGALI, January 12, 2026 — Rwanda National Police has rotated 160 police officers from the RWAFPU3-7 team, who returned to Kigali after a one-year deployment in South Sudan under the United Nations Peacekeeping Mission in South Sudan. The outgoing team, led by SSP Devotha Nyinawumuntu, was based in Juba and immediately replaced by the RWAFPU3-8 team, commanded by SSP Donatha Iribagiza.
The police officers’ duties in South Sudan included restoring peace and security, protecting civilians, safeguarding United Nations personnel and operations, and promoting the well-being of local populations.
At Kigali International Airport, the incoming team was received by CP Yahaya Kamunuga, Commissioner of Police, who thanked the returning officers for their dedication and professionalism. He said:
“You have returned to Rwanda to continue serving your country. You may find that things have changed. But your integrity and dedication must remain the same.”
On behalf of the outgoing team, SP Vincent Mwine Rubimbura, deputy leader of RWAFPU3-7, highlighted key community engagement initiatives carried out during their deployment. In addition to protecting civilians and UN personnel, the team worked to strengthen relations with the local population through activities such as community service, school renovations, distribution of mosquito nets and school supplies, and providing medical care and clean water to vulnerable families.
SP Rubimbura noted that these efforts have enhanced trust and cooperation between the police and local communities, reinforcing the overall peacekeeping mission.

title: AFC/M23 Accuses Burundi’s President of Role in Attacks on Banyamulenge
excerpt: GOMA, February 13, 2026 — Corneille Nangaa, leader of the opposition coalition AFC/M23, has condemned Évariste Ndayishimiye over what he described as the continued targeting of Banyamulenge civilians in South Kivu province, eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. In a statement
title_en: AFC/M23 Accuses Burundi’s President of Role in Attacks on Banyamulenge
excerpt_en: GOMA, February 13, 2026 — Corneille Nangaa, leader of the opposition coalition AFC/M23, has condemned Évariste Ndayishimiye over what he described as the continued targeting of Banyamulenge civilians in South Kivu province, eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. In a statement
body_en:
GOMA, February 13, 2026 — Corneille Nangaa, leader of the opposition coalition AFC/M23, has condemned Évariste Ndayishimiye over what he described as the continued targeting of Banyamulenge civilians in South Kivu province, eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo.
In a statement released February 13, Nangaa denounced ongoing military operations allegedly carried out by Congolese government forces alongside Burundian troops against both civilians and AFC/M23 positions.
He also criticized the Burundian leader, who is expected to assume a senior continental role, accusing him of contributing to crimes against the Banyamulenge population.
Call for International Intervention
Nangaa urged the international community and African institutions to act quickly to prevent wider ethnic tensions in the Great Lakes region and to assist affected civilians.
Background to Burundian Deployment
The Burundi deployed troops to the DRC under a bilateral agreement aimed at fighting armed groups operating in the region, including RED Tabara, FNL-Nzabampema, and FOREBU.
According to the AFC/M23, the mission later expanded, with Burundian forces allegedly participating in operations in Banyamulenge-inhabited areas across the territories of Uvira, Fizi, and Mwenga, particularly in Minembwe commune.
Road Closures and Humanitarian Impact
For several months, roads linking Minembwe residents to markets and health facilities have reportedly been closed. Burundian army spokesperson Brig. Gen. Gaspard Baratuza previously stated the restrictions were imposed because some residents were suspected of collaborating with hostile armed groups.
The accusations come amid escalating tensions in eastern DRC, where multiple armed actors and foreign forces remain engaged in a complex conflict with significant humanitarian consequences.

body_en:
WALIKALE, February 13, 2026 — Armed groups of the Wazalendo Alliance, backed by the Democratic Republic of Congo government, are clashing for control of the Batakirwa area in the Bafuna group, Walikale Territory.
The confrontation pits the NDC-R, led by Guidon Shimiray Mwissa, against Uhuru-RDC, commanded by Mashite Kashira. On February 11, 2026, Mashite deployed fighters to three mineral-rich villages in Batakirwa, warning the NDC-R that any attempt to enter would trigger fighting.
Local leader Kibaki reported that Uhuru-RDC fighters have been intimidating civilians, accusing them of supporting the NDC-R, forcing him to flee to Walikale town. He told Actualite newspaper:
“The population is in great danger. The armed groups are terrorizing civilians, associating them with their enemies.”
Kibaki urged the DRC government to take action against these armed groups, which are already engaged against the AFC/M23 alliance, warning that failure to intervene could escalate the conflict.

title_en: AFC/M23 and MONUSCO Hold Ceasefire Implementation Talks in Goma
excerpt_en: GOMA, February 13, 2026 — Leaders of the AFC/M23 coalition and the MONUSCO met in Goma on February 13 to discuss the implementation of the ceasefire. On the AFC/M23 side, the meeting included Corneille Nangaa, the coalition’s General Director, and military officials such as Col N
body_en:
GOMA, February 13, 2026 — Leaders of the AFC/M23 coalition and the MONUSCO met in Goma on February 13 to discuss the implementation of the ceasefire.
On the AFC/M23 side, the meeting included Corneille Nangaa, the coalition’s General Director, and military officials such as Col Nzenze Imani John, head of intelligence. Representing MONUSCO was its Acting Director, Vivian van de Perre, who arrived in Goma on February 12. Her plane landed at the local airport, the first operational flight since late January 2025, when AFC/M23 took control of the facility.
Upon arrival, van de Perre stated that discussions would focus on partners responsible for monitoring the ceasefire, and proposed that the airport be reopened in phases to facilitate the mission.
The UN Security Council has mandated MONUSCO to monitor the ceasefire in areas from which AFC/M23 withdrew in Uvira Territory, an agreement reached with the DRC government during the Doha peace talks in Qatar.
Jean-Pierre Lacroix, UN Under-Secretary-General for Peacekeeping Operations, said on February 12 that MONUSCO troop deployment will be phased, beginning with reconnaissance aircraft to ensure security. The reconnaissance flights to Uvira will depart from Goma airport, suggesting that AFC/M23 may need to facilitate access for the mission.

title: Rwanda Police Receives Firefighting Vehicle Worth Over Rwf 1 Billion
excerpt: KIGALI, February 13, 2026 — The Rwanda Police has received a firefighting vehicle valued at over Rwf 1 billion from RPC Ltd, a joint venture behind the Rusumo Hydropower Plant. The handover took place at the Rwanda Police headquarters in Kigali, attended by RPC Ltd management, po
title_en: Rwanda Police Receives Firefighting Vehicle Worth Over Rwf 1 Billion
excerpt_en: KIGALI, February 13, 2026 — The Rwanda Police has received a firefighting vehicle valued at over Rwf 1 billion from RPC Ltd, a joint venture behind the Rusumo Hydropower Plant. The handover took place at the Rwanda Police headquarters in Kigali, attended by RPC Ltd management, po
body_en:
KIGALI, February 13, 2026 — The Rwanda Police has received a firefighting vehicle valued at over Rwf 1 billion from RPC Ltd, a joint venture behind the Rusumo Hydropower Plant. The handover took place at the Rwanda Police headquarters in Kigali, attended by RPC Ltd management, police officials, and other stakeholders.
The donated vehicle, a MAN Model TGS 31,400 truck, comes equipped with modern firefighting equipment suitable for residential and high-rise buildings, valued at €759,100 (over Rwf 1.3 billion).
Eric Mpayimana, CEO of RPC Ltd, said the donation is part of broader community initiatives beyond electricity provision:
“We chose to donate firefighting vehicles to the countries where our hydroelectric power plant—Burundi, Tanzania, and now Rwanda—operates, to provide assistance in the event of a fire and to build local firefighting capacity.”
Mpayimana noted that RPC’s activities also include building markets, youth centers, and health centers, contributing to regional unity across the three countries.
ACP Rutikanga Boniface, spokesperson for the Rwanda Police, described the vehicle as a major boost for protecting people and property, noting that current resources are insufficient for fire emergencies:
“Infrastructure is growing, cities and businesses are expanding, and rescue operations are increasingly necessary. This vehicle will enhance our capacity, and we plan to deploy similar vehicles in other areas.”
Boniface added that the donation also reflects awareness of fire risks linked to electricity usage:
“RPC provides electricity to heat homes, but misuse can cause fires. Receiving this vehicle shows consideration for the safety of those using electricity in the event of an accident.”
Rangira Bruno, Mayor of Kirehe District, where the power plant is located, described the donation as an important step in community care initiatives that RPC Ltd is implementing in partnership with the government.

title: AFC/M23 Denounces DRC Ceasefire Announcement as Misleading
excerpt: GOMA, February 13, 2026 — Corneille Nangaa, Chairman of the AFC/M23 Alliance, has denounced the announcement by the Office of the President of the Democratic Republic of Congo that President Félix Tshisekedi has “accepted” a ceasefire requested by the Angola government, calling i
title_en: AFC/M23 Denounces DRC Ceasefire Announcement as Misleading
excerpt_en: GOMA, February 13, 2026 — Corneille Nangaa, Chairman of the AFC/M23 Alliance, has denounced the announcement by the Office of the President of the Democratic Republic of Congo that President Félix Tshisekedi has “accepted” a ceasefire requested by the Angola government, calling i
body_en:
GOMA, February 13, 2026 — Corneille Nangaa, Chairman of the AFC/M23 Alliance, has denounced the announcement by the Office of the President of the Democratic Republic of Congo that President Félix Tshisekedi has “accepted” a ceasefire requested by the Angola government, calling it misleading as attacks by the DRC army continue.
On February 13, the Presidential Office stated that acceptance of the ceasefire would include no expansion of military bases, no reinforcement of forces in conflict areas, and halting foreign support. Nangaa, however, emphasized that AFC/M23 remains committed to the Doha peace process, which is grounded in respecting political obligations and achieving peace through dialogue.
Nangaa accused the DRC government of attempting to launch new negotiations while existing talks are still ongoing, warning that this approach risks undermining earlier progress and delaying solutions to urgent issues. He said:
“Contrary to the declaration of acceptance of the ceasefire, the Kinshasa government has demonstrated through verified actions the continuation of the war. Attacks in densely populated areas, the use of mercenaries, and indiscriminate shootings affecting civilians demonstrate its choice to continue the war, violating its commitments.”
He added that the Kinshasa government’s declaration is propaganda aimed at misleading the population and the international community, while concealing the continuation of its military operations.
Meanwhile, Benjamin Mbonimpa, Permanent Secretary of AFC/M23, told journalists in Goma that DRC government forces launched further attacks on the morning of February 13.

excerpt_en: KAMPALA/KIGALI, February 14, 2026 — The Chief of Staff of the Uganda People's Defence Force, Gen. Muhoozi Kainerugaba, has once again declared his affection for Rwanda and its people, confirming that he will soon travel to Kigali for an official visit. In a message posted in the
body_en:
KAMPALA/KIGALI, February 14, 2026 — The Chief of Staff of the Uganda People's Defence Force, Gen. Muhoozi Kainerugaba, has once again declared his affection for Rwanda and its people, confirming that he will soon travel to Kigali for an official visit.
In a message posted in the early hours of February 14, 2026, on the social media platform X, Gen. Muhoozi expressed his deep admiration in Kinyarwanda, stating: “I love Rwanda and Rwandans very much. I will soon be visiting my Uncle Afande Paul.”
The Ugandan army chief was referring to Paul Kagame, whom he has frequently described as both a mentor and a family figure. Gen. Muhoozi has often publicly referred to President Kagame as his “uncle” and a role model.
Earlier this week, Gen. Muhoozi first announced his intention to visit Rwanda and revealed plans to meet President Kagame during his stay in Kigali. His latest statement reinforces growing expectations of renewed high-level engagement between the two neighboring nations.
On several occasions, Gen. Muhoozi has emphasized the historic ties and long-standing friendship between Uganda and Rwanda, highlighting their shared political and military history as the foundation of bilateral cooperation.
The anticipated visit comes amid continued efforts to strengthen diplomatic and security relations between the two countries, which share deep historical, cultural, and strategic links in the Great Lakes region.
