title: Former Women Combatants Urged to Safeguard National Unity
excerpt: KIGALI, February 14, 2026 — Former female fighters from different armed groups in Rwanda have been called upon to strengthen reconciliation and preserve national unity during the General Assembly of the Ndabaga Community, held on Saturday. The community brings together women who
title_en: Former Women Combatants Urged to Safeguard National Unity
excerpt_en: KIGALI, February 14, 2026 — Former female fighters from different armed groups in Rwanda have been called upon to strengthen reconciliation and preserve national unity during the General Assembly of the Ndabaga Community, held on Saturday. The community brings together women who
body_en:
KIGALI, February 14, 2026 — Former female fighters from different armed groups in Rwanda have been called upon to strengthen reconciliation and preserve national unity during the General Assembly of the Ndabaga Community, held on Saturday.
The community brings together women who participated in the country’s liberation struggle — including members of the Rwandan Patriotic Front (RPF-Inkotanyi), former soldiers of the RPF, and ex-combatants from the defeated Forces armées rwandaises (EX-FAR). Participants were encouraged to share experiences and develop initiatives that promote cohesion and social progress.
The name Ndabaga refers to a historical symbol meaning “a girl who became a warrior and went to battle,” reflecting the members’ military service while recognizing their identity as women.
Promoting Skills and Self-Reliance
The head of the community, retired Lieutenant Mbabazi Diane, urged members to prioritize mutual learning and development projects aimed at improving their living conditions.
“Our objective as Ndabaga members is to strengthen our skills so we can improve our daily lives,” she said.
To support economic empowerment, the community is partnering with Airtel Rwanda Communications on a 30-million-Rwandan-franc tailoring project. The initiative will begin with a pilot group before expanding nationwide if successful.
According to organizers, tailoring was chosen because many members had limited access to formal education, and the project offers a practical pathway toward financial independence.
Unity and Reconciliation Emphasized
Leaders reminded participants that, despite ongoing development efforts, they must remain ambassadors of reconciliation and unity and guide others away from division.
“As people who contributed to the country’s liberation, we must lead by example and demonstrate the value of Rwandan unity,” Mbabazi added.
Personal Transformation
Member Umurungi Musiime Florence, who joined the Ndabaga Community in 2004, said participation helped her regain confidence and rebuild her life.
She explained that being surrounded by peers encouraged her to return to school, continue contributing to society, and pursue personal development.
The Ndabaga Community says its activities aim not only at economic empowerment but also at reinforcing long-term social cohesion and post-conflict healing in Rwanda.

title: UN Plans Aerial Reconnaissance Before Peacekeepers Deploy to Uvira
excerpt: KINSHASA, February 11, 2026 — The United Nations will deploy reconnaissance aircraft before sending peacekeepers to Uvira Territory in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, as part of a phased plan to monitor a ceasefire in the volatile border region. The announcement was made by
title_en: UN Plans Aerial Reconnaissance Before Peacekeepers Deploy to Uvira
excerpt_en: KINSHASA, February 11, 2026 — The United Nations will deploy reconnaissance aircraft before sending peacekeepers to Uvira Territory in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, as part of a phased plan to monitor a ceasefire in the volatile border region. The announcement was made by
body_en:
KINSHASA, February 11, 2026 — The United Nations will deploy reconnaissance aircraft before sending peacekeepers to Uvira Territory in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, as part of a phased plan to monitor a ceasefire in the volatile border region.
The announcement was made by Jean-Pierre Lacroix, Under-Secretary-General for Peacekeeping Operations, during his working visit to the country on February 10.
Mandate Backed by the UN Security Council
The move follows the January 2026 withdrawal of fighters from the city of Uvira by the M23/AFC coalition, which requested the deployment of neutral forces to prevent reprisals against civilians by government troops.
The United Nations Security Council has mandated the UN mission MONUSCO to oversee implementation of the peace arrangement — a framework accepted by both the Congolese authorities and the armed group.
Phased Deployment for Security Reasons
According to Lacroix, troops will not be deployed immediately. Instead, reconnaissance aircraft will first collect intelligence on security conditions before personnel are transported.
He warned that sending helicopters without prior assessment could expose peacekeepers to attack.
“We will not send helicopters to take our personnel into areas where there are dangers or where drones are present,” Lacroix said, adding that security guarantees are required before the mission proceeds.
He also called on international partners and the parties involved to ensure the safety of peacekeepers as they begin monitoring the ceasefire.
Flights from Goma
The reconnaissance aircraft are expected to operate from Goma International Airport, currently under the control of the AFC/M23 coalition. The airport has remained closed since January 2025, and UN officials did not confirm whether reopening is imminent.
Gradual Arrival of Peacekeepers
Once aerial surveillance is completed, a small contingent of troops will be deployed to Uvira, with numbers increasing progressively depending on developments on the ground.
The UN says the cautious rollout is intended to prevent incidents and build confidence while stabilizing the region after months of fighting.

title: Foreign Contractors Linked to Erik Prince Involved in Uvira Offensive
excerpt: KINSHASA, February 11, 2026 — Foreign military contractors linked to American security entrepreneur Erik Prince were deployed in South Kivu to assist the national army of the Democratic Republic of the Congo during operations aimed at retaking the city of Uvira from the M23/AFC c
title_en: Foreign Contractors Linked to Erik Prince Involved in Uvira Offensive
excerpt_en: KINSHASA, February 11, 2026 — Foreign military contractors linked to American security entrepreneur Erik Prince were deployed in South Kivu to assist the national army of the Democratic Republic of the Congo during operations aimed at retaking the city of Uvira from the M23/AFC c
body_en:
KINSHASA, February 11, 2026 — Foreign military contractors linked to American security entrepreneur Erik Prince were deployed in South Kivu to assist the national army of the Democratic Republic of the Congo during operations aimed at retaking the city of Uvira from the M23/AFC coalition, according to security and diplomatic sources.
The coalition seized Uvira on December 9, 2025, and advanced toward Makobola, prompting heavy counter-offensives by Congolese special forces units known as the Hiboux and Cheetah groups. The army used heavy weapons, warplanes, and drones as it attempted to push the fighters toward the South Kivu highlands. Foreign contractors were reportedly brought in to operate drone systems, while Israeli advisers focused on training two Congolese special units to conduct operations both day and night.
On January 17–18, the AFC/M23 withdrew its fighters from the city following a request from the United States, which had pledged the resumption of peace talks in Doha, Qatar, if the movement complied. Government troops and allied Wazalendo fighters re-entered Uvira on the morning of January 18 without major clashes, ending the immediate need for the contractors on the battlefield.
After the withdrawal, the personnel returned to their initial assignment — helping authorities monitor mining revenues and combat embezzlement linked to the country’s mineral sector. One official indicated they had been mobilized to support the recapture of the city using all available resources before resuming financial oversight activities.
Security officials say the government may again rely on the contractors if hostilities resume, suggesting their role could shift back to combat support depending on developments on the ground.

title: South Africa Announces Withdrawal of Troops from Eastern DRC
excerpt: KINSHASA, February 10, 2026 — South Africa has announced it will withdraw its troops from the UN peacekeeping mission in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, citing the need to consolidate its military forces, financial constraints, limited operational results, and a renewed
title_en: South Africa Announces Withdrawal of Troops from Eastern DRC
excerpt_en: KINSHASA, February 10, 2026 — South Africa has announced it will withdraw its troops from the UN peacekeeping mission in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, citing the need to consolidate its military forces, financial constraints, limited operational results, and a renewed
body_en:
KINSHASA, February 10, 2026 — South Africa has announced it will withdraw its troops from the UN peacekeeping mission in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, citing the need to consolidate its military forces, financial constraints, limited operational results, and a renewed focus on domestic priorities.
The troops are part of MONUSCO, where South Africa has maintained between 700 and 800 soldiers, primarily within the Force Intervention Brigade (FIB) — a unit authorized to conduct offensive operations against armed groups.
The withdrawal, announced on February 8, is scheduled to take place gradually from the first quarter of 2026 through December 2026.
While Pretoria has officially framed the move as strategic and financial, critics argue the decision is also influenced by broader political and economic interests, particularly in mineral-rich regions of eastern Congo. South African deployments have largely been concentrated in North Kivu, South Kivu, and Ituri — provinces known for deposits of gold, coltan, gas, and copper.
Since the 1990s, South Africa has publicly justified its military engagements across the continent as part of efforts to restore peace and stability. However, observers note that troop deployments have frequently coincided with areas of significant natural resource wealth.
Allegations have also surfaced over the years accusing certain elements within the mission of involvement in illegal mining activities, including the illicit trade of gold and coltan. Some reports claim that military-controlled airports were used in mineral transactions and that intermediaries facilitated cross-border trading networks. These allegations have not led to formal international prosecutions but continue to fuel debate over the economic dimensions of foreign troop deployments.
South Africa remains one of the largest contributors to MONUSCO’s Force Intervention Brigade, whose mandate differs from traditional UN peacekeeping contingents by allowing proactive combat operations against armed groups.
The gradual withdrawal marks a significant shift in regional security dynamics, raising questions about the future balance of forces in eastern Congo and the long-term sustainability of international stabilization efforts.

The returnees — 110 children, 38 women, and 13 men — crossed into Rwanda through the La Corniche main border post, linking Rubavu with Goma. Upon arrival, they were received by local officials, including Prosper Mulindwa, Mayor of Rubavu District.
They were immediately transported to a temporary transit center in Kijote, located in Nyabihu District, where they are undergoing short-term orientation and reintegration support.
The repatriation followed resolutions adopted during a tripartite meeting between Rwanda, the DRC and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees held in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, on July 24, 2025. Prior to their return, the group had been residing in a temporary camp in Goma, after fleeing various parts of eastern Congo.
Addressing the returnees, Mayor Mulindwa questioned why any Rwandan should still consider themselves refugees, stating that Rwanda has abolished refugee status for its nationals and guarantees protection to its citizens.
“A person who remains outside the country believing they are a refugee is pursuing a losing cause,” he said, urging them to contact others still in eastern Congo and encourage them to return home.
Among the returnees was Nyiransabimana Ancille, 64, who said she fled Rwanda in 1994 and has now returned to the former Mutura Commune, expressing readiness to contribute to local development.
Authorities stated that once the returnees receive their national identity documents, they will receive government reintegration assistance. Adults over 18 are to be granted $188, minors under 18 will receive $113, and each individual will also be provided with essential food supplies valued at 45,000 Rwandan Francs to support their transition back into normal life.
The repatriation marks another step in ongoing regional efforts to facilitate voluntary returns and reduce the presence of Rwandan nationals in armed groups operating in eastern Congo.

excerpt_en: NORTH KIVU, February 10, 2026 — The M23/AFC coalition, fighting the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, says it has added 7,532 newly trained commandos to its ranks following training at the Tshanzu military center in Rutshuru Territory. According to the movement,
body_en:
NORTH KIVU, February 10, 2026 — The M23/AFC coalition, fighting the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, says it has added 7,532 newly trained commandos to its ranks following training at the Tshanzu military center in Rutshuru Territory.
According to the movement, the recruits underwent extended preparation that included combat techniques and physical engagement training before being deployed toward active front lines in eastern Congo.
The group’s military chief, Sultani Makenga, told the new fighters that their predecessors had already defeated coalition forces aligned with the Congolese army, which he claimed included foreign troops, militias and mercenaries.
“Your comrades have done a great job on the battlefields. The enemy brought different groups — Burundians, the FDLR and foreign mercenaries — but they were defeated,” he said during the address.
Makenga urged the recruits to join ongoing operations and support fighters already engaged in combat, instructing them to maintain discipline and avoid harming civilians or engaging in looting and drug use.
“Your comrades are waiting for you. Help liberate people who have suffered for a long time and do not become a burden to them,” he added.
The announcement comes as the movement continues expanding its manpower after capturing Goma in January 2025. The group says that in September and October 2025, more than 16,000 fighters graduated from the Tshanzu and Rumangabo camps and were subsequently deployed to combat zones.
The reported increase in fighters highlights ongoing militarization in eastern Congo despite repeated diplomatic initiatives aimed at restoring stability in the region.

title: AFC/M23 Announces Plans to Establish Telecommunications Company in Areas Under Its Control
excerpt: Masisi, February 16, 2026 – The AFC/M23 coalition, which is fighting against the Democratic Republic of the Congo, has announced plans to establish a telecommunications company in territories under its control, aiming to restore communication services for local populations. The a
title_en: AFC/M23 Announces Plans to Establish Telecommunications Company in Areas Under Its Control
excerpt_en: Masisi, February 16, 2026 – The AFC/M23 coalition, which is fighting against the Democratic Republic of the Congo, has announced plans to establish a telecommunications company in territories under its control, aiming to restore communication services for local populations. The a
body_en:
Masisi, February 16, 2026 – The AFC/M23 coalition, which is fighting against the Democratic Republic of the Congo, has announced plans to establish a telecommunications company in territories under its control, aiming to restore communication services for local populations.
The announcement was made on February 16, 2026, by Bahati Musanga Erasto, the governor of North Kivu appointed by AFC/M23, during a visit to residents in the town center of Kitshanga, located in Masisi Territory.
Accusations Against Kinshasa
Addressing residents, Governor Bahati accused the government in Kinshasa of deliberately cutting off telecommunications services in areas controlled by the coalition, alleging that the move was intended to harm civilians living in those areas.
“It is the government of Kinshasa that interrupted the transmission. We are working to ensure this does not happen again. We are putting in place an alternative transmission system; no one will interrupt it because it belongs to us. It will reach Goma, Kitshanga, and everywhere else. No one will touch these antennas again to disrupt transmission,” he said.
According to Bahati, only the cities of Goma and Bukavu currently have functioning telephone services, while other localities remain cut off, depriving residents of access to modern communication technologies.
Uncertainty Surrounding the Project
Details about how the project will be implemented remain unclear. It is not known whether AFC/M23 intends to launch a new telecommunications company or partner with an existing operator already active in other countries.
The announcement comes amid ongoing tensions in eastern DRC, where control over territory, public services, and strategic infrastructure remains a central issue in the broader conflict.

title: France Clarifies Presence of Troops in Kisangani Amid Social Media Speculation
excerpt: Kinshasa, February 17, 2026 – The Embassy of France in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has dismissed claims of a secret deployment of French troops to Kisangani, stating that the personnel seen in the city are part of an ongoing military training partnership with the Democra
title_en: France Clarifies Presence of Troops in Kisangani Amid Social Media Speculation
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, February 17, 2026 – The Embassy of France in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has dismissed claims of a secret deployment of French troops to Kisangani, stating that the personnel seen in the city are part of an ongoing military training partnership with the Democra
body_en:
Kinshasa, February 17, 2026 – The Embassy of France in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has dismissed claims of a secret deployment of French troops to Kisangani, stating that the personnel seen in the city are part of an ongoing military training partnership with the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Since February 15, 2026, photos circulating on social media have shown French soldiers in Kisangani, the capital of Tshopo Province, prompting speculation about their possible involvement in the conflict in eastern DRC.
The speculation intensified amid claims that Kisangani serves as a strategic hub where the Congolese army and foreign mercenaries prepare air operations targeting positions held by the AFC/M23 armed group, including areas where civilians are present.
“No Secret Deployment”
In response, the French Embassy emphasized that the presence of French troops is part of a transparent and longstanding bilateral military cooperation program.
“The French military is training the DRC military, at the request of the DRC government. It is a normal bilateral partnership; it will not be sent there in secret. We have openly announced the activities based on our partnership,” the Embassy said in a statement.
According to French officials, the cooperation includes training Congolese soldiers in jungle warfare techniques. The Embassy shared images of training sessions conducted in Kisangani in 2022 as well as more recent sessions from February 2026, underscoring the continuity of the program.
The clarification comes as tensions remain high in eastern DRC, where fighting between government forces and AFC/M23 rebels continues to shape regional security dynamics.

title: Kenya Foils Al-Shabaab Attack, Seizes Weapons in Nairobi
excerpt: Nairobi, February 18, 2026 – The Kenyan military, led by soldiers from the Counter-Terrorism Service (CTS), successfully thwarted a planned attack by suspected Al-Shabaab operatives, authorities announced. The operation, carried out on February 18, 2026, followed careful monitori
title_en: Kenya Foils Al-Shabaab Attack, Seizes Weapons in Nairobi
excerpt_en: Nairobi, February 18, 2026 – The Kenyan military, led by soldiers from the Counter-Terrorism Service (CTS), successfully thwarted a planned attack by suspected Al-Shabaab operatives, authorities announced. The operation, carried out on February 18, 2026, followed careful monitori
body_en:
Nairobi, February 18, 2026 – The Kenyan military, led by soldiers from the Counter-Terrorism Service (CTS), successfully thwarted a planned attack by suspected Al-Shabaab operatives, authorities announced.
The operation, carried out on February 18, 2026, followed careful monitoring of the suspects’ movements, communication networks, and other links. Acting on intelligence reports, CTS personnel intercepted a large cache of weapons, including 600 rounds of ammunition, small and large firearms, and explosives, intended for use in various parts of Nairobi City.
“The plans of the Al-Shabaab terrorist group to kill many Kenyans have been foiled by the intelligence service,” the CTS statement said.
Planned Attacks During Ramadan
Initial investigations indicated that the group had planned attacks during the fasting month of Ramadan. Officials also revealed that the suspects had considered kidnapping foreigners as part of their operation.
Kenyan security agencies emphasized that ongoing investigations aim to uncover additional activities linked to the planned attacks.
Crackdown on Funding Networks
Over the past two weeks, intelligence services identified 13 accounts used to fund terrorist activities, involving citizens from Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania. All accounts were subsequently closed, disrupting the financial networks supporting the planned operations.
The successful intervention highlights Kenya’s continued vigilance against terrorism and its commitment to protecting civilians from potential threats.

title: DRC Military and FDLR Accused of Burning Banyamulenge Homes in South Kivu
excerpt: South Kivu, February 18, 2026 – The armed group MRDP-Twirwaneho has accused the DRC military coalition, including FARDC troops and allied FDLR forces, of burning Banyamulenge homes in several villages of South Kivu Province during recent clashes. The statement, issued on February
title_en: DRC Military and FDLR Accused of Burning Banyamulenge Homes in South Kivu
excerpt_en: South Kivu, February 18, 2026 – The armed group MRDP-Twirwaneho has accused the DRC military coalition, including FARDC troops and allied FDLR forces, of burning Banyamulenge homes in several villages of South Kivu Province during recent clashes. The statement, issued on February
body_en:
South Kivu, February 18, 2026 – The armed group MRDP-Twirwaneho has accused the DRC military coalition, including FARDC troops and allied FDLR forces, of burning Banyamulenge homes in several villages of South Kivu Province during recent clashes.
The statement, issued on February 18, 2026, was a response to claims made by acting DRC military spokesperson Lt. Col. Mak Hazukay, who had accused Twirwaneho of the destruction. Twirwaneho rejected these allegations, calling them “baseless and shameless.”
“Contrary to what the FARDC announced, soldiers of the government coalition—including the DRC army, allied groups, and foreign forces—during their operations and so-called ‘strategic response’ were the ones who burned the houses of Banyamulenge civilians in Kalingi, Gakenke, and Kalongi,” the group said.
Impact on Civilians
A local resident reported that airstrikes by government forces have targeted communities in Minembwe Commune and surrounding areas for nearly two weeks.
“This is the second week that planes have been shooting at the population. They started at Point-Zéro, then moved to Bidegu, and finally Kalongi, where houses were burned and residents fled to Ilundu. Villages were destroyed,” the resident said.
The witness condemned the attacks, questioning how government forces could claim to be fighting Twirwaneho while targeting civilian homes and infrastructure, including hospitals.
Allegations of Cover-Up
Twirwaneho further alleged that while criminal activities continue in Minembwe and border areas, the DRC government is conducting a campaign to conceal these actions, allowing destruction and attacks to remain undetected.
The accusations underscore escalating tensions in South Kivu, where civilians continue to bear the brunt of military operations in a complex and volatile security environment.

title: DRC Hands Over Rubaya Mines Controlled by AFC/M23 to US Investors
excerpt: Kinshasa, February 19, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government has handed over mines in the Rubaya area of Masisi Territory, long controlled by the AFC/M23 group, to US investors, officials confirmed. A government document listing Rubaya and other mining sites wa
title_en: DRC Hands Over Rubaya Mines Controlled by AFC/M23 to US Investors
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, February 19, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government has handed over mines in the Rubaya area of Masisi Territory, long controlled by the AFC/M23 group, to US investors, officials confirmed. A government document listing Rubaya and other mining sites wa
body_en:
Kinshasa, February 19, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government has handed over mines in the Rubaya area of Masisi Territory, long controlled by the AFC/M23 group, to US investors, officials confirmed.
A government document listing Rubaya and other mining sites was submitted to US representatives on February 5, 2026, during the inaugural meeting of the Joint Cooperation Committee in Washington. The committee was established under a cooperation agreement signed in December 2025, focusing on the mining and processing of precious metals.
The list of mines provided by the DRC was intended for review by US investors to confirm the presence of essential minerals and identify any potential obstacles to extraction.
Government Perspective
DRC Minister of Economy, Daniel Mukoko Samba, emphasized that the government remains responsible for mines, even those not under its direct control.
“The fact that the Rubaya site is not under the control of government forces today does not mean that we, the DRC government, will not hand them over to our partners,” he said.
AFC/M23 Reaction
Bertrand Bisimwa, Deputy Director for Political, Diplomatic, and Governance Affairs of AFC/M23, criticized the handover, calling it a sign of government weakness.
“Selling publicly assets that one does not own or does not control is a way of fighting and surviving,” Bisimwa said.
The Rubaya mines, under AFC/M23 control since May 2024, are highly strategic, containing up to 15% of the world’s Coltan, making them a key resource in the global minerals market.
The handover marks a significant development in the DRC-US mining partnership, even as the DRC government grapples with limited control over territories in the east.

title: Ugandan General Says DRC No Longer a Haven for Rwandan Armed Groups
excerpt: Musanze, Rwanda, February 20, 2026 – Gen. Maj. Paul Muhanguzi, Commander of the 2nd Division of the Ugandan Army, stated that the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is no longer a safe haven for armed groups targeting Rwanda’s security, despite both countries being members of the
title_en: Ugandan General Says DRC No Longer a Haven for Rwandan Armed Groups
excerpt_en: Musanze, Rwanda, February 20, 2026 – Gen. Maj. Paul Muhanguzi, Commander of the 2nd Division of the Ugandan Army, stated that the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is no longer a safe haven for armed groups targeting Rwanda’s security, despite both countries being members of the
body_en:
Musanze, Rwanda, February 20, 2026 – Gen. Maj. Paul Muhanguzi, Commander of the 2nd Division of the Ugandan Army, stated that the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is no longer a safe haven for armed groups targeting Rwanda’s security, despite both countries being members of the East African Community (EAC).
Gen. Maj. Muhanguzi led a Ugandan military delegation to Rwanda, starting at the Rwandan Demobilization and Rehabilitation Commission (RDRC) headquarters in Mutobo, Musanze District, on February 19, 2026. The mission focused on understanding programs that support the reintegration of former armed group members, including FDLR fighters, and their families from the DRC.
Commitment to Regional Security
He emphasized that the DRC’s inclusion in the EAC should mean the elimination of armed threats:
“Congo also requested to join East Africa. After joining, we should not have criminals in Congo. Rwanda would not have an enemy from Uganda, and Uganda would not have an enemy from Rwanda. However, we also want Congo not to have enemies who attack Uganda, who attack Rwanda,” Gen. Maj. Muhanguzi said.
Reintegration of Former Fighters
The General praised FDLR fighters who have returned to Rwanda, acknowledging their potential to contribute positively to the country:
“A country is not built by one person, it is built by all the people. I also congratulate President Kagame for being able to lead Rwanda, and you too, when the time comes, will know the truth and return home,” he added.
Since 2001, the RDRC has repatriated 12,602 former armed group members, though reports indicate that some, particularly from the FDLR, remain in DRC forests.
The visit highlights ongoing regional cooperation between Rwanda and Uganda to enhance security, reintegration programs, and peace-building efforts in the Great Lakes region.

title: AFC/M23 Condemns International Silence Amid Ongoing Civilian Killings in South Kivu
excerpt: South Kivu, February 20, 2026 – The AFC/M23 coalition has criticized the international community for remaining silent as DRC government forces and allied groups continue to target civilians in South Kivu Province. According to AFC/M23 spokesman Lawrence Kanyuka, forces from the D
title_en: AFC/M23 Condemns International Silence Amid Ongoing Civilian Killings in South Kivu
excerpt_en: South Kivu, February 20, 2026 – The AFC/M23 coalition has criticized the international community for remaining silent as DRC government forces and allied groups continue to target civilians in South Kivu Province. According to AFC/M23 spokesman Lawrence Kanyuka, forces from the D
body_en:
South Kivu, February 20, 2026 – The AFC/M23 coalition has criticized the international community for remaining silent as DRC government forces and allied groups continue to target civilians in South Kivu Province.
According to AFC/M23 spokesman Lawrence Kanyuka, forces from the DRC, Burundi, FDLR, Wazalendo, and foreign mercenaries have carried out killings in the communes of Minembwe, Mikenge, Karingi, and other parts of the highlands.
“These intolerable acts of cruelty against humanity are being carried out with the appalling and unjustified silence of aid workers, human rights organizations, and diplomatic institutions,” Kanyuka said.
Targeting Vulnerable Populations
He emphasized that the attacks disproportionately affect women, children, and the elderly, and are intended to inflict massive harm on the civilian population, in clear violation of international humanitarian law.
Ceasefire Violations
The coalition reiterated that the DRC government continues to violate the ceasefire agreement signed in Doha, Qatar, as well as other peace resolutions adopted in Washington, United States.
“This belligerent behavior threatens to reverse the progress made toward lasting peace and stability in the region,” Kanyuka warned.
The statement underscores the growing tensions in South Kivu and calls for urgent international attention to prevent further humanitarian crises.

title: DRC Seeks US Military Training and Intelligence Cooperation in Exchange for Minerals
excerpt: Kinshasa, February 20, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is seeking military training, equipment, and intelligence cooperation from the United States under a growing security and economic partnership. The DRC aims to exchange access to strategic mineral deposits for e
title_en: DRC Seeks US Military Training and Intelligence Cooperation in Exchange for Minerals
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, February 20, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is seeking military training, equipment, and intelligence cooperation from the United States under a growing security and economic partnership. The DRC aims to exchange access to strategic mineral deposits for e
body_en:
Kinshasa, February 20, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is seeking military training, equipment, and intelligence cooperation from the United States under a growing security and economic partnership.
The DRC aims to exchange access to strategic mineral deposits for enhanced US military support, building on a cooperation agreement signed on December 4, 2025, which allows American investors to mine and process key minerals.
Minerals Linked to Technology and Defense
On February 5, 2026, the DRC provided the US with a list of specific mineral deposits, including those essential for electric car batteries, electronics, and military equipment.
Security Cooperation Plans
Reports indicate that a classified security clause is part of the December agreement, potentially enabling the US to:
Train DRC military personnel
Provide advanced military equipment
Exchange intelligence to strengthen regional security
The initiative was outlined in a document prepared by the DRC President’s security advisor, Désiré Cashmir Eberande Kolongele, and signed by DRC Foreign Minister Thérèse Kayikwamba Wagner and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Ongoing US Engagement
In January 2026, a US military delegation led by Col. Michael Gacheru visited the DRC to discuss bilateral cooperation on peace and security, building on existing US support that includes financial aid, technical assistance, and police equipment.
The DRC government has indicated it seeks expanded military assistance, aiming to strengthen its armed forces while ensuring continued access to strategic minerals for industrial and defense applications.

title: AFC/M23 to Release 230 DRC Soldiers and Former Child Fighters
excerpt: Goma, February 20, 2026 – The AFC/M23 coalition announced plans to release 230 DRC soldiers captured in Goma last year, along with former Wazalendo fighters and child soldiers, signaling a gesture toward peace and reconciliation. The announcement was made by AFC/M23 Director-Gene
title_en: AFC/M23 to Release 230 DRC Soldiers and Former Child Fighters
excerpt_en: Goma, February 20, 2026 – The AFC/M23 coalition announced plans to release 230 DRC soldiers captured in Goma last year, along with former Wazalendo fighters and child soldiers, signaling a gesture toward peace and reconciliation. The announcement was made by AFC/M23 Director-Gene
body_en:
Goma, February 20, 2026 – The AFC/M23 coalition announced plans to release 230 DRC soldiers captured in Goma last year, along with former Wazalendo fighters and child soldiers, signaling a gesture toward peace and reconciliation.
The announcement was made by AFC/M23 Director-General Corneille Nangaa Yobeluo following talks with EU Commissioner for Conflict Resolution and Humanitarian Aid, Hadja Lahbib, who visited Goma on February 20.
Details of the Release
41 former child soldiers from FARDC and Wazalendo will be released.
About 100 women from FARDC and Wazalendo captured in Rumangabo will also be freed.
230 FARDC soldiers held at the Katindo military camp will be released as a gesture of goodwill.
Nangaa emphasized, “We are not war mongers. We are prioritizing political talks because that is what will bring peace. If the DRC government does not respect them and wants to continue the war, we will defend ourselves as we usually do.”
Background
In April 2025, 1,359 DRC soldiers and police officers who had sought refuge in camps under MONUSCO, the UN peacekeeping mission, were repatriated to Kinshasa after negotiations between the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) and AFC/M23.
The release underlines AFC/M23’s focus on dialogue and political solutions as a path to peace, while maintaining the group’s readiness to defend its positions if hostilities persist.

title: RDF and UPDF Strengthen Border Security to Boost Regional Stability
excerpt: Musanze, Rwanda, February 20, 2026 – The Rwanda Defence Forces (RDF) and Uganda People’s Defence Forces (UPDF) concluded the seventh meeting of the Heads of Defence Forces along the shared border, reaffirming their commitment to enhance border security and promote regional stabil
title_en: RDF and UPDF Strengthen Border Security to Boost Regional Stability
excerpt_en: Musanze, Rwanda, February 20, 2026 – The Rwanda Defence Forces (RDF) and Uganda People’s Defence Forces (UPDF) concluded the seventh meeting of the Heads of Defence Forces along the shared border, reaffirming their commitment to enhance border security and promote regional stabil
body_en:
Musanze, Rwanda, February 20, 2026 – The Rwanda Defence Forces (RDF) and Uganda People’s Defence Forces (UPDF) concluded the seventh meeting of the Heads of Defence Forces along the shared border, reaffirming their commitment to enhance border security and promote regional stability.
The three-day talks, held in Musanze District, reviewed progress on decisions from the sixth meeting in Kabale, Uganda (September 30 – October 2, 2025), and addressed ongoing challenges along the border.
Key Focus Areas
Strengthening border security measures
Combating illegal crossings, human trafficking, illicit trade, livestock theft, fraud, and impersonation
Coordinating import and export monitoring, including illicit liquor control
Both militaries emphasized the importance of continued dialogue, joint activities, and public participation through Civil-Military Interaction (CIMIC) programs, environmental protection initiatives, and joint exercises.
Statements from Military Leaders
Maj. Gen. Ruki Karusisi, Commander of the RDF 5th Division, praised the professionalism, trust, and constructive atmosphere, noting that the discussions strengthened the resolve of both sides to maintain peace and security along the border.
Maj. Gen. Paul Muhanguzi, Commander of the UPDF 2nd Land Division, affirmed Uganda’s commitment to implement the meeting’s decisions and to continue addressing emerging border issues. He also thanked the leadership of both countries for their guidance in enhancing bilateral military cooperation.
The meeting underscores the strong partnership between Rwanda and Uganda, highlighting continued efforts to secure borders, foster regional stability, and prevent cross-border crimes.

title_en: DRC Distributes Cash to Soldiers and Wazalendo Amid Ongoing Battles
excerpt_en: South Kivu, DRC – February 21, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government has begun distributing cash payments to its national army soldiers and Wazalendo fighters actively engaged against the AFC/M23 coalition in South Kivu province. The distribution started on 11
body_en:
South Kivu, DRC – February 21, 2026 – The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government has begun distributing cash payments to its national army soldiers and Wazalendo fighters actively engaged against the AFC/M23 coalition in South Kivu province.
The distribution started on 11 February 2026, following a visit by a Ministry of Defense team to Uvira on February 10. According to reports, each DRC soldier received $400, while Wazalendo fighters were given $200 each.
The Ministry’s team was reportedly divided into six groups to monitor payments in Uvira, the Rusizi Valley, Baraka, Fizi, Minembwe, and Makobola.
The cash distribution follows AFC/M23’s withdrawal from Uvira in January and coincides with the DRC government’s intensified efforts to reclaim lost territory. Governor Jean-Jacques Purusi Sadiki, appointed to South Kivu province, reiterated that President Félix Tshisekedi intends to retake Kamanyola, Bukavu, Goma, and Bunagana, emphasizing that the army would advance in the coming days.
Since late January, clashes have escalated across South Kivu, including Sange, Mukoko, Gakenke, Point-Zéro, Rugezi, Biziba, Kundondo, Mitamba, and Kirungwa. On 17 February, DRC and Wazalendo forces attacked AFC/M23 positions in the Mulenge and Lemera highlands, supported by Burundian troops. On 18 February, coalition forces targeted MRDP-Twirwaneho positions in Minembwe commune, while AFC/M23 positions near the Lemera football stadium were also attacked.
These operations have involved heavy weaponry, warplanes, and drones, despite ongoing regional and international diplomatic efforts to halt fighting.
Although President Tshisekedi accepted the principle of a ceasefire proposed by Angola on 13 February, attacks on AFC/M23, Twirwaneho positions, and civilian homes continued before and after the proposed date.
Political analysts suggest that Tshisekedi’s strategy—simultaneously escalating military operations while showing readiness for dialogue—is aimed at consolidating the DRC government’s leverage ahead of potential peace talks. They urge regional and international mediators to take concrete steps to curb violence rather than relying on declarations alone.
CONCLUSION
This period was marked by a complex interplay of escalating military operations and high-stakes diplomacy in the Great Lakes region. Although President Félix Tshisekedi of the DRC publicly accepted an Angola-brokered ceasefire scheduled for 18 February 2026, its effectiveness remained uncertain as military actions—including drone strikes and airstrikes—continued against AFC/M23 and Twirwaneho positions. Rwanda expressed skepticism about Kinshasa’s commitment to peace, citing the DRC’s ongoing use of heavy artillery, airstrikes, and foreign mercenaries.
Security concerns remained deep-rooted. Rwanda, supported by members of the U.S. Congress, highlighted the DRC’s alleged continued cooperation with the FDLR, a group linked to the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi. Kigali stated that its defensive measures would only be lifted once the FDLR is fully dismantled. Meanwhile, the humanitarian situation in South Kivu deteriorated, with Banyamulenge civilians targeted through drone attacks and the burning of homes, prompting condemnation and accusations of genocide from political leaders and community organizations.
Beyond the conflict, Rwanda remained active on the international stage, advancing strategic, technological, and social initiatives:
Strengthened global ties: The opening of a new Danish embassy in Kigali and continued bilateral cooperation with Barbados and Italy.
Technological and social progress: Talks with Russia on developing nuclear energy and the launch of the digital consular platform “Nshuti” to support the Rwandan diaspora.
National unity and reconciliation: Efforts to reintegrate former combatants and genocide convicts, promoting a unified Rwandan identity (“Ndi Umunyarwanda”) to counter lingering genocide ideology.
In conclusion, while Rwanda continues to advance internal development and international partnerships, the regional security landscape remains volatile, characterized by mutual distrust between Kinshasa and Kigali and highlighting the urgent need for impartial international mediation to address the root causes of the violence.
By Jeff Buleli

title: Kamikaze Drone Attack on Kisangani Airport Thwarted
excerpt: Kisangani DR Congo, February 2, 2026 — The civilian Bangboka International Airport in Kisangani, northern Democratic Republic of Congo, was targeted by kamikaze drones overnight between Saturday and Sunday, according to the Tshopo provincial government. Local authorities confirme
title_en: Kamikaze Drone Attack on Kisangani Airport Thwarted
excerpt_en: Kisangani DR Congo, February 2, 2026 — The civilian Bangboka International Airport in Kisangani, northern Democratic Republic of Congo, was targeted by kamikaze drones overnight between Saturday and Sunday, according to the Tshopo provincial government. Local authorities confirme
body_en:
Kisangani DR Congo, February 2, 2026 — The civilian Bangboka International Airport in Kisangani, northern Democratic Republic of Congo, was targeted by kamikaze drones overnight between Saturday and Sunday, according to the Tshopo provincial government.
Local authorities confirmed that eight enemy drones were intercepted and neutralized before reaching their target. The runway, which is also used by FARDC attack drones and fighter jets conducting strikes against AFC/M23 positions more than 400 kilometers away, was not damaged.
In a televised address, provincial officials stated that the drones were “equipped with unconventional munitions and submunitions” and failed to reach their objectives. No group has claimed responsibility, but authorities have accused the AFC/M23 and Rwanda of orchestrating the attack, alleging it was intended to undermine the Washington peace agreement.
The provincial government has called for calm and urged residents to resume normal activities, insisting there is “no reason to travel” at this time.

Goma DRC February 2, 2026 — The National Union of Congolese Press (UNPC) in North Kivu has been ordered to vacate its offices in Goma by RTNC provincial authorities. The building, donated by MONUSCO, will cease operations as of today.
Journalists say the move is linked to AFC/M23 control of RTNC and denounce it as pressure on press freedom. They vow to continue working despite the risks.

body_en:
Niamey, January 29, 2026 — Two Tuareg marabouts were summarily executed by Nigerien security forces following their arrest in the Niamey 2000 neighborhood. The victims, including Ahmad Ag Almouner Ag Madda, a respected elder from Tessit, Gao, were taken by military personnel in the morning and found dead by late afternoon.
No official charges were filed, and the fate of a third man arrested with them remains unknown. Their burial is scheduled for January 30 at Yantala cemetery.
Calls are growing for an independent investigation into these extrajudicial killings amid rising communal tensions.

title_en: IMF Warns Security Spending Is Derailing DRC Budget Targets

body_en:
Kinshasa, February 4, 2026 — The International Monetary Fund (IMF) says security spending is the main cause of budget deviations in the Democratic Republic of Congo, following its second program review.
The IMF reports that prolonged fighting in eastern DRC led to an increase in security expenditures of about 1.2% of GDP, forcing repeated adjustments to fiscal targets and reducing funds for social and investment programs.
Two key targets were missed: limits on emergency spending and minimum levels of social spending. While the IMF approved a higher deficit ceiling due to security pressures, it warned that continued reliance on emergency procedures threatens fiscal discipline and remains the program’s primary vulnerability.

title_en: MONUSCO Boosts Ceasefire Monitoring Support Between DRC and AFC/M23
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, February 4, 2026 — The UN Stabilization Mission in the DRC (MONUSCO) announced it has strengthened its preparedness to support the ceasefire monitoring and verification mechanism between the Congolese government and the AFC/M23, following talks facilitated in Doha by Qa
body_en:
Kinshasa, February 4, 2026 — The UN Stabilization Mission in the DRC (MONUSCO) announced it has strengthened its preparedness to support the ceasefire monitoring and verification mechanism between the Congolese government and the AFC/M23, following talks facilitated in Doha by Qatar.
MONUSCO confirmed it is authorized under UN Security Council Resolution 2808 (2025) to assist in implementing a permanent ceasefire, and will provide technical and logistical support through the ICGLR-backed mechanism (EJVM+).
The Mission is expected to deploy an initial team to Uvira in the coming days to monitor compliance, as parties reaffirmed their commitment to the Doha Peace Framework signed on November 15, 2025.

Mulolya, North Kivu, February 3, 2026 — Four civilians were killed and six motorcycles burned in an ambush by ADF rebels on the Oicha–Mulolya–Mamove road, about 10 km west of Oicha, the main town of Beni territory.
The attack occurred around 8:00 a.m., with rebels coming from west of Mamove, which was itself attacked two days earlier. This brings the death toll in the area to nine civilians in three days.
Another ambush was reported in Malibo the same day, though targeted farmers escaped to Oicha. Traffic remains suspended, and victims’ bodies were taken to the Oicha General Hospital morgue.
The FARDC Deputy Chief of Staff is currently assessing the security situation in Beni.

excerpt_en: Paris, February 25, 2026 – French President Emmanuel Macron held talks with DRC President Félix Tshisekedi at the Élysée Palace on Wednesday, focusing on the security and humanitarian situation in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo as well as strengthening bilateral cooperation
body_en:
Paris, February 25, 2026 – French President Emmanuel Macron held talks with DRC President Félix Tshisekedi at the Élysée Palace on Wednesday, focusing on the security and humanitarian situation in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo as well as strengthening bilateral cooperation between Paris and Kinshasa.
The meeting comes amid ongoing diplomatic efforts to address the conflict in North and South Kivu, where fighting between armed groups and government forces continues to fuel a severe humanitarian crisis. According to officials from both countries, the two leaders discussed regional peace initiatives and the role of international partners in supporting stability in the Great Lakes region.
Macron and Tshisekedi last met on January 23, 2026, during a working visit by the Congolese president to Paris. That meeting also focused on the humanitarian situation in eastern DRC and ways to reinforce political, economic, and security cooperation between the two countries.
France recently welcomed Tshisekedi’s agreement to support a ceasefire proposal put forward by Angola, urging all parties involved in the conflict to respect the initiative. Paris has also stressed the need to fully implement the Washington Peace Agreement of December 4, 2025, calling on regional actors to honor their commitments and contribute to the de-escalation of tensions.
During their discussions, the two presidents also addressed the Democratic Republic of Congo’s candidacy for the leadership of the International Organisation of La Francophonie (OIF). Kinshasa has expressed interest in playing a greater role within the Francophonie, with the organization expected to elect its next Secretary-General at the Francophonie Summit scheduled for November 2026 in Cambodia.
Beyond the security situation, the meeting allowed Macron and Tshisekedi to review broader areas of cooperation, reflecting the longstanding partnership between France and the Democratic Republic of Congo, particularly in diplomacy, development, and multilateral engagement.
By Jeff Buleli
